articleTitle: Thermal Design & Performance of a 300 mm Wafer Scale System
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: The thermal design and performance of the system packaging for a 300 mm wafer scale system is described. The system, which was water cooled, had a total thermal maximum design power of approximately 27 kW. The cooling system consisted of a silicon microchannel cooler, upper and lower cold plates, and (90) heat spreaders. The system packaging had a layered structure with laminates and power conversion components attached to the wafer mounted to the microchannel cooler, a lower layer consisting of pluggable vertical I/O cards and a large I/O planar board above which was an upper layer of pluggable high-voltage vertical cards and a large high-voltage planar. Additionally, eight external I/O cards, which plugged onto the I/O planar board, provided optical links to and from the system.

articleTitle: Robust Pothole Detection in Adverse Weather Conditions using Thermal Imaging and Image Processing
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Potholes on roads pose significant risks, contributing to road accidents and vehicle damage. Common strategies for detection, such as manual reporting and vibration-based sensors, have drawbacks like high setup costs and night vision limitations. This study explores the effectiveness of thermal imaging for pothole detection, utilizing a diverse dataset and applying augmentation techniques. The research exclusively employs a self-developed convolutional neural network (CNN) within deep learning. Results indicate a remarkable accuracy rate of 98%, surpassing pre-trained models. This study highlights the promising potential of thermal imaging in pothole detection, emphasizing its innovative application for improved road safety and maintenance.

articleTitle: Experimental investigation of the heat spreading performance of oscillating heat pipes for electronics cooling applications
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Oscillating heat pipes (OHPs) typically consist of a meandering or serpentine channel or tube that contains alternating liquid slugs and vapor plugs distributed along the length of the channel. Heat transport into and out of the channels results in fluid motion due to vapor bubble generation and growth (heat input) and vapor bubble shrinkage and collapse (heat removal), which, respectively, occur at the so-called evaporator and condenser sections of the OHP. OHPs are commonly used to transport heat laterally from a heat source to a heat sink. However, they can also be employed to effectively spread heat laterally within the plane of the OHP from hotspots on one side of the OHP to a heat sink on the opposite side; we refer to this configuration as a vertical heat spreading stack. The local vaporization and condensation processes inherent to OHPs allow them to mitigate unfavorable effects associated with high heat fluxes and localized hot spots where, for example, concentrated heat sources can result in large temperature spikes when relying on a purely conduction-based approach. This work focuses on evaluating the performance of OHPs in managing localized areas of high heat flux. Potential applications include electronics cooling and in-package thermal management. A vertical heat spreading test apparatus is developed to characterize the thermal performance of the aluminum OHPs with hotspots of sizes 4 mm x 4 mm and 4 mm x 10 mm and heat fluxes of up to 100 W/cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>. The effects of different working fluids and fluid fill ratios are studied. A performance map of the OHPs is presented that explores the dependence of thermal resistance on the hotspot size, location, heat flux, working fluid and fluid fill ratio.

articleTitle: Development and Performance Evaluation of Additively Printed In-Mold-Electronic Sensors
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: The field of printed electronics has seen increased research momentum over the last ten years and has begun to break into sectors like consumer electronics, healthcare, and transportation. In-mold electronics (IME), a procedure that involves the integration of printed electronic circuits into injection-molded parts, is another cutting-edge application area for printed electronics. In this procedure, flexible, thin substrates made of polyethylene terephthalate glycol (PETG) or polycarbonate (PC) are printed with electronic circuitry before being inserted into molds. The substrate and printed circuit are then enclosed in the molten plastic that has been poured into the mold. The end result is a single, integrated part that combines the mechanical qualities of the plastic part with the functionality of the electronic circuit. Using IMEs offers several benefits such as weight and bulk minimization along with maintaining ergonomic design, which makes printed IMEs an apt technology for the development of interactive and tactile sensors. IME technology can enable sensors to be seamlessly integrated into parts of an automobile often interacted with by humans resulting in a sleek and unobtrusive design. The current study aims to integrate various such additively printed sensors with in-mold electronics conforming to the steering wheel of an automobile. The candidate sensors chosen for this study are electrodermal activity sensor (EDA) which measures the changes in conductivity produced in the skin due to increases in the activity of sweat glands and a pulse oximeter sensor which measures blood oxygen saturation. The circuits for these sensors have been printed using a gravure offset printing technique on PETG and PC substrates. Initially, a component attachment study has also been conducted on PETG and PC substrates using electrically conductive adhesive (ECA) for component attachment, to determine a feasible ink and ECA curing profile. The printed sensors have then been subjected to vacuum thermoforming over an aluminum mold so as to achieve thermoformed sensors. The printed sensors have then been subjected to performance evaluation and subsequent comparison with their theoretical output.

articleTitle: Compliant Direct Attach Liquid Cooling
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Increasing device power and the desire to operate systems with higher ambient temperature for reduced cooling facility power are driving a need for improved electronic system thermal solutions. Liquid cooling is one area of significant effort toward this goal. To create a reliable system, however, most high-power device thermal solutions are implemented in a lidded configuration. This configuration requires that the generated heat transit two thermal interface materials (TIM) and the lid. A lower thermal resistance approach is direct attach, where the liquid cooled heat sink is coupled with a single TIM to the device silicon. Generally, such an approach makes significant demands of the TIM, requiring substantial mechanical compliance and robustness. One solution to reducing these demands is to move at least some of the compliance requirements into the heat sink by making the heat sink conformable. Prior work has shown one very effective but expensive demonstration of this approach. In this work we present a different compliant direct attach heat sink approach that shows promise to be high performance, reliable, and cost competitive. A thin, flexible cold plate with distributed pressure loading is combined with a pad TIM resulting in overall junction to water thermal resistance values as low as 19 C-mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>/W. The cold plates are constructed in a mesh configuration utilizing two different stacked sheet assembly processes with total cold plate thickness ranging from 2-5 mm. Some versions are post-processed to reduce pressure drop. Thermal resistance for these cold plates was measured utilizing a uniform power test vehicle. Thermal performance and pressure drop results were obtained across a range of coolant flows. Initial power-cycling data with up to 7000 full-power cycles showed no negative change in thermal performance, indicating the potential for good reliability. Model results for the base mesh structure were matched against the experimental results and used to predict junction temperature improvement relative to a lidded structure for power maps more representative of high-performance product. These results showed potential peak temperature improvement of 14 °C or more for one representative power map with a peak power density of ~3 W/mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>. Overall, this technology shows substantial promise for significant product temperature reduction at competitive thermal solution cost.

articleTitle: Thermal performance of 0.7mm-thick ultra-thin vapor chambers with composite mesh-groove wick
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: This work presents the performance test results for 140 × 80 × 0.7 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> ultra-thin vapor chambers (UTVCs) with a sintered composite mesh-groove wick under a horizontal or reverse horizontal orientation. Also tested are UTVCs with identical form factors but with a sintered two-layer 200 (2×200) mesh wick. These novel copper-water UTVCs simply comprise a top plate etched with arrayed pillars as the condenser and a wicked bottom plate as the evaporator and liquid path. The pillars provide strong structural support, extended condensation area, and direct shortcuts for liquid return. The thickness of the vapor duct forming between the pillars is 0.33 mm. The evaporator is heated by a 30 × 30 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> dummy heater; the condenser with a footprint of 140 × 80 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> is cooled by a cold plate with running water of 50 ºC. Under the horizontal orientation, the maximum heat transfer rate for the composite mesh-groove wick reach 487 W, superior to those of 259 W for the 2×200 mesh wick. The minimum vapor chamber resistances are 0.031±0.01 K/W for both kinds of wick. Under the reverse horizontal orientation, the maximum heat transfer rate is slightly decreased but the minimum vapor chamber resistances is slightly improved for both wicks due to the gravity effect.

articleTitle: Reliability Analysis of Sintered Silver (S-Ag) for Die Attachment Using a Four-Point Cyclic Isothermal Bend Test Approach at High Temperature and Strain Rates
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: With the increase in electronics devices densification, Sintered Silver (S-Ag) has gained considerable popularity due to its exceptional thermal conductivity, enhanced electrical conductivity, high melting point, and low-temperature sintering characteristics. However, due to the limited number of mechanical and thermal behavior studies of S-Ag, reliability datasets are required to understand the strength and failure modes of sintered silver bond layer. The key objective of this research is to seek reliability assessment through lifetime modeling of S-Ag under dynamic loading conditions at high temperatures to mimic a scenario close to real life environments. To facilitate this purpose, custom made four-point bend testing equipment is designed to utilize repeated mechanical loading and expedited fatigue testing under constant elevated temperatures, replacing conventional temperature cycling approaches. Board-level sintered silver die attachment samples was subjected to a high range of temperatures: 125°C, 150°C, and 175°C. Corresponding strain rate and the empirical data was captured to enable prediction of reliability based on varying mechanical and thermal conditions. The outcome of this experiment is expected to give worthy insight regarding the applicability and performance of S-Ag in electronic packaging and contributes to support current efforts to enhance reliability and durability in high-temperature and high-strain-rate conditions, with potential applications to electronics for emerging technologies and industries.

articleTitle: High Heat Flux Thermal Management using CuW Microchannel Heat Sinks and FC3283
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Microchannel heat sinks (MCHS) have become a common cooling technique for addressing the thermal management limitations of high-powered devices. Introducing cooling fluid into the device packaging by forced convective, single-phase liquid cooling in microchannel heat sinks can lead to reduced thermal resistances and, in turn, reduce the temperature of the device at higher powers. Improving the cooling efficiency can allow for a wider range of performance, such as higher heat fluxes, increased lifetime, and decreased size. This paper discusses the performance of copper tungsten (CuW) microchannels used with a dielectric coolant (FC3283) to dissipate high heat fluxes up to 600 W/cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> over a 0.25 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> area. CuW is thermal expansion matched to GaAs, a common laser diode substrate, and FC3283 is a dielectric refrigerant compatible with cooling of power electronics. This offers a direct practical solution for advanced cooling of laser diode bars. The microchannels used in this study were approximately 365 µm deep and 100 µm wide resulting in a hydraulic diameter of 160 µm. The experiments were performed at a variety of applied power loads and repeated for seven different flow rates to determine optimal performance. The inlet temperature of the cooling fluid was kept constant at 10°C. The resulting thermal resistance ranged from 0.99 K/W at the lowest flow rate, to 0.61 K/W at the highest flow rate. The overall thermal performance of the CuW microchannels using FC3283 proved to be an encouraging option for the future development of laser diode bars and other high-power microelectronics.

articleTitle: Static and Dynamic Thermal Modelling of Si Photonic Thermo-Optic Phase Shifter
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: An experimentally validated finite element thermal model of a thermo-optic phase shifter with integrated metal heater is presented. The model is validated with optical measurements of the heater power required for π phase shift, and with electrical measurement of heater resistance. Length-dependent device performance is investigated, as well as design features for improved heater efficiency: substrate undercut and insulation trenches. Next to static performance, also dynamic performance is discussed. An analytical dynamic model is used to explain the difference in heating and cooling time constants which are often reported in literature.

articleTitle: Low Electrical Conductivity Glycol Coolants as Alternative to Perfluorinated Fluids for Electronics Cooling Applications
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS/PFOS) are being phased out due to environmental and health concerns. Low electrical conductivity ethylene glycol-water solutions were studied to understand if these coolants can be a viable alternative to PFAS/PFOS. Glycol-water fluids demonstrate excellent thermo-physical properties, but ions from various sources can cause the electrical conductivity to rise continuously. A deionizer containing mixed bed (MB) resin particles can maintain low electrical conductivity, but limited studies have been done to understand the effect of a glycol solution on the ion exchange capacity and performance of the MB resin.In our research, MB resin was exposed to Dynalene low electrical conductivity ethylene glycol-water 50 wt% solution (LCEG 50 wt%) as well as ultrapure deionized water (UPW) at different temperatures and time intervals up to 12 weeks. Results demonstrated that the MB resin has a continuous usage temperature range from -25°C to 93°C in LCEG 50 wt%, with the fastest ion exchange occurring between 22.8°C to 70°C. There was a minor loss (less than 7%) in ion exchange capacity for LCEG 50 wt% and UPW at room temperature after 12 weeks, while a notable reduction in capacity was observed at 93°C after the same timeframe: 68% loss for LCEG 50 wt% and 47% loss for UPW. It was also observed that the anionic resin degradation in LCEG 50 wt% was 2.5 times higher on average compared to degradation in UPW. Results show that resin performs better in UPW than in LCEG 50 wt% but can still be used to effectively maintain low electrical conductivity in glycols.

articleTitle: Characterization of the Mechanical Response and Microstructure of iSAC Lead-Free Solder
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: The Anand viscoplastic constitutive model is commonly used to represent the rate-dependent deformation behavior of lead-free solder materials. This model is characterized by nine parameters, and is a well-established component within various commercial finite element analysis software packages such as ANSYS and ABAQUS. Reliability predictions for electronic assemblies are known to be highly sensitive to the input Anand parameters, so that their accurate determination by experiments is critical.In this study, a new lead-free doped solder material referred to as iSAC has been mechanically characterized. The iSAC material includes the traditional Sn-Ag-Cu (SAC) elements found in most lead-free solders, along with tailored amounts of Bi, Ni, Zn, and Ge to enhance interface characteristics, manufacturability, and assembly reliability. Cross-sectional samples of iSAC joints were first analyzed to determine their microstructure, and chemical composition analysis was performed using Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDS).Miniature tensile samples of the iSAC material with controlled microstructures were then fabricated by a reflow process in glass tubes. Uniaxial tensile tests were then performed on reflowed rectangular cross-section solder specimens over a range of temperatures and strain rates. Using the stress-strain data, the mechanical properties of the iSAC material were determined and compared to other lead-free alloys. In addition, the nine Anand parameters for the iSAC solder were characterized using the measured uniaxial response at 15 different pairs of temperature and strain rate. Good correlation was obtained between the Anand model predictions and the measured experimental data.

articleTitle: Methodology to evaluate the thermal performance of the encapsulated phase change materials based nanofluid coolant
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Thermal management has become critically important for the power electronics industry due to the continuous growth in the demand for high-density power devices. Modern fabrication techniques are constantly helping to produce compact and smaller devices, however, at the same time, the heat dissipation surface area has also been compacted. Hence, thermal management has become a grave challenge in these devices for engineers and researchers. Various solutions have been proposed and many researchers are working all over the world to mitigate the heat dissipation issue in power electronics. One such solution is to use the Phase Change Materials (PCMs) for the cooling of these devices. PCMs store a great quantity of heat and help to maintain the temperature in electronic devices. Unfortunately, PCMs have low thermal conductivity and they are difficult to integrate with cooling systems effectively. For one, any melting must be contained so that it can be repeatedly utilized. Some have attempted to create secondary PCM heat exchangers in connection with convective liquid cooling to control liquid temperatures, however, it would be even more effective if PCMs’ latent heat could be directly integrated with coolants. Taking the benefit of the high latent heat of the PCMs, a new kind of composite PCMs was synthesized. The idea was to hold the PCM inside the shell material so that the PCM remains isolated from the coolant carrier when suspended as a slurry. As an added benefit, a higher thermally conductive shell material assists with thermal transport within the internal PCM. These composite PCMs are called encapsulated phase change materials (ePCMs) and they can provide various advantages such as an enhanced rate of heat transfer due to large surface area and high heat capacity. There is no standard methodology available to test the thermal performance of the ePCMs-based nanofluids. In this paper, we have attempted to validate the customized flow loop experimental setup which was designed to evaluate the thermal performance of the ePCM-based fluid.

articleTitle: Immersion Oil Thermal Performance Characteristics and Comparisons
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Immersion oil selection is one of the important tasks to enable efficient immersion cooling. In addition to the safety and reliability consideration, thermal characteristic is the key point. In this paper, three off-the-self immersion oils have been investigated via thermal characteristic comparison and CFD simulation. Kinematic viscosity, coefficient of thermal expansion, thermal conductivity, and thermal capacities are important thermal characteristics and have been compared. The cooling performance of these immersion oils has been compared via CFD simulation. Factors such as flash points that have an impact on safety and reliability have also been included. This paper provides a correlation for thermal performance consideration as well as points out the flash point limitation when selecting proper immersion oils.

articleTitle: Drop Shock Test of PCB at Elevated Temperature
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: The electronics industry has faced an ongoing reliability challenge with lead-free solder materials since the implementation of the restriction of hazardous substances (RoHS) Directive. Among the various lead-free solder options, SAC-based solders have gained substantial popularity as replacements for the traditional SnPb (Tin-Lead) solder. Board-level drop shock testing of these solder materials is an essential criterion for evaluating reliability. The conventional approach in drop shock testing has primarily involved room temperature conditions. However, a substantial knowledge gap exists concerning solder joint behavior in real-world operating temperatures. Therefore, this study aims to conduct drop shock tests at elevated temperatures to effectively bridge the critical gap and ensure the reliability of solder joints in real-world practical conditions. In this study, drop shock performance testing of the SAC305 alloy has been performed at both room temperature and an elevated temperature of 75°C. The experiments followed the joint electron device engineering council (JEDEC) drop test standards, featuring a peak acceleration of 1500G and a 0.5 ms duration. After the drop tests, Weibull analysis was employed to assess the drop shock reliability under each test condition. Additionally, microstructure analysis was conducted to accurately identify the failure location and the failure modes. The results revealed a substantial reduction in the reliability of solder joint when subjected to elevated temperatures. Furthermore, microstructure analysis identified a change in the failure mode at elevated temperatures.

articleTitle: PCM-impregnated heat sinks for transient thermal management of GaN electronic chips
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Heat sinks impregnated with phase change material (PCM) are considered promising solutions for transient thermal management of future high-heat-flux GaN transistors. Existing PCM-impregnated heat sink designs, however, suffer a low cooling performance in their steady-state operation as the PCM layer sits between the cooling fins and the chip. This study introduces a novel lung-inspired PCM-impregnated heat sink design to volumetrically distribute the cooling air through and within the PCM and the solid fins. As such, the proposed PCM heat sink reduces the thermal resistance between the electronic chip and the cooling fluid during both steady and transient operational modes. The cooling performances of three lung-inspired PCM-impregnated heat sink designs at various PCM volumetric ratios are first numerically evaluated under a transient heat input scenario. Then, the transient cooling performance of the optimized PCM-impregnated heat sink design is further investigated using three representative heat sink body materials of a high thermal conductivity polymer, alumina, and aluminum. The results indicate a PCM-impregnated heat sink made of a high thermal conductivity material is still needed for transient thermal management in many industrial electronic chips. Also, it was found that a PCM-impregnated heat sink made of ceramic might be suitable for military-grade electronic chips. The insights gained from this study could help the design of advanced PCM-impregnated heat sinks for optimum thermal management of future high-heat-flux electronic chips.

articleTitle: Cooling Capability Enhancement in Single-Phase Immersion using Targeted Flow
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Single-phase immersion cooling has emerged as a promising technology to help overcome energy consumption and sustainability challenges in the data center industry, promising some of the lowest Power Usage Effectiveness values (PUEs) and highest system power densities. However, thermal design power for server CPUs, GPUs, and emerging AI accelerators (collectively referred to herein as xPUs) have increased dramatically in recent years and are often exceeding the cooling capacity of existing single-phase immersion configurations. In this paper, we investigate the effect of different convective schemes on temperature of xPUs in single-phase immersion cooling systems. Significant increases in xPU cooling capability are demonstrated for optimized heat sink geometries that leverage targeted fluid delivery to the heat sink, either through local pumping at or near the xPU socket or via redirection of the cold return flow from the Coolant Distribution Unit (CDU). Compared to natural convection, cooling capability increases in excess of 100%. It appears feasible within reasonable engineering design limits using these methods, thereby making immersion a viable low-cost alternative solution for higher TDP parts that could otherwise be cooled by the use of liquid cold plates only.An experimental characterization is done to evaluate the potential of a novel cooling scheme for single-phase immersion in polyalphaolefin (PAO)-based synthetic oil coolant. Measured xPU case temperatures are used to evaluate the thermal cooling capability for the proposed heat sink solution. Results show that multiple design methodologies are available for greatly increasing power dissipation capability in these systems. A detailed comparison is made to cooling performance in the natural convection and/or mixed convection environment of traditional immersion cooling heat sinks. We believe that a new class of thermal solutions based on these targeted flow approaches will significantly extend the design space for single-phase immersion cooling of server systems. Such a targeted flow approach also has the potential to make the thermal performance of the high-power density xPUs agnostic of variations in the server configurations, tank flow maldistribution across servers, or varying component workloads. The results show a cooling capability enhancement of 21% at 1 lpm when compared to the immersion-optimized heat sink at the same flow rate at a negligible pressure drop value. This performance is 42% better than the natural convection heat sink in PAO 6.

articleTitle: Mitigation of distortion in fiber laser welded ultra-thin vapor chamber
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: The ever-increasing demand for higher integration and performance in mobile devices underscores the necessity of finding superior cooling solutions. Miniaturization results in a larger heat flux and local high temperatures that impact the lifetime and reliability of these devices. Vapor chambers (VC) are extensively utilized in the thermal management of electronic systems due to their passive operation, reliability, and effective heat transport. However, there remains a need to manufacture much thinner vapor chambers to address tight space limitations while ensuring the required thermal performance and sufficient structural integrity. The purpose of this work is to fabricate ultra-thin vapor chambers (UTVC) meeting these requirements by utilizing a novel fiber laser welding process to join stainless steel. The unavoidable issue of distortion due to welding is tackled by developing finite element models to simulate heat transfer and stress development. Various methods for mitigating welding-induced distortion are examined. Characteristic parameters, including laser power, travel speed, and cooling and clamping systems, are thoroughly studied and optimized. The results indicate that minimizing the net heat input during welding, along with adequate cooling and constraining of the central region of the vapor chamber, significantly reduces waviness and distortion to meet tolerance requirements.

articleTitle: A novel Design for Improving Heat Dissipation Capacity of Single-Phase Immersion Cooling System with the Perturbation Mechamism
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: With the explosive demands for high performance computing, especially the emerging artificial intelligence generated content (AIGC) with large language model (LLM) on stage, higher performance CPUs and GPUs are constantly being innovated to meet the demand of higher computability. Higher performance also means more heat is generated from CPUs and GPUs. The recent trend in the industry that the thermal design power (TDP) of data center microprocessors is projected to increase from 350 watts to 1200 watts, or above in the coming 3 years.The study in this paper has increased the overall heat transfer capability by improving the upward speed of dielectric coolant with a novel perturbation design. The experimental method is to use Intel 4th Gen Xeon Scalable Processors along with Intel Open IP immersion cooling system for actual measurement, the CPU Tjunction temperature with the novel perturbation design is achieved at least 13.27% lower than that without perturbation design. This paper also details such novel perturbation design mechanism and engineering results to conclude single phase immersion cooling solution is capable of addressing the challenge of data center cooling for up to 1500W TDP or above high heat flux processors.

articleTitle: Performance Enhancement of Advanced Integrated Circuits Via CVD Diamond Embedding in a Chip
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: We report the impact of integration of CVD diamond layers in chip and package of advanced INTEL processors. The integration significantly reduces the the junction temperatures by 20°C and allows a performance increase that is equivalent to advancing a full technology node.

articleTitle: Development and Performance Evolution of Thermoformed In-Mold Gravure Offset Band-Pass Filters due to Thermal Cycling
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Gravure offset printing is new form of printing developed as a process of relief printing which shows a promising technique for printed electronics. The reliability of thermoformed in-mold additively fabricated circuits has not been previously studied. In-mold electronics has the potential for light weighting of the automotive platform and a reduced carbon footprint. Further, additive printing has several advantages such as high throughput, high resolution and large-area printability which makes it particularly suited to the automotive industry. The research focuses on the process-reliability interaction of a demonstrator band-pass filter on thermoformed substrate using the gravure offset printing method, silver inks and one interconnect material, namely ECAs (Electrically Conductive Adhesives). The substrates will then be thermoformed in the shape of the steering wheel and encapsulated using one encapsulant material namely encapsulant A The circuits were then subjected to thermal cycling at -40°C-85°C for a significant number of cycles to analyze the reliability performance of the functional circuits.

articleTitle: Transport mechanisms governing the evaporation of a sessile droplet in its pure vapor environment
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Droplet evaporation has been drawing the attention of researchers as it is a critical process in many different areas of science and technology. Most numerical and experimental research has focused on the evaporation process of droplets surrounded by air. Hence, the literature on droplet evaporation in a pure vapor environment is still open to progress. The fundamental difference between evaporation into air and pure vapor is the diffusion of vapor and air molecules at the gas phase, which substantially affects the evaporation of droplets surrounded by air. In the absence of air, the phase change at the interface can be defined by Hertz-Knudsen-Schrage equation based on kinetic theory. The current study presents a numerical model of drying water droplets on a solid substrate surrounded by pure vapor. The model accounts for both buoyancy and thermocapillarity-driven convections inside the droplet. When the thermocapillarity effect (Marangoni convection) is omitted, a single Rayleigh cell generated by the buoyancy occurs inside the droplet. This convection, driven by buoyancy, has a minor influence on energy transport. However, when the thermocapillary effect is accounted for, single or multiple Bénard-Marangoni cells occur inside the droplet, resulting in more vigorous convection, enhancing mass and energy transport and reducing the droplet lifetime. During the drying process, the change in the strength and mode of Marangoni convection induce a nonmonotonic variation in evaporation rate with decrasing contact angle.

articleTitle: Reduced Physics Modeling of Two-Phase Flow through High-Density Cooling Structures
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Increasing power density in high performance microprocessors has driven research into high performance and energy efficient methods of cooling including both single-phase and two-phase liquid cooling. These approaches employ coldplates with complex high-density cooling structures such as fine-pitch microstructures, linked-pin-fins, metal foams, etc., to achieve high heat transfer coefficients. The development of coldplates, especially for two-phase cooling, with such complex cooling structures requires computationally efficient high fidelity thermal models to evaluate the device and system performance under different cooling configurations and operating environments. In this work, a novel reduced physics model based on porous media approximation was developed with homogeneous equilibrium model assumptions for the two-phase flow in the coolant flow domain. For an exemplar complex cooling structure, this reduced physics model produced pressure drop values close to those obtained from full-physics simulations while utilizing significantly less computational nodes and >100X less computational time.

articleTitle: Modularized Thermal and Mechanical Cold Plate Based High Power Memory Liquid Cooling Solution
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: With the increasing demand of High-Performance Computing (HPC) in Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML), the system power and cooling requirement is tremendously changed which are driven by CPU, GPU and memory power increasing. The power density of single DRAM and memory is continuously increasing with the memory technology evolution from DDR3 to DDR5. Furthermore, the memory channels and quantity for the server system is also increased based on system platform design requirement. All these bring cooling challenges in air cooling system. With this background, the liquid cooling memory solution is proposed to support higher power memory with smaller memory pitch in the system. This paper introduces the memory liquid cooling development history and proposes the new concept of double side liquid cooling solution to break though current cooling limitation in memory liquid cooling. The thermal analysis with DDR5 memory thermal model is performed to demonstrate the memory cooling capability of proposed solution. Besides thermal design, the mechanical solution is also an important part of the cooling solution design. The liquid cold plate fitting with system design and tube routing need to be considered. The contact between cold plate and hot swapped memory also needs to be taken into account in the memory liquid cooling mechanical design. With the thermal and mechanical modularized design proposed in this paper, the prototype of the concept is tested, and the test results show the promising results to support high power memory.

articleTitle: Embedded manifold microchannel cooling for chiplet thermal management
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: The chiplet architecture enhances chip performance, but it also leads to heat accumulation, necessitating efficient cooling techniques. Recent studies have demonstrated embedded manifold microchannel cooling (EMMC) as a promising thermal management technique. However, there is still a lack of comprehensive investigation on embedded cooling for chiplet architechture. This study introduces the idea of EMMC into the chiplet architecture and proposes the embedded chiplet cooling (ECC), where microchannels are directly etched onto chips and integrated with 3D-printed manifolds. The proposed method ensures all chips to operate under designated heat loads. Under the highest tested heat flux of 81W/cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> and flow rate of 0.8LPM, the average temperature rise is mitigated to 66.0°C. Results also demonstrate that total thermal resistances decrease with increased flow rates, achieving a total thermal resistance of 0.30K/W at a flow rate of 0.8LPM. Moreover, higher flow rates improve temperature uniformity; when the flow rate increased from 0.4LPM to 0.8LPM under a heat flux of 46.7W/cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>, the standard deviation of chips' temperatures decreased from 8.85°C to 3.09°C Additionally, the proposed cooling technique compensates for height disparity and warpage within chip, ensuring reliability and enabling embedded cooling in more complex scenarios.

articleTitle: An innovative examination of composite PCM capacitor
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: PCMs possess excellent properties for use in the thermal management solutions world. However, their low thermal conductivity poses a challenge. This work compares two capacitors with conduction methods, lattice and plate fins, with two reference capacitors, aluminum-only and PCM without conduction enhancement. This work presents a new method to assess PCM efficiency. It was found that the lattice capacitor has the most efficient heat conduction method for PCM while the heat rate decreases.

articleTitle: Compact Modeling of Distributed Flow Resistances for Data Center CFD
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Objects such as cable trays and piping bundles are often modeled as 3D resistances or porous blocks. In this compact approach, a uniform pressure drop (loss coefficient) per unit distance is typically prescribed in each coordinate direction. But how does the CFD user know what loss coefficient values to specify? Whereas flow characteristics of 2D resistances can be adequately estimated from only an open-area ratio, 3D resistances are considerably more complex. Handbooks cannot cover all possible arrangements of distributed objects, are awkward to use, and offer unknown accuracy. Further, in practical applications, the data center CFD user can typically only estimate the open flow area through each coordinate direction. Accordingly, we idealize the flow resistance through each direction of the distributed resistance as equivalent to that of a thick extrusion of a 2D porous plate of corresponding open-area ratio. We determine the loss coefficients of the extruded porous plates by detailed CFD thereby extending an existing and well-validated empirical correlation from two to three dimensions. We also investigate the use of a nonuniform flow resistance distribution within the porous block and a downstream momentum source (to compensate for not explicitly modeling small-scale airflow jets). We find that this additional complexity does not appreciably improve the accuracy of the compact model for the scenarios analyzed.

articleTitle: Thermal Characterization of a Two-Phase Integrated Heat Sink with Different Heat Source Locations
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: The objective of this research is to thermally characterize a heat sink with integrated two-phase heat transport which was fabricated using laser powder bed fusion to demonstrate the potential of employing additive manufacturing (AM) design flexibility for the integration of two-phase heat spreading for variety of applications. The vertically finned heat sink base and fins are entirely hollow and is designed to spread heat throughout the heat sink using the internal two-phase heat flow. The heat sink base is interchangeable and has a porous wick region which is also additively manufactured. The wick structure provides capillary pumping of the working fluid to the heat source, which can be placed at any location on the heat sink base. In the present analysis, the thermal performance of the heat sink is examined in terms of thermal resistance for different locations of the evaporator heat source. Previous research suggests that shifting the heat source away from the center location can result in a slight improvement in thermal performance. The results showed that lower spreading resistance offered by the two-phase integrated heat sink in the bottom mode can reduce the temperature of the heating section by up to 77-87 °C compared to the middle mode using 9 ml, 12 ml and 15 ml of acetone as a working fluid.

articleTitle: 3D-IC In-Design Thermal Analysis and Optimization
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: The three-dimensional integrated circuit (3D-IC) technology can offer efficiency, power, and performance in packaging. As part of the system-level endeavor to fully support the application of this technology, we have designed and implemented the next-generation 3D-IC thermal analysis workflow. It features generic fully heterogeneous integration, customizable connection types and bump distribution, automatic meshing, and transient and stress simulation capabilities. This workflow can perform thermal analysis from the level of a single die, to a package complete with a board.Additionally, this workflow has great potential for in-design optimization. We have conducted experiments with a machine learning based tool to optimize physical parameters in a stacking. This thermal workflow can be used for pre-layout suggestion, post-layout optimization, and TSV distribution optimization in 3D-IC designs. The stress simulation has also be enabled in this solver, further providing the capability to perform optimization analysis based on stress simulation targets.

articleTitle: Effects of Temperature on Prepreg & Glass Style in Printed Circuit Board (PCB) - Impact on Solid State Drive
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Prepregs in printed circuit board (PCB) may cause warpage and copper pad cracks during reliability testing, which may eventually lead to failure of solid state drive (SSD). To design more dimensionally stable PCBs, it is essential to understand the elastic properties of prepregs with different glass styles and resins at various temperatures. In this study, the effect of temperature on the Young's modulus of resins with different glass styles (1067, 1086, 1080, 7628, and 2116) was investigated. Additionally, prepregs with different resins (R1, R2, R3, and R4) were evaluated to understand the effect of resin on the Young's modulus at various temperatures. The thermal decomposition temperature of the prepregs were also investigated. The results indicate that the Young's modulus of glass style 7628 is significantly higher than that of the other glass styles, making it a promising candidate for applications where dimensional stability is critical. Furthermore, the thermal decomposition temperature of the prepregs was found to be relatively high indicating that they can withstand high temperatures without degradation.

articleTitle: Long-Term Reliability Test on An Air Assisted Liquid Cooling System
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: The power density of advanced-node semiconductors used in HPC applications has been increasing. Simultaneously, the adoption of advanced packaging techniques such as 2.5D, 3D, and heterogeneous integration has posed significant challenges for cooling these HPC applications. It has become evident that traditional air-cooling methods are insufficient for cooling HPC systems, necessitating the use of liquid cooling. However, liquid cooling technologies come with their own set of challenges which are currently being identified and understood by the industry. Air-assisted Liquid Cooling (AALC) system is one of the solutions that can be adopted into the data center without the need of the infrastructure-wise upgrade. To gain confidence in this technology, ensuring the reliability and sustainability of this system is of utmost importance. To achieve this, we have conducted an extensive long-term reliability test over one year duration, continuously monitoring the system's operation and performance in an accelerated environment. In this paper, we will discuss the setup of the long-term reliability test, examine the degradation of system performance over time, and explore our methods for monitoring the test while it is in operation.In addition, one notable challenge is the reliability of materials that come into direct contact with the coolant, as it can lead to potential corrosion and material incompatibility issues. This can result in cooling efficiency degradation in the event of microchannel blockages by corrosion byproducts and more critically can lead to catastrophic failure in the affected CPUs, racks, and possibly the whole facility. In this study, we will also show how we identify and address the root causes of issues encountered during this collaborative effort and lesson learned.

articleTitle: Effects of Datacenter Cooling Subsystems Performance on TUE: Air vs. Liquid vs. Hybrid Cooling
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Datacenter cooling systems consist of several subsystems operating in tandem. Each of these subsystems is characterized by a nondimensional Coefficient of Performance (COP) defined as the ratio of the desired cooling effect to the input power required to produce it. The various COPs combine for each cooling approach and can be used to calculate the system Total-Power Usage Effectiveness (TUE) from a derived closed form equation.Using this general result, the sensitivity of the TUE to the COP of the various subsystems can be studied, and the performance of hybrid systems can be compared to fully air or liquid cooled systems. For systems cooled by either direct liquid or immersion, the TUE ultimately isn’t affected very much by the pTUE of the liquid subsystems, as the TUE of the cooling system depends primarily on the performance of the primary loop, which is where the heat is ultimately rejected to the ambient air.For a hybrid DLC-air system, the TUE depends in addition on the COP of the air-cooling system; the dependence on the fraction of the heat load acquired by the DLC system is linear

articleTitle: Server-Level Test System for Direct-To-Chip Two-Phase Cooling of Data Centers Using a Low Global Warming Potential Fluid
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Cooling of data centers is becoming increasingly challenging with the surging power density, and direct-to-chip two-phase cooling is a promising solution with high cooling capacity and efficiency. Due to the difficulty in accurately modeling two-phase heat transfer under complex configurations, experimental investigations of direct-to-chip two-phase cooling under practical conditions are needed. In this work, we developed a server-level thermohydraulic experimental test system to characterize the performance of this novel and promising cooling solution. The system is a fluid circulation loop consisting of a test server sled, a refrigerant reservoir, a condenser, and a liquid pump. Refrigerant R1233zd(E) is used in this work, which has a low global warming potential of 1. The test server sled has two mounted thermal test vehicles (TTVs) with a maximum power rating of 1000 W each, which are used to simulate two Intel Sapphire Rapids CPUs. Two microchannel cold plates are attached onto the two TTVs to provide cooling by vaporizing the liquid refrigerant flowing inside. Case temperatures, fluid temperatures and pressures, pressure drops across multiple components in the loop, and liquid flow rate are measured using sensors implemented in the cooling loop. Preliminary tests demonstrated sable and efficient cooling of CPU power up to 1000 W with case-to-fluid thermal resistance below 0.02 K/W. At these power levels, we also showed that the flow rates between two parallel cold plates are balanced when the heat is applied nonuniformly. Our work establishes a server-level test system capable of characterizing various working parameters and system configurations, providing valuable insights into both the fundamental understanding and the practical realization of the two-phase direct-to-chip cooling solution for data centers.

articleTitle: Air Cooling and Water Cooling for Data Center High-Speed I/O Interconnects
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Quad Small Form-factor Pluggable-Double Density (QSFP-DD) high-speed I/O interconnect system is the smallest form factor being able to support ultra-high data speed. Furthermore, the data speed of QSFP-DD system is increasing rapidly during the last 5 years, driven by the ultra-high data speed applications, such as Cloud Computing and 5G/6G network. However, the increase in data speed comes at the cost of increase in power dissipation, which has increased from about 5 W/port to 30 W/port during the last 5 years. As a result, air cooling solution, which was conventionally used for QSFP-DD, is no longer adequate to manage the increasing thermal loads. More advanced cooling solutions, such as water-cooled cold plate are needed. In the current work, a series of tests and simulations were conducted on QSFP-DD air-cooled heat sink and water-cooled cold plate applications based on the optimizations done in prior publications. The study provided a guideline to meet the thermal design targets for QSFP-DD.

articleTitle: The Study of Liquid Cooling Solution on 51.2T Switch
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Al/ML application hyper-growth in recent years is rapidly driving the increased switching bandwidth in data centers, which brings the increased thermal challenge for high performance switches with traditional air cooling solutions. Thermal design power of the latest generation 51.2T ASIC called Tomahawk 5(TH5) from Broadcom is up to 763W. The required thermal performance for air-cooled heat sink represented by Rca should be within 0.05°C/W to maintain 105°C of maximum junction limit, which could be still achieved by the large size VC heat sink in 2U chassis, however it costs larger space for heat sink and higher fan power consumption.In this paper, liquid cooling as an alternative solution of traditional air cooling solution was studied to identify thermal feasibility and thermal improvement for 51.2T ASIC in 2U chassis. First, three different cold plate solutions were explored for thermal performance comparison with CFD simulation analysis. Second, thermal performance of the three different cold plates and air-cooled VC heat sink were compared through experiments, the experiment result presents that thermal performance of the best cold plate solution is about 40% better than the target thermal performance of 0.05°C/W. Furthermore, thermal simulation results have good agreement with the experimental results with 5.7% error, and it can be used as reference of cold plate liquid cooling design and simulation.

articleTitle: Thermal Performance of Microchannels Heat Sink with Fins on side walls
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: The main objective of this study is to investigate the thermal performance of straight microchannel heat sinks with fins on sidewalls. A mathematical model is developed and used to carry out the simulation-based study to examine the performance of the microchannel heat sink. The mathematical modeling is done by building a CAD model of the heat sink and carrying out the thermal analysis using the ANSYS Fluent software. From the CFD study, numerical results are obtained for different operational and geometrical conditions. The study shows that using a straight microchannel with pin fins on side walls is better at lower ranges of Reynolds number lower than 400; however, at Reynolds number higher than 400 the straight microchannel with smooth sidewalls shows better performance. Moreover, at a higher Reynolds number than 800, the pressure drop increases significantly. Furthermore, increasing the size of pin fins for both triangle and square fins enhances thermal resistance but also leads to higher pressure drop. To address this trade-off, the study employs FOM analysis, where Design 1 with smaller triangle-shaped fins outperforms Design 2, averaging an FOM value of 24.58 at Reynolds numbers between 250 and 1500. Similarly, for square fins, Design 3 performs better compared to Design 4, with an average FOM value of 38.38 at Reynolds numbers from 250 to 1500.

articleTitle: The Study on cold plate liquid cooling solution for high performance server
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: IT equipment power is increasing rapidly to meet the continuously increased demand of computing performance. Intel Next generation CPU-Granite Rapids will reach maximum 500W Thermal Design Power (TDP) and AMD Turin CPU will have maximum TDP more than 600W. Traditional air cooling has great thermal challenge especially for high density servers. And liquid cooling provides more superior and efficient cooling to meet thermal requirements for future IT equipment and decrease data center power usage effectiveness (PUE). This paper introduced the engineering practice of cold plate liquid cooling solutions for dual latest generation 350W Intel Sapphire Rapids CPU and DDR5 DIMMs in 1U and half-width node of server. Two liquid cooling solutions were designed with different CPU cold plate designs, similar DIMM cold plate design along with different hose routings. Experiments on thermal performance of CPU cold plates, DIMM cold plates associated with the node level liquid cooling solutions were conducted to study the impact on thermal performance in terms of coolant inlet temperature, coolant flow rate, air cooling fan speed, etc. Furthermore, thermal simulation analysis using Simcenter Flotherm for liquid cooling solution was conducted, and simulation results have good agreement with the experimental results, the thermal resistance error was within 5%, the pressure drop error was within 10% and it can be used as reference of cold plate liquid cooling design and simulation.

articleTitle: Numerical study and analysis on lowering the resistiveness of lateral heat spreading in a passively cooled notebook
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: The current generation's demand for laptops is trending towards low-noise, cooler, and high-performance systems. For low noise, fanless systems are preferred, which depend on the surface area of the system for cooling through natural convection. Thermal solutions in fanless systems are limited to the printed circuit board (PCB) area and have a hotspot in the same region. To increase cooling capability for maintaining low temperatures at high power, heat needs to be spread to the relatively cooler locations of the system. The better spreading can be measured by resistiveness in lateral heat spreading (RLHS). The lower RLHS would help to increase power capability at lower temperatures. To aid this spreading of heat, an efficient heat transport mode is designed, which increases the power capability by ~2W in the same fanless system. Heat is transported from the System on Chip (SoC) region to the palmrest area of the notebook via multiple heat pipes. As the palmrest area is typically cooler, it serves as the condenser of the heat pipe and enables effective transport of the heat through the heat pipe without any fans. The numerical study is done using a finite volume method (FVM) in computational fluid dynamics (CFD) with design optimization to get maximum cooling capability. The simulations and results are presented only for the base of the laptop without the display, and cooling enhancement up to 2W is seen with better spreading of heat compared to the baseline case.

articleTitle: Thermal Management and Integrated Heat Spreader Assembly Challenges of Products with Variable Die Heights
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: The recent emergence of High-Performance Computing (HPC) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) has reemphasized the significance of advanced packaging for semiconductor devices. Heterogenous Integration (HI) facilitates the delivery of performance needed for these products by providing the opportunity of assembling different functional dice in a single package. Numerous silicon and assembly technologies have been evaluated across the industry to push the boundaries of current capabilities and to develop state-of-the-art products. The focus is not only on planar integration, but on vertical die stacking as well. The stacked silicon design adds further intricacy due to high power density. An integrated heat spreader (IHS) can be employed to improve heat dissipation from the dice. This paper will primarily focus on the thermal interface materials (TIM) selection procedure and the integrated heat spreader assembly challenges of products with variable die heights. It was found that the Solder TIM provides significant performance improvement over the Polymer TIM in AI use conditions.

articleTitle: Thermal cyclic fatigue life evaluation of BGA solder joints using approximate formula for strain range behavior
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: When electronic equipment is used in places where temperatures vary widely, such as in automobiles, it is necessary to correctly evaluate the fatigue life of the equipment to guarantee system safety. One of the most vulnerable parts of electronic devices is the solder joints that connect the electronic components to the board. Therefore, it is necessary to evaluate the fatigue life of the solder joints to investigate the fatigue life of the devices.It takes huge amount of time and costs to conduct fatigue experiments on actual components. Therefore, simulation is used to evaluate the fatigue behavior including the crack propagation today. However, it may take at least 4 or 5 hours, and some cases it may take a week for a long simulation. In order to reduce the time required for solder life evaluation, it would be useful to have a method to predict the life of a solder from the condition before the crack propagates. If this method is established, only the condition before crack propagation needs to be analyzed. Thus, the time required for solder lifetime evaluation is expected to be reduced to about one-tenth of the current time.This study targets the fatigue life of solder balls in BGA packages and aims to develop an approximate formula to predict the behavior of the nonlinear strain range while considering the dispersion of joint structure. The fatigue life can be calculated from the nonlinear strain range. To develop the approximate formula, the distribution of strain range with relation to the crack initiation distance was analyzed by Finite Element Analysis, and the mechanism of the dispersion was discussed by the analytical results. The case of solder joints shape and the connection method has also been analyzed, and it was confirmed that these formulas evaluate the lifetime accurately.

articleTitle: Embedded cooling to meet the 2kW thermal design power of HPC chips in the future
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: The rapid development of large models like GPT-4 has led to a significant increase in demand for high performance computing. This surge in transistor density has result in heat generation surpassing kW levels, necessitating more efficient heat dissipation methods. In this paper, a silicon-based staggered strip fin manifold embedded cooling scheme for high-performance computing chips is proposed. The top slit and bottom microchannel wafers are etched on two silicon wafers, and thereafter assembled employing the Cu-Sn bonding process, finally bonded to manifold to form the cooling vehicle. Copper serpentine resistors are prepared for heating and an infrared camera is utilized to observe the global temperature. Under a heat power of 1150 W, the average temperature rise is 34.6 °C, the thermal resistance is 10.8 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>K/W when using deionized water as the coolant at the volume flow rate and pressure drop of 1 L/min and 13.5 kPa, respectively. The thermal resistance agreed with the simulation results within 1.5 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>K/W. Consequently, at a temperature rise of 60 °C and a flow rate of 1 L/min, a total power of 2000 W will be effectively dissipated.

articleTitle: The model and influence factors of thermal interaction in chiplet 2.5D integration
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: By integrating heterogeneous chips with different materials and functions into a single system, chiplet architecture technology can break through a variety of limitations on the system-on-chip (SoC). However, it presents new challenges in terms of thermal interaction. In this paper, a collective parameter model based on thermal resistance network for chiplet 2.5D integration is presented in this paper. The relationship equation between chiplet temperature rise and thermal resistance is formulated. The collective parameter model identifies several factors that mitigate the passive chiplet temperature rise caused by thermal interaction. These influence factors include increasing the chiplet spacing, decreasing the interposer thickness, either increasing the TIM thermal conductivity or increasing the convective coefficient and the thermal conductivity of the heat sink. Finite element simulation is utilized to verify the trends predicted by the collective parameter model. The trends obtained by finite element simulation agree with the predictions of the collective parameter thermal resistance model. In this paper, the determinants of the thermal interaction for 2.5D chiplet integration are clarified.

articleTitle: Immediate thermal evaluation of power modules independent of the number and placement of chips
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: The demand for power modules is increasing in line with the electrification of automobiles to realize a sustainable society. Among these, there is a demand for more compact and higher-frequency power modules. Currently, many companies are using elements that are available in the market, rather than those developed independently. However, in the design of power modules, evaluation of thermal performance is important because high cooling performance, insulation, and reliability are required. Therefore, the structure of the power module must be designed so that the critical temperature of the device is not exceeded even when a current is applied. However, performing the analysis each time for various design requirements would lead to development delays. Therefore, the goal of this research is to create a data sheet that allows thermal evaluation to be performed in a single analysis, regardless of element size, number of elements, and element spacing.If a graph showing the relationship between output current and switching frequency is created as a way to simultaneously evaluate the relationship between heat generation due to switching losses, heat generation due to conduction losses, and constraints due to module thermal performance, the relationship between rated temperature, which is a constraint condition, and output current and switching frequency, which are design requirements, can be simultaneously evaluated. This eliminates the need to evaluate the maximum temperature by simulation every time the current condition is changed.<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">[1]</sup>However, once the number and arrangement of elements are changed, it is necessary to perform several simulations to approximate the curve, even when preparing this data sheet. To eliminate this complication, this study attempted to approximate the thermal evaluation when two elements are arranged in different arrangements from the analysis results for the most basic structure of one element. Specifically, we measured the temperatures at a certain distance from the analysis for a single element and introduced a coefficient that evaluates the thermal spread based on the difference between the temperature and the maximum temperature. This and the concept of chip area were introduced, and using the fact that thermal resistance is approximately halved when it reaches 4, the error was corrected using the above coefficient to allow evaluation of thermal resistance. At this time, we analyzed the case where the two elements are placed in parallel and the case where they are placed diagonally, respectively, and showed that the approximation by the present method is valid for both cases. Furthermore, we also evaluated the two elements when they were joined together, i.e., when the size of the element was effectively doubled. The results showed that once the module structure is determined, the necessary data sheets for the design requirements can be obtained by a one-time analysis of the module structure.

articleTitle: Reliability of Additively Printed In-Mold Electronics Using ECA in Sustained High-Temperature Operation
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: The utilization of additive in-mold technologies within the automotive industry necessitates the availability of extended reliability data in challenging environments and the presence of acceleration factors for predicting its anticipated lifespan. However, the reliability data of these flexible in-mold electronics under harsh automotive conditions remains scarce. The study focuses on the interactions of materials and manufacturing techniques to ensure the longevity and performance of in-mold flexible electronic systems in the face of challenging automotive environments. The impact of materials, fabrication techniques, and testing protocols on the reliability of in-mold flexible electronics under sustained high-temperature operation has been studied. For this study, printed thermoformed samples are subjected to continuous, prolonged exposure to high temperatures to replicate the harsh conditions typically encountered by automotive components. For printing conductive traces as well as interconnect materials, nScrypt direct write platform is used. In-mold capable silver ink is used as conductive traces, and stretchable electrically conductive adhesive (ECA) is used as interconnect materials. Thermoformable polycarbonate sheet is used as substrate materials. Heat-assisted vacuum thermoforming has been used to fabricate in-mold architectures.

articleTitle: Thermal Management of Multiple High-Heat-Flux Heat Sources using Additively Manufactured Two-Phase Cold Plate
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: A hybrid two-phase cooling system (HTPCS) was developed for the thermal management of multiple high-heat flux heat sources located randomly (i.e., without a specific pattern) across a cold plate. The heat removal inside the cold plate took place based on the evaporation from wick structures. The significance of this cold plate lies in (i) its fabrication through one single additive manufacturing (AM) process, and (ii) the independent heat removal from individual heater through an evaporator wick inside a channel beneath each heater. Each channel had its own inlet and outlet manifolds, enabling the heat removal process from each heater to operate independently of the others. The cold plate was fabricated from AlSi10Mg and operated with the refrigerant R245fa. The results were compared with those of a pumped two-phase loop including an additively manufactured plain cold plate without evaporator wicks. The increased number of menisci and improved rewetting capabilities of evaporator wicks, attributed to the porous nature of the wicks, led to lower thermal resistances and an increased upper limit of operation for HTPCS compared to the plain cold plate, respectively. The HTPCS operated above 369-385 W/cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> without any signs of partial dryout with pumping power below 1.6 W. The corresponding measured thermal resistances at this range of heat fluxes resulted in values around 0.15-0.20 K-cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>/W. In comparison, the plain cold plate operated up to the range of 302 to 310 W/cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>, with measured thermal resistances approximately at 0.18 to 0.23 K-cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>/W. The high thermal performance of the HTPCS, coupled with its streamlined fabrication process, positions the developed HTPCS in this study as a promising technology for thermal management of multiple high-heat-flux heaters.

articleTitle: Assessment and Comparison of Interface Fracture Toughness in Potting/Substrate Material Systems using ENF and CNF Bi-material Specimen
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Electronics in aerospace and defense applications may be subjected to harsh environments during storage, transport, handling, and over a prolonged use life of the system. Reliable operation of electronics in such harsh environments is needed under high-g acceleration loads, high temperature, and high humidity. Potting compounds are often used to mitigate the harmful environmental effects by providing an additional element of structural support to the electronic assemblies. Interfacial delamination of potting is often a precursor to system failure. In this paper, the interfacial strength evolution has been quantified using a product-design agnostic test specimen. Two different specimen geometries have been studied to assess the effect of mode-mixety including the end-notch-flexure (ENF) and central notch flexure (CNF). The fracture toughness has been measured under monotonic and fatigue loads. Paris constants were developed for potting/substrate assemblies. The effect of mode-mixety has been on the measured fracture toughness.

articleTitle: Experimental and Numerical Study of Two-Phase Immersion Cooling for High-Power Chips
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: As the demand for high-performance computing continues to rise, so does the power consumption of semiconductor devices. How to cool these high-power chips efficiently and effectively has become a significant challenge.In recent years, immersion cooling technology has garnered increasing attention. Immersion cooling has advantages such as high heat transfer coefficients, high cooling capacity, low power consumption, and a compact form factor. The fundamental principle of immersion cooling is that electronic components, such as processors, are immersed in a dielectric liquid that is nonflammable. Heat is removed from the components directly through the dielectric liquid. According to the boiling point of the dielectric liquid, it can be divided into two approaches: single-phase and two-phase immersion cooling.This study adopts both a numerical and experimental approach to investigate the cooling of high-power chips by using a two-phase immersion cooling method.For numerical simulation, the six-equation Eulerian two-fluid model in OpenFOAM is adopted. In order to simulate the complex process of fluid boiling phenomenon, RPI heat flux partitioning model is chosen to simulate fluid boiling process. The model incorporates the momentum exchange term between the gas and liquid phases to account for differences in density and relative velocity.The two-phase immersion cooling experiment is performed in a 600mm x 450mm x 320mm tank with an 800W heat source, a condenser and a mesh type BEC (boiling enhancement coating). Fluorez FL-50 is adopted as working fluid for two-phase immersion cooling. The water inlet of the condenser is fed with a constant temperature chilled water. A pressure balancing device is implemented to maintain tank gas pressure around 1 atm. For comparing with numerical results, the liquid temperature around the chip, chip case temperature, gas temperature is measured in the experiment.In this study, a classical DEBORA test result of subcooled flow boiling is chosen to validate the numerical method first. In addition, a parametric comparison of numerical and experimental results of cooling high-power chips using a two-phase immersion cooling method is performed. The simulation and experimental results indicate that the difference in chip case temperature stays below 3.4% under steady-state condition.

articleTitle: Hexagonal Boron Nitride Nanosheets Filler Infiltrated Polymer Composite Films for Thermal Management Applications
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Thermally conductive and electrically insulating nanofillers are ideal materials in a polymer for the synthesis of thermal compounds to dissipate the heat from sensitive electronic devices.
