In the operating region, the eSSDs are expected to perform at any workload with full performance without triggering thermal throttling for a given operating environment specification. However, generating an operating curve is a very time-consuming task, as each point on the curve requires several iterations of either simulations or tests. In addition, it is not unusual that some component specs or powers could change during the product development cycle. Thus, it may take a few iterative cycles before generating an accurate operating curve. To address this concern, in this paper, we propose an operating curve fast prediction method using machine learning and a modified binary search algorithm. Our regression machine learning model can find the equations to predict the temperature of critical components (e.g., NAND package, ASIC package, and DRAM package) and enclosure hotspots for different ambient temperatures and airflow rates based on a designed simulation or test matrix. After equations are found, the boundary points on the operating curve are obtained by running a modified binary search given the temperature limits of the enclosure and critical components. The validation study has shown that the temperature predictions from the machine learning model for all critical components in different working conditions align with the Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations with good accuracy. Moreover, if the thermal limits are updated later, our fast prediction method can update the operating curve automatically.

articleTitle: Experimental analysis and measurement of hotspot location with thermal test vehicle in mobile SOC
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: In a situation where the required performance of Mobile Application Processors (AP) is increasing gradually, and power consumption is also on the rise, control technology is needed to ensure that temperature remains within defined limits. During chip design, temperature sensors are strategically placed near hotspots based on temperature distribution analysis through simulations. Temperature sensors for individual CPU cores are positioned near hotspot locations based on single-core operation, resulting in a phenomenon where the hotspot location shifts during multi-cores operation due to thermal coupling with surrounding heat sources. This can lead to an increase in discrepancies between the temperature values measured by the sensors and the actual temperature of the hotspot within the core. Mobile AP chips are housed within packages, and additional packages are stacked on top of the AP. Consequently, it is not possible to measure the chip's temperature distribution from the outside during operation. However, due to the limited number of temperature sensors, accurately measuring the temperature distribution of a single CPU core is challenging. In this paper, a thermal test vehicle (TTV) was developed to measure the phenomenon of hotspot location shifting within the CPU block of Mobile System-On-Chip (SOC) APs during multi-cores operation scenarios. The TTV was used in conjunction with the functioning Mobile AP chip to measure the temperature distribution within cores and the shifting of hotspot locations under different scenarios while the chip was in operation.

articleTitle: Thermal Performance of Transient Liquid Phase Diffusion Bonded Multi-Layer Cold Plate
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: The performance of CPU/GPU are updated year by year, and in recent years the heat generation of these chips have increased significantly. For High Performance Computing (HPC) cooling or High-end server cooling, single phase Direct Liquid Cooling (DLC) is becoming primary cooling solutions. The latest thermal design power (TDP) of CPU/GPU has reached > 600W level, and high-performance cold plate is a key factor for next generation cooling solutions. Traditional parallel fin type microchannel cold plates have been adopted, and to enhance their thermal performance, narrower fin pitch cold plates have been developed. However thinner fin thickness results in lower fin efficiency, and high pressure drop. In this paper, an innovative cold plate design is presented with evaluated thermal performance, pressure drop, and manufacturing cost. The Multi-Layer Cold Plate (MLCP) consists of multiple etched sheets laminated by Transient Liquid Phase (TLP) diffusion bonding. In thermal performance comparison between MLCP and parallel fin cold plate, the MLCP showed 20% improvement in thermal performance at similar pressure drop. TLP diffusion bonding enables MLCP to be manufactured continuously with high capacity and reasonable cost. The cost depends on etching sheet size. For a sheet size of 65mm x 45mm it is confirmed that MLCP can be manufactured at the same cost as parallel fin.

articleTitle: Characterization of Gap Pad Thermal Interface Material by Enabling Pressure and Thermal Mapping Capabilities
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Most electronic components generating heat will require external cooling solutions to keep device temperatures within specified limits, ensuring optimal performance and reducing degradation over time. The typical solution utilizes a heatsink or spreader to cool the component in combination with a Thermal Interface Material (TIM). Thermal Interface Materials are widely used in the tech industry and enable improved heat transfer to achieve reliable operation of electronic devices. In some instances, gap pads are the preferred TIM because of their multiple benefits such as being able to accommodate uneven air gaps and rough surfaces, as well as their ease of application. Typically, gap pads are used for low-power components cooled through the primary thermal solution, such as power delivery components or microprocessors with low-power consumption.For Personal Computing (PC) cooling applications, it is necessary to make accurate predictions of gap pad performance for a variety of power scenarios. This broad range of power scenarios means the hotspot can be located anywhere within the electronic component's surface. When applying a gap pad between two surfaces, it is known that the gap pad thickness is not uniform across the totality of the surfaces, and that there will be a thickness profile. This happens for multiple reasons including surface warpage of the surfaces. Because of this, assuming a uniform gap pad performance (or conductivity) can translate into significant errors.In this paper, the authors present how to capture local variations of gap pad performance that enable accurate modeling for multiple power scenarios, regardless of the hotspot location. This was done using a realistic, system-like test setup, capturing real pressures with pressure-mapping sensor and direct heating from silicon test chips. As the material is heated the pressure-mapping sensor was used to capture the load and pressure changes over the entire heating area. Parallelly, embedded sensors on the silicon test chip were used to generate an accurate temperature profile across the test chip area. This pressure mapping and temperature mapping were used to assess the accuracy of the predictions. This procedure enabled the team to measure the thermal performance of gap pads ranging 0.5mm to 1.5mm of thickness, under pressure conditions ranging 2 to 60 psi. As a result, it was possible to demonstrate that the use of pressure maps allowed the thermal model to capture the thermal resistance variations caused by the TIM thickness alterations. Fundamentally, the methodology provided valuable insight into the interaction between the overall thermal performance, the load distribution across the surfaces and the location of the hottest point on that surface. Even though gap pads are not new in the industry, this methodology of performance validation using realistic system conditions will enable more accurate predictions and optimized cooling designs for future systems.

articleTitle: Novel Nano-indentation Dynamic Mechanical Thermal Analysis (NiDMTA) Technique for Characterizing Viscoelastic Properties of Polymeric Materials in Semiconductor Packages
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: In this paper, we demonstrate a novel Nano-indentation Dynamic Mechanical Thermal Analysis (NiDMTA) technique to measure storage and loss moduli of a polymeric material over combined frequency and temperature sweeps. Specifically, the frequency sweep between 1Hz and 100Hz is enabled by dynamic Nano-indentation with a flat-ended diamond punch tip, and the temperature sweep is achieved by a sample heating stage that can reach maximum 300°C. We applied the NiDMTA technique to characterize an adhesive material used in semiconductor packaging. Subsequently, the frequency-temperature dependent complex modulus data were used to construct the master curve based on the Time-Temperature Superposition Principle (TTSP) and fit the Williams–Landel–Ferry (WLF) shift function along with the Prony series parameters of the generalized Maxwell model. The resulting instantaneous and equilibrium moduli of this adhesive material are 12.37MPa and 5.35MPa, respectively, and the identified viscoelastic material model can be readily used in Finite Element Analysis (FEA) simulations. The new NiDMTA technique enables small-scale viscoelastic characterization for polymeric materials used in semiconductor packages and beyond.

articleTitle: Dependence of Oscillation Frequencies on Operating Conditions in an Oscillating Heat Pipe
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Oscillating heat pipes (OHPs) have proven to be effective heat spreaders and as such have been widely studied. Their behavior, however, is difficult to predict due to the strong coupling between mechanisms governing heat transfer and fluid flow, and the large number of influencing parameters. This work utilizes a numerical solution framework to predict the frequencies of the liquid slug oscillations. A parametric study is performed to analyze the dependence of the oscillating frequencies on the operating conditions. A simplified analytical model reveals the dependence of the frequencies on the operating parameters and provides guidelines for a better OHP design.

articleTitle: The Study on Improving CFD Simulation Accuracy for Heat Sink Design Optimization in Single-Phase Immersion Cooling System
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Data center sustainability has becoming one top priority in the industry nowadays, mainly driven by cooling efficiency challenge of data center high heat flux components such as high thermal design power (TDP) microprocessors in high density rack server as well as the related regulation and enforcement of sustainability locally and worldwide. Power usage effectiveness (PUE) is one of mainstream indicators for environmentally sustainable data center. Lower PUE highly matters in the existing data center reconstruction or new built data center. Recent research and engineering practice in ecosystem has proved the feasibility of immersion cooling technology for hyper scale data center deployment to achieve PUE 1.1 or lower. However, ramping up immersion cooling solutions for massive production scaling in the industry still need address the challenges from the phase of design, validation to deployment and maintenance. Parameters setting of thermal simulation utility for immersion cooling system design accuracy is one pain point nowadays as mainstream setting parameters are with best known methods of air cooling, which accumulated for decades. Deviating significantly from the principles of air cooling system design, immersion cooling hinges on the manipulation of liquid density variations to induce fluid circulation, but weakened by gravitational effects. This paradigm shift necessitates a meticulous reassessment of parameter configurations and the meticulous selection of thermal simulation tools tailored specifically for immersion cooling scenarios. In this study, the commercial version of Foltherm XT, a computational fluid dynamics (CFD) utility, is used with optimal parameters setting for thermal simulation of immersion cooling system design. Intel immersion cooling engineering system (aka. Open IP immersion cooling reference system) is used for engineering validation to prove the accuracy of immersion cooling thermal simulations with optimal parameters. Validation results have concluded the coolant flow field is dominated by laminar flow where FC-40 of 3M Fluorinert Electronic liquid used to cool high density servers with Intel Xeon scalable processors, and less than 2.5% deviation between simulation and engineering validation eventually achieved. To demonstrate the value and benefit of this study on high CFD simulation accuracy for immersion cooling, an advanced heat sink design optimal for single immersion cooling system is introduced with the conclusion drawn that heat sink in louver design way hit the sweetest spot of performance, cost and capacity for single-phase immersion cooling system, where its thermal resistance has achieved 7% lower than typical 1U air heat sink (44+2 fins and 0.3 mm fin thickness) widely used nowadays.

articleTitle: Hydraulic Performance Analysis of an Additively Manufactured Multipass Microchannel Heat Exchanger
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Heat exchangers operating in extreme environments need to meet strict size, weight, and power consumption (SWaP) requirements to enable an efficient thermal system. The development of high-performance, low-cost, and highly compact metal heat exchangers can be attractive and beneficial to multiple sectors, like aerospace, power generation, and electronics. This study investigates the implementation of the microchannel approach in the heat exchanger design to optimize heat transfer and endure high-pressure scenarios in such challenging environments. However, the design's complexity and compact nature pose significant challenges to traditional fabrication methods. To overcome this issue, direct metal laser sintering, as one of the additive manufacturing (AM) methods, was employed to customize and fabricate such type of heat exchanger with lower cost and achieve small fins (0.18 mm width) and channels (0.3 mm width). Upon creating a demonstration unit, experimental characterization was conducted, and the results were compared with model predictions to evaluate the heat exchanger’s hydraulic performance in laminar and turbulent flow regimes while accounting for roughness factors. This study demonstrates the feasibility of fabricating a compact microchannel heat exchanger using AM, while offering insights into its hydraulic performance through both empirical and computational techniques.

articleTitle: Multi-resolution method for thermal resistance matrix based on 2D Haar wavelet
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Optimal thermal-aware design (TAD) with limited resources essentially requires the accurate thermal resistance matrix (TRM) that represents the relationship between temperature and power with proper spatial resolution. The TRM has been widely used for temperature sensor placement and floor-plan optimization in board and on-die design. However, the large size of TRM with fine spatial resolution usually causes the computational burden by consuming a lot of time for design optimization. In this paper, the systematic scheme that reduces the TRM size is being proposed. By using multi-resolution (MR) approach, it is presented that the size of TRM can be reduced, which can save computational resources to achieve a steady-state temperature map. By using this method, several case studies saving 70~90% of computation time are presented to demonstrate that the proposed systematic scheme is effective and useful for time efficient optimization of on-die floor-plan and temperature placement when designing SOC that include multiple heterogeneous cores.

articleTitle: An Integrated Simulation Framework for Thermal-Mechanical Performance Analysis of Two-phase Microchannel Evaporators
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: In this work we present an integrated simulation framework that has been developed to numerically predict the thermal and mechanical performance of parallel two-phase microchannel evaporators for thermal management of electronic components. The simulation framework is realized by integrating an in-house two-phase flow simulator with the Ansys Mechanical Finite Element Analysis (FEA) solver. The in-house two-phase flow simulator is based on established heat transfer and pressure drop correlations and is capable of calculating two-phase heat transfer for a wide variety of parallel microchannel designs, coolant fluids, inlet flow conditions and applied heat loads. The ANSYS FEA solver, on the other hand, allows efficient computation of a three-dimensional microchannel evaporator temperature distribution for complex thermal boundary conditions, such as localized hot spots on a packaged electronic component, and the stress distribution within the microchannel evaporator due to internal fluidic pressure. The framework is validated against experimental data obtained from literature and then utilized to predict the performance of a parallel microchannel evaporator in the presence of a nominal background heat flux and several localized hot spots on the electronic component. Refrigerants with low global warming potential are studied as the cooling fluid and the inlet flow conditions are varied with respect to mass flow rate and subcooling. Both uniform and non-uniform flow across the parallel channels are considered for each refrigerant to understand the impact of flow maldistribution on mitigating hot spot temperature rise. Finally, the effect of the internal pressure developed due to the two-phase flow on the mechanical integrity of the evaporator is also studied. This integrated approach thus allows understanding the effect of a range of parameters such as refrigerant type, flow maldistribution, parallel channel geometry, and localized hot spots on both the thermal and mechanical performance of the evaporator. A comprehensive performance map is also generated to aid in identifying the optimal refrigerant type and flow conditions for a given electronics cooling application.

articleTitle: Experimental Thermal Characterization of Thin Film low-k Dielectric Materials
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: In this paper, we present the experimental thermal characterization of thin film dielectric materials with low dielectric constant (low-k) for Back-End of Line (BEOL) application realistic thickness values in the range from 10 to 120 nm. The proposed methodology is a combination of the 3-omega method and a 2-step model fitting procedure to extract the substrate and dielectric thin film thermal conductivity. The amplitude of the 3<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">rd</sup> harmonic of the voltage signal shows a high sensitivity to both the substrate and thin film thermal conductivity for an applied harmonic voltage or current signal. The method is validated by comparing the extracted Si and SiO2 thermal conductivity with reported literature data. The characterization method is applied to a low-k dielectric material and reveals a thermal conductivity of 0.33 ± 0.02 W/m-K, independent of the film thickness.

articleTitle: Temperature and pressure dependent thermal interface material characterization using packaged thermal test vehicle assemblies
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: This study introduces a novel thermal characterization methodology for thermal interface materials under in-situ application scenarios, where thermal interface materials are applied between a thermal test chip assembly with a warped die and a cold plate, while it is under varying compression loads. A thermal test chip with integrated heaters and sensors, which can detect temperature variations caused by non-uniform contacts, measures the temperature distribution within the chip. Steady state measurements with uniform heating are adapted for package level thermal characterization, where normalized junction temperature increase distributions are examined and compared for different thermal interface materials. Furthermore, in combination with thermal finite element analysis, transient measurements with local heating are used to extract intrinsic thermal properties of different thermal interface materials.The proposed methodology is applied to characterize various commercial thermal interface materials with different bond line thickness, compressibility and thermal conductivity under varying clamping pressure and cold plate temperatures. Characterization results are documented in terms of extracted effective thermal conductivity and normalized temperature increase distribution at the chip junction.

articleTitle: Thermal Analysis of Dual-sided Cooling for Backside Power Delivery Networks (BSPDN) on 2.5D Glass/Silicon Interposer Package
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: This study explores advanced cooling strategies for Backside Power Delivery Networks (BSPDN) within a 2.5D interposer-based package integrated with a logic die and High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) modules. Comparative modeling analysis of cooling techniques reveals that utilizing topside direct-on-chip microjet cooling alongside a glass-based interposer package has the potential to decrease HBM temperatures significantly, potentially by a factor of 5. This reduction is achieved by minimizing the thermal coupling between the logic and HBM components. In addition, dual-sided cooling utilizing topside microjet cooling and glass/silicon interposer embedded microchannel cooling is proposed to address the thermal bottleneck of BSPDN configurations owing to the lower thermal conductivity SiO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> bonding layer. The modeling results indicate that the proposed dual-sided cooling approach can decrease the logic maximum temperatures by 22% while simultaneously mitigating the thermal coupling between the logic and HBM components.

articleTitle: Co-Design of 300 mm Wafer Scale Package
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: A novel packaging configuration was developed for a 300 mm wafer scale system. A number of these systems have been operated at power levels up to about 16 kW for over a year using a thermal test wafer. The power subsystem can provide a total of 22.5 kA of current for the 0.8 V and 1.2 V power domains to the wafer, and the I/O subsystem can provide an aggregate system bidirectional bandwidth of 128 GByte/s using PCIe Gen3 optical links, and a local HBM bandwidth through the laminate of 512 GByte/s per reticle site and 37.9 TByte/s per wafer. The system is nearly all water cooled.

articleTitle: Thermal Characterization of Two-Phase Cooling using Embedded Microchannels in a High Current Density Electric Motor
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: The transportation sector is rapidly transitioning from fossil fuels to hybrid and fully electric propulsion alternatives. Aviation presents a challenging application in this transition, in part due to the strict power density (kW/kg) targets required for propulsion using electric motors. Scaling of traditional motor designs to higher powers increases the component weight as well as that of auxiliary infrastructure, specifically, the thermal management system that must also increase in capacity. Integration of advanced cooling methods within the motor windings has the potential to enable operation at increased powers without compromising the overall system weight. In this study, an additively manufactured stator section prototype with embedded microchannels for cooling is constructed to demonstrate the high current density operation of Litz wire coils. The cooling performance is characterized using two-phase flow of a dielectric refrigerant (R1233zdE) and tested under steady-state conditions. Wall-embedded thermocouples inserted along the flow length of the channels, as well as an electrical-resistance-based average coil temperature measurement, enable characterization of the flow boiling heat transfer coefficient and ground insulation thermal resistance. Under this cooling configuration, a peak current density of 30.4 A/mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> was achieved at a safe operating peak coil temperature of 128 °C with a heat transfer coefficient of 2530 W/m<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>K. This thermal performance allows for high electric loading of machines to meet the propulsion power density requirements of electrified aviation.

articleTitle: Multi-objective design optimization of pin-fin cold plates for electric vehicle battery packs using convolutional neural networks and genetic algorithms
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Lithium-ion batteries generate heat while charging and discharging, requiring battery thermal management systems (BTMS) to mitigate adverse thermal effects impacting battery performance, safety, and longevity. As future electric vehicles (EVs) demand battery packs of higher energy densities that charge faster, more advanced BTMS are becoming increasingly critical. This work contributes to surrogate-model-based design optimization methodologies that are accelerating the design process of BTMS and their integrated liquid-cooled cold plates. This work proposes a novel surrogate-model-based design optimization approach to enable rapid design iterations of cold plates and satisfy ever-stringent EV thermal management needs. The approach is demonstrated through a case study addressing the optimal channel geometry of a pin-fin cold plate for a modular pack design used in the battery pack of Ford’s Mach-E EV model. This work’s approach produces optimal cold plate channel geometries based on battery-module-specific design features, including battery cell heat generation profiles, packaging materials, and heat spreading characteristics. Latin Hypercube sampling and numerical three-dimensional conjugate heat transfer models are used to construct a training database for deep encoder-decoder hierarchical (DeepEDH) convolution neural network (CNN) models. These trained DeepEDH-CNN models replace the numerical simulations during a multi-objective optimization with the Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II). The optimal pin-fin positions and radii yield a cold plate design that reduces maximum temperatures, temperature gradients, and cooling power consumption by 4.87 K, 5.1 K (22.2 %), and 7.93 Pa (9.0 %) respectively. This work demonstrates the capabilities of the proposed approach as a generalized methodology for BTMS design optimization, holding the potential to accelerate the thermal performance enhancements demanded by EV fast charging and next-generation battery packs.

articleTitle: Development of a Novel Analytical Model for Liquid Synthetic Jets and Introduction of Their Application in Immersion Cooling Systems
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: A synthetic jet, generated near the orifice of a synthetic jet actuator, emerges from a cavity with a periodically actuated wall. The vortical structures produced by synthetic jet actuators, due to their effective mixing and boundary layer agitation capabilities, present potential for applications in a wide range of electronics cooling applications. One potential application can be the integration of synthetic jet actuators inside immersion cooling tanks where there is a lack of effective targeted flow control. The study of synthetic jets encompasses their generation, formation, and both near- and far-field flow behaviors. However, for liquid synthetic jets, there is a notable deficiency in research across published literature. The first step in designing and studying liquid synthetic jets should begin with an examination of their generation. While lumped element models offer considerable versatility for designing synthetic jet actuators, such models for liquid synthetic jet actuators are currently lacking. Therefore, this study aims to adapt fluid dynamic-based lumped element model of air based synthetic jets and extend it to liquid synthetic jets, addressing this gap in the field. Synthetic jet actuators working with Shell immersion cooling fluid and water are modelled and results are compared with three dimensional CFD simulations. Studied devices were able to generate SJs at velocities of 6.15 m/s for water, and 6.8 m/s for synthetic oil system. It was observed that Helmholtz frequency happens in liquid system however at significantly higher frequencies, in comparison to air synthetic jet actuators. Phase lag between diaphragm actuation and jet exit velocity is also observed at wall resonance frequency, a phenomenon which needs to be considered in future studies. It can be concluded that presented lumped element model is an excellent tool for designing and rapidly assessing liquid synthetic jet actuators in the development process. However, in order to accurately characterize their heat transfer capabilities, detailed CFD simulations with compressibility consideration and further experiments are required.

articleTitle: Development of a Hybrid Single/Two-phase Capillary-based Micro-cooler using Copper Inverse Opals Wick with Silicon 3D Manifold for High-Heat-Flux Cooling Application
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Previously, we reported two-phase capillary-based cooling using narrow (200 to 1000 µm) heater bridge copper inverse opal (CIO) wicks with heat flux level of 1400 Wcm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-2</sup> and superheat ≈ 10 ℃. Here, we demonstrate the area scaling of the proposed technology to a large-area micro-cooler for high-heat-flux cooling of microprocessors and power electronics. We developed a hybrid single/two-phase micro-cooler that relies on capillary-wicking in a 25-µm-thick CIO with an open silicon microchannel 3D-manifold for liquid delivery and vapor extraction, achieving a high heat flux ≈ 400 Wcm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-2</sup> over a heated area of 10 × 10 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>. For a range of inlet water flowrates from 5 to 60 g(min)<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-1</sup>, we achieved total thermal resistances and vapor qualities of 0.68 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>℃W<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-1</sup> to 0.2 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>℃W<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-1</sup> and 0.55 to 0.12, respectively. The flowrates are 10× smaller than those of conventional single- or two-phase microchannel cooling technology. The corresponding two-phase thermal resistances ranges from 0.05 to 0.02 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>℃W<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-1</sup> with temperature superheat of 8 to 6 ℃, respectively. While the overall performance of the large-area (10 × 10 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>) capillary-based micro-cooler degraded compared to the previous demonstration of the technology for a heated area of 5 × 5 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>, however, preliminary CFD modeling indicates that an improved manifold design will be able to achieve comparable performance.

articleTitle: Methodology to Generate a Steady State Thermal Computational Fluid Dynamic Model of Consumer Laptop
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) has proven to be an invaluable tool for technology enterprises, and the domain of personal computing applications is no exception. CFD empowers us to simulate consumer laptops, comprehend their behavior across various scenarios, and project meaningful results, all without the need to physically replicate and test every scenario. This translates into substantial time and cost savings. However, achieving accurate results from CFD simulations is not a straightforward task. It demands the meticulous provision of all relevant data to the software. Creating a complete computer model that accurately replicates the thermal behavior of a consumer computer requires a comprehensive system correlation based on the characteristics of the actual system.The complete design of a personal laptop can be broken down into two main subsystems: the mechanical system and the thermal system. The mechanical system includes factors such as the physical component dimensions, their arrangement, and the materials used. In the case of the computer selected for this research, the thermal system involves elements of the airflow generated by the fans, thermal solution characterization, and measurements of system power and temperature at relevant points. This paper's main objective is to outline a methodology for gathering these inputs and identifying the most relevant components and details to incorporate into a CFD model that is representative of a physical laptop. The aim is to strike a balance between simplicity for ease of software analysis while still achieving accurate results.To investigate the thermal characteristics, experiments were conducted during the laptop's realistic operation. This involved the use of thermocouples to record real-time temperature data of the computer skins and thermal solution, an acoustic chamber to study system acoustics, and an airflow chamber to analyze both system and fan airflow patterns. In parallel, it was crucial to obtain precise measurements of the mechanical stack within the physical computer. This included determining the exact component locations, component geometries, and calculating the system's air gaps, all of which have a direct impact on thermal performance. These mechanical measurements were carried out using calipers and a coordinate measuring machine (CMM). Concurrently, the CFD model was developed to accurately replicate the actual laptop. Subsequently, steady-state simulations were executed to validate the modeled temperatures and system impedance, using them as indicators to assess the accuracy of the correlation between the CFD model and the consumer laptop.This study aimed to assess the correlation between a real system and the CFD model, with a particular focus on critical aspects of the system's performance: chassis temperatures, fan-generated noise, and thermal capability. When comparing the data collected in the tests and the data obtained from the simulation, the findings reveal a 6% difference in chassis temperatures, which are important to consider due to ergonomic limits. Additionally, there is less than 10% variation of the system impedance which indicates the similarity between both. This correlation opens numerous possibilities for future research, including the creation of models with different components or features to meet market demands.

articleTitle: An Unsteady Homogeneous Two-Phase Flow Model for Microchannel Oscillating Heat Pipes
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Microchannel oscillating heat pipes (OHPs) are promising heat transfer devices for electronic chip cooling due to their wickless construction and high heat transfer capability. Despite the simple geometry of OHPs, their complex transport mechanisms and multiple regimes of operation presents a modeling challenge. The widely accepted slug-plug model is based on a two-phase slug flow pattern, and assumes that evaporation and condensation of a thin liquid film surrounding the vapor bubbles governs the heat transfer process. The flow oscillation of OHPs operating at low power as predicted by the slug-plug model generally agrees with experiments. But as power increases, the flow exhibits a variety of typical bubbly and churn flows which might render the slug-plug model unapplicable. In this work, we use a one-dimensional (1D) unsteady homogenous two-phase model to capture flow instabilities which is one of the mechanisms for the operation of OHPs with more highly dispersed vapor and liquid. The proposed model assumes that the two-phase flow is homogeneous and numerically solves three sets of coupled partial differential mass, momentum, and energy conservation equations. We applied this model to simulate the periodic fluctuation modes of the fluid velocity field inside a portion of OHP which consists of five turns microchannel under a background pressure surge. The fast-oscillating motion of the two-phase mixture transports energy along the microchannel with a time delay between the evaporator heat input and condenser heat rejection. Currently, the model does not consider the compressibility of vapor and other physical mechanisms that are also needed to model the complete closed-loop OHP. Therefore, to model the open-loop response, a unidirectional pressure drop boundary condition is applied as a step function to assure that oscillation of the flow occurs due to intrinsic flow instabilities, rather than an externally driven cyclic pressure drop. Overall, the simulation results provide insights into the physical modeling of flow instabilities inside microchannel OHPs at high heat flux operation and this work will be extended in the future to model a complete closed-loop OHP based on the two-phase homogeneous flow model.

articleTitle: Quantile-based Long Short Term Memory Remaining Useful Life prediction of Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor Field-Effect Transistor
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Accurate prediction of the remaining useful life (RUL) of a degrading component is crucial to prognostics and health management for electronic systems, to monitor conditions and avoid reaching failure while minimizing downtime. However, the shortage of sufficiently large run-to-failure datasets is a serious bottleneck impeding the performance of data-driven approaches, and in particular, those involving neural network architectures. Here, we develop a new data-driven prognostic method to predict the RUL using an ensemble of quantile-based Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural networks, which represents the RUL prediction task to a set of simpler, binary classification problems that are amenable for prediction with LSTMs, even with limited data. We demonstrate that this approach obtains improved RUL estimation accuracy for power MOSFETs, especially with a small training dataset that is characterized by a wide range of the RUL.

articleTitle: Predicting Accurate Hot Spots in a More Than Ten-Thousand-Core GPU with a Million-Time Speedup over FEM Enabled by a Physics-based Learning Algorithm
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: The classical proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) with the Galerkin projection (GP) has been revised for chip-level thermal simulation of microprocessors with a large number of cores. An ensemble POD-GP methodology (EnPOD-GP) is introduced to significantly improve the training effectiveness and prediction accuracy by dividing a large number of heat sources into heat source blocks (HSBs) each of which may contains one or a very small number of heat sources. Although very accurate, efficient and robust to any power map, EnPOD-GP suffers from intensive training for microprocessors with an enormous number of cores. A local-domain EnPOD-GP model (LEnPOD-GP) is thus proposed to further minimize the training burden. LEnPOD-GP utilizes the concepts of local domain truncation and generic building blocks to reduce the massive training data. LEnPOD-GP has been demonstrated on thermal simulation of NVIDIA Tesla Volta™ GV100, a GPU with more than 13,000 cores including FP32, FP64, INT32, and Tensor Cores. Due to the domain truncation for LEnPOD-GP, the least square error (LSE) is degraded but is still as small as 1.6% over the entire space and below 1.4% in the device layer when using 4 modes per HSB. When only the maximum temperature of the entire GPU is of interest, LEnPOD-GP offers a computing speed 1.1 million times faster than the FEM with a maximum error near 1.2°C over the entire simulation time.

articleTitle: Microhardness Analysis of Reflowed Solder Joints: Effect of Paste Alloy and Paste Volume
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: The assessment of microhardness in reflowed solder joints is a critical aspect of quality assurance in various industries. It allows for identifying defects and weaknesses in solder connections, ensuring the reliability of electronic devices and mechanical components. The microhardness of solder joints directly affects their mechanical strength, making it crucial for applications exposed to mechanical stresses and temperature fluctuations. This study examines the effects of solder paste alloy and paste volume on the microhardness of reflowed solder joints. Solder spheres composed of SAC 305 and solder pastes, including SAC305, SAC-Bi, and SAC-Bi-Sb, were applied at varying paste-to-sphere volume ratios, specifically at 0.1, 0.3, and 0.5. The tested component was a 15 x 15 mm CABGA208. A micro-Vickers hardness tester was employed to indent seven joints for each combination using appropriate standard load to measure hardness. Subsequently, an average microhardness value was calculated for each combination. The results indicated that the doped alloys, specifically SAC-Bi and SAC-Bi-Sb, exhibited significantly higher hardness levels compared to SAC305. Furthermore, the study emphasized a significant influence of paste volume on microhardness, with a general trend indicating that higher paste volume resulted in increased solder joint hardness. However, this trend did not apply to SAC305, where paste volume did not yield any observable impact on hardness. These results were subject to comprehensive statistical verification and were confirmed through ANOVA and Linear Regression analysis.

articleTitle: Liquid to Refrigerant Cooling System Challenges, Characterization, and Operational Limits: A Case Study
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: As data processing demands are on the rise, efficient cooling systems are becoming vital for conserving energy, space, and ensuring optimal performance. While air cooling is a straightforward and convenient method for electronic thermal management, it may struggle to manage higher heat flux effectively. Consequently, liquid cooling techniques have gained significant attention for their ability to manage the increased thermal loads generated by smaller chip sizes. In the present work, a facility-level Liquid-to-Refrigerant (L2R) system is experimentally characterized under various operational conditions. The selected system consists of an indoor chiller, an outside condenser unit, and multiple server racks. The system is capable of handling up to 200 kW of thermal load. However, various limitations are observed and studied both on the primary and secondary sides of the system. The impacts of these constraints on the stability and reliability of the chosen system are thoroughly investigated. Various Performance parameters are discussed, along with different operation aspects. Finally, recommendations for best practices related to the studied parameters are carefully documented.

articleTitle: Resilient Polymer Nanocomposites for Type II Thermal Interface Materials
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Thermal interface materials (TIMs) in electronics are typically used between the heat source and heat sink to enhance heat dissipation. TIMs are continuously exposed to harsh conditions such as temperature cycling, mechanical stress, humidity, vibration, and shock, which can lead to failure and hinder efficient thermal conduction. Both thermal and mechanical properties are equally important for electronic reliability and performance. However, mechanical properties are often overlooked in the literature compared to thermal properties. This study emphasizes the fabrication of TIMs based on thermoplastic elastomer (TPE) nanocomposites with mechanical robustness and sufficient thermal conductivity. The form factor of the TIM is Type II, an elastomeric thermal pad. Mechanical robustness in the TIMs is achieved through triblock copolymers of polystyrene-block-polyisoprene-block-polystyrene (SIS). Thermal conductivity of these robust films is enhanced by incorporating functionalized 2D hexagonal boron nitride (BN) nanoplatelets. Above 20 vol.% BN, both in plane and cross plane thermal conductivities decrease. Additionally, the incorporation of the nanoplatelets increases surface roughness, elastic modulus, and mechanical hysteresis. We observe that an increase in nanofiller content negatively impacts mechanical performance without necessarily improving thermal conductivity. Thus, understanding the balance of mechanical and thermal performance is critical for optimization. The results obtained through this research can offer valuable insights for designing elastomeric thermal pads.

articleTitle: Prediction of Failure at FCBGA Interfaces under Thermo-Mechanical Loads Using a Competing Risk Cohesive Zone Model
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Electronics on the automotive platform plays a vital role in ensuring the safe and efficient operation of automobiles. To enhance the durability and reliability of Flip-Chip Ball Grid Array (FCBGA) packages, underfill materials are employed to reinforce the interfaces between substrates and semiconductor dies. These underfills (UF) serve as protective barriers, safeguarding the chips from various environmental factors such as moisture, shock, vibration, and radiation. Furthermore, underfills play a pivotal role in minimizing plastic deformation during temperature fluctuations and provide crucial mechanical support to solder connections. Their significance is particularly pronounced in underhood electronics, where FCBGAs endure prolonged exposure to extreme thermo-mechanical stresses. Delamination is one of the most prevalent failure modes encountered at the chip/underfill (UF) interfaces. A bi-material specimen has been fabricated to measure the fracture propensity of the chip/underfill and EMC(Epoxy Mold Compound) to substrate interfaces. These specimens have been isothermally aged at high 100°C and 150°C for varying durations spanning from 30 to 360 days. Separately, a set of bi-material specimens have been subjected to humidity exposure for 10 hours to 120 hours at 60°C/60%RH. The interfacial fracture toughness has been measured across a spectrum of loading conditions. Mode-I and mode-II stress intensity factors are determined for the monotonic loading conditions. The Paris constants (A, n) have been determined in fatigue loading using the Paris power law, which relates the crack growth rate and stress intensity factor. The Paris constants serve as direct indicators of the evolution of interfacial properties under prolonged exposure to elevated temperatures and fatigue loading. Cohesive zone parameters have been computed for the chip/UF and substrate/UF interfaces. To predict the interfacial delamination at FCBGA interfaces, a predictive cohesive zone model has been developed and simulated.

articleTitle: Thermal Analysis of High Current Vertical Power Delivery Network with Embedded Microchannel Cooling
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Advancements in high-performance computing (HPC) demand densified interconnect and assembly methods in power delivery networks (PDN). A challenge accordingly emerges with system-on-package (SoP) solutions using vertical power delivery networks (VPDNs), where heat dissipation from the die and the integrated voltage regulator (IVR) is a primary concern. This paper presents a numerical thermal analysis of two VPDN designs: distributed on- and in-interposer dual-phase multi-inductor hybrid (DPMIH) converters. Positioned vertically beneath the die for a 12 V-to-1 V single-stage, high-current power conversion using gallium nitride (GaN), these configurations are evaluated in scenarios with and without embedded microchannel cooling. With microchannel cooling, the analysis incorporates 103 microchannels, each 200 µm wide and 100 µm high, employing water as the working fluid. The aim is to maintain device temperatures below 90 °C during 1 kW power delivery to a monolithic 3D (M3D) die while minimizing pumping losses for microchannel cooling and ensuring total efficiency exceeds 80 % at a high current density. Numerical results show that without embedded microchannel cooling, the maximum system temperatures reach approximately 126.1 °C and 155.5 °C for on- and in-interposer configurations, respectively. Conversely, embedded microchannel cooling with a flow rate of 0.05 kg/s reduces maximum system temperatures to 54.6 °C and 74.6 °C for on- and in-interposer configurations, respectively. For maintaining temperatures just below the threshold of 90 °C, on-interposer conversion requires a flow rate over 0.015 kg/s, with pumping power consumption of at least 9.2 W, whereas in-interposer conversion demands a minimum flow rate of 0.025 kg/s, consuming 39.4 W of pumping power.

articleTitle: Numerical Investigation of Flow Boiling in Fin-Enhanced Microgaps Using an Improved Lee Model
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Modeling flow boiling in finned micro-gaps commonly employed in cold plates for thermal management of microelectronics remains a complex challenge due to the lack of a model that can accurately represent interfacial heat and mass transfer, across a range of conditions. Among the phase change models used in computational fluid dynamics and heat transfer (CFD/HT) modeling of flow boiling, the Lee model has gained popularity. The Lee model assumes that phase change occurs at a constant saturation temperature and does not account for the incipience superheat required for the onset of nucleate boiling (ONB). In this paper, we present an improved Lee model that considers both the change in saturation temperature with pressure and the required surface superheat for the ONB. We assess the improved model’s performance against the original Lee model for a fin-enhanced micro-gap with nonuniform heating. The current CFD/HT study uses the dielectric fluid HFE-7200, which allows for near junction, or direct contact cooling of electrically active components. We also investigate the impact of variation in the contact angle on the improved Lee model predictions of the two-phase flow regimes.

articleTitle: Experimental Measurements of the Effective Thermal Conductivity and Contact Resistance of Compressed and Uncompressed Metal Foam for Applications to Cold Plates
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Open-cell metal foams have attractive properties such as high surface area density and moderate pressure drop such that they are under exploration as an alternative to traditional finned structures in air-cooled heat sinks or liquid-cooled cold plates for electronics cooling. Recent studies in metal foam technology have shown that mechanical compression decreases the foam porosity and increases the surface area density, both of which increase the thermal performance of a metal foam cold plate under the right conditions. The current study focuses on experimental measurements of the effective thermal conductivity of compressed metal foam, motivated by applications using single and two-phase liquid flow. Experimental measurements are reported for the effective thermal conductivity and contact resistance of compressed and uncompressed copper, aluminum, and silicon carbide foams. An ASTM standard two-bar method was used with the two-sample technique in which two samples of different thicknesses are measured under identical conditions to extract both the effective thermal conductivity and contact resistance. Samples of copper, aluminum and silicon carbide foams with compression ratios (CR) of 1, 2, 3, 4, and 6 were tested. It was found that previously derived experimental correlations for k<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">eff</inf> for uncompressed foam fail to capture the behavior of compressed foam. A simple correction to an existing correlation was found to successfully correlate the measured effective thermal conductivity to the solid phase thermal conductivity and sample porosity. The effective thermal conductivity for all samples increased by a factor of ten with compression leading a decrease in porosity from 90% to 50%. Similarly, thermal contact resistance without an interface material was found to also correlate with sample porosity as the number of contact areas at the solid interface increases with decreasing porosity (i.e. with increasing compression). Contact resistance was significantly decreased when a thermal interface material was used to attach the foam sample. Without the TIM, the contact resistance was a strong function of contact pressure.

articleTitle: Liquid Metal Concentration Effects on Thermal and Mechanical Properties in Elastomers
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: The escalating power density and consumption in electronic devices necessitate package-level heat-dissipating components with high isotropic thermal conductivity. Although polymers offer advantages such as low density, high strength, easy processability, chemical stability, and cost-effectiveness, they typically exhibit low intrinsic thermal conductivity values. Previous studies have explored the incorporation of gallium alloys into elastomeric matrices to enhance the composite material’s overall conductivity. However, conventional approaches involve aligning the thermally conductive filler, resulting in high thermal conductivity but significant thermal anisotropy. Yet, cross-plane thermal conductivity plays a vital role in dissipating heat from active devices and transmitting it to the surrounding environment. In this study, we investigate the impact of varying concentrations of eutectic gallium indium alloy (EGaIn) liquid metal within an elastomeric matrix without inducing filler alignment. Utilizing inplane and cross-plane thermal and mechanical characterization techniques, we aim to understand how this factor influences the isotropic enhancement of thermal conductivity and the mechanical performance of the material. Our findings reveal that, in the absence of induced alignment, thermal conductivity demonstrates a more isotropic increase with the concentration of liquid metal compared to alternative methods, all while maintaining mechanical performance similar to the matrix. These discoveries pave the way for advancements in bulk polymer-based composite materials for electronic applications.

articleTitle: Development of In-Mold Integration of EDA Sensors Via Additive Printing
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Wire harnesses account for a significant weight of the vehicle. The emergence of advanced driver assistance systems has seen the emergence of a number of safety features, including lane departure warning, driver alertness monitoring, cross-traffic alert, guidance, navigation, and control. Touch surfaces in the automotive platform are presently used for little more than aesthetic appeal. However, the integration of human-machine interfaces on the touch surfaces requires additively printed in-mold electronics. The processes for the printing of sensors in addition to the integration of surface mount electronics for signal processing are not yet known for additively printed conformal electronics. This research focuses on developing robust and reliable PCBs for wearable electro-dermal activity (EDA) biosensors, particularly on substrates that are thermoformable. Electrodermal sensors measure the surface conductance of the skin to determine the state of the autonomous nervous system. The Electrodermal Activity (EDA) sensors are used for their ability to monitor a multitude of biosignals within the human body. These wearables could acquire biosignals with high accuracy, which makes them beneficial in scenarios like assessing a driver’s emotional and medical condition during various driving scenarios. The potential real-world implications of such monitoring are considerable, from safety applications to medical diagnostics. The purpose of using thermoformable substrates was due to their ability to be reshaped to provide unprecedented design flexibility, such as mounting on any curved surface. The other focus was to accurately measure skin conductance and response as biosignals for real-time driver monitoring. The approach will involve using the Voltera additive print platform for the fabrication of EDA sensors along with the signal processing circuits for the measurement of surface conductance. The influence of the sintering time temperature, print speed, print volume, and thermal profile during thermoformed circuit performance has been studied. The bio-signals have been measured under a range of real-life use conditions. The measured response of the thermo-formed circuits has been compared to medical-grade sensors to assess the error, consistency, and stability of the measured response. The thermo-formed EDA sensors showed a comparable performance with minimal errors relative to the medical grade measurement platform. In addition, the sensor effectively monitored stress levels with high precision through developed stress detection algorithms with combination of AI and physics-based model.

Author Keywords: Fabrication of Additively Printed In-mold Electronics
AI-based Machine Learning of EDA Sensor

articleTitle: Direct-On-Chip Hotspot Targeted Microjet Cooling for Ultra-fast Inference at Scale Running on Groq Language Processing Unit (LPU)
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: This paper investigates the thermal management strategies targeted at hotspot mitigation based on the Groq Language Processing Unit (LPU™) architecture with functionally sliced power map. To address this challenge, this study explores the concept of direct-on-chip hotspots targeted microjet cooling corresponding to the power map through the entire LPU™ chip. The customized heat transfer coefficient map can be achieved by tailoring the inlet nozzle diameter and pitch, as well as the flow conditions to match the hotspots within the chip, or high-power densities. Based on the modeling results, this direct-on-chip microjet cooling can successfully address the potential temperature non-uniformity from different functional blocks within the logic die. It achieves a temperature nonuniformity within 4 ℃ across the logic die and significantly reduces the thermal coupling between LPU™ and the nearby chiplet in an exploratory use case scenario setting.

articleTitle: Biodegradable Substrates For Sustainable Aerosol-Jet Additively Printed Electronics
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Flexible hybrid electronics (FHE) have gained popularity due to their speed and soft tooling, and their applications in various sectors like consumer electronics, automotive, healthcare, and transportation. Historically, printed circuits used volatile organic solvent-based inks, which have been criticized for their environmental impact. However, water-based inks have emerged as a promising alternative, offering a significantly reduced environmental footprint. This study aims to explore the application of biodegradable PET substrates in the aerosol jet printing process, which is known for fabricating 3D and 2D surfaces on micron scales. Key components were attached to the circuits using electrically conductive adhesives. The evaluation included a detailed analysis of component performance, mechanical stability, and electrical performance. The study also examined the electrical properties of the circuits, focusing on resistance values across varying sintering temperatures and durations. Preliminary findings suggest that modifying these parameters can enhance electrical properties, with optical methods used to characterize printed trace outcomes. This paper presents a pioneering foray into the utilization of biodegradable PET substrates in sustainable electronics manufacturing, offering insights into potential enhancements in environmental sustainability without compromising on functional efficacy.

articleTitle: Pool Boiling Reliability Tests and Degradation Mechanisms of Microporous Copper Inverse Opal (CuIOs) Structures
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: The rising power density in electronic systems requires thermal management solutions that are both high-performing and reliable. Porous materials such as Copper Inverse Opal (CuIOs) have unique structural features, including high permeability and high thermal conductivity, to enhance pool boiling performance. However, there is little understanding of the degradation mechanism of such porous materials under pool boiling conditions. In this study, samples of 10 μm thick CuIOs with 4.8 μm diameter, covering silicon substrate of area 11 mm × 11 mm, with various heated areas ranging from 2.5 mm × 2.5 mm to 10 mm × 10 mm, were tested in 100 °C deionized water at a constant heat flux of 110 Wcm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">−2</sup> for 3-to-7 days. The combined effect of erosion and corrosion caused structural degradation of the CuIOs. The directly heated area had the most severe degradation while the edge of the heater and the unheated area showed progressively less degradation, maintaining some CuIOs structure even after the 7-day reliability test. Among all the tested samples with various heater sizes, the 2.5 mm × 2.5 mm heater sample – in which the heater size was designed to be comparable to the water bubble characteristic length – had the largest critical heat flux (CHF) up to 300 Wcm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">−2</sup> with a superheat ~ 13 °C. Additionally, CuIOs with a smaller heated area performed better in terms of reliability. This study offers preliminary insights into CuIOs degradation mechanisms, contributing to the development of more robust thermal management solutions. We expect that electroless plating of CuIOs with gold (Au), nickel (Ni), and atomic layer deposition (ALD) aluminum oxide (Al<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>) in combination with appropriate application-specific coolants will further improve the reliability and lifetime of the CuIOs.

articleTitle: Embedded Microchannel Cryogenic Cooling for Silicon Crystal Monochromators using Liquid Nitrogen and Liquid Argon
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Crystal monochromators are often the primary optics in hard X-ray synchrotron beamlines. Management of power load is critical to their design. The thermal deformation of the crystal not only broadens the rocking curve, resulting in a reduction of flux and worse energy resolution but also distorts the wavefront. This distortion adversely affects beam angular divergence and coherence preservation. Strict requirements on stability and deformation must be met, as new-generation synchrotron sources deliver brighter beams of X-rays. More aggressively, the root-mean-square (RMS) height error of the crystal atomic plan should be smaller than 30 pm for Si (111), 8 pm for Si (333). To address these thermal challenges associated with the ultrahigh peak heat flux (48.59 W/mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>) and thermal expansion effects, cryogenic cooling emerges as a promising solution for silicon crystal monochromators due to their high thermal conductivity up to 2500 W/(m ∙ K) and low thermal expansion coefficient properties under cryogenic temperature. This paper introduces a pioneering method employing internal microchannel cryogenic cooling with liquid Nitrogen (LN<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>) and liquid Argon (LAr) to mitigate thermal deformation in high-power silicon crystal monochromators. A finite element method (FEM) has been developed to predict the temperature performance and surface deformation by applying intrinsic properties of Si material and the cooling system parameters. Simulation results show that LN<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> cooling demonstrates significant advantages over water cooling, notably reducing vertical displacement by approximately 41.34 times due to the exceptional thermal conductivity of silicon (K<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">Si</inf> = 1300 W/(m ∙ K)) at cryogenic temperatures around 95 K. In addition, our studies show that the thermal deformation of the silicon crystal under 100 W power can be reduced to around 0.28 nm residual RMS height error for liquid Nitrogen cooling, while 7.6 pm residual RMS height error for liquid Argon cooling.

articleTitle: Changes in the response of an inertial MEMS sensor due to changes in the temperature of the working environment
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: The work analyzes the operation of the analog reading path of the MEMS accelerometer in the ASIC system. It is a block of an integrated circuit that has been physically made and measured. Performance analysis captures the main points of the system that limit the quality of its operation as a whole. Simulation tests of the system were used for the analysis, performed at the design stage of its diagram and then topography, due to the inability to measure signals at all stages of processing by the readout system in the form of an integrated structure. The work focused particular attention on the analysis of influence temperature variation on the useful digital data obtained at the output) that appears in the analog path of the ASIC system and its dependence on temperature.The analysis used commonly known statistical tools, in particular the standard deviation, showing how the output value from the analog-to-digital converter system changes as a function of temperature, and line charts showing the dispersion of these values for a stationary system (depending on the orientation of the system -1 g, 0 g or 1 g).

articleTitle: Modeling of the Temperature Cycling Performance of BGA Packages with Hybrid SAC-LTS Joints and Various Bi Concentration Gradients
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Low Temperature Solders (LTS), typically Sn-Bi alloys, are increasingly being adopted in surface mount technology (SMT) assembly due to their ability to reduce warpage during assembly by enabling lower reflow temperatures. Hybrid solder joints, formed by reflowing LTS pastes with SAC solder bumps on a Ball Grid Array (BGA) package, exhibit a varying Bi concentration - higher at the PCB side and lower towards the component side. Bi diffusion in SAC alloys can prevent crack propagation by restricting the coarsening of intermetallic compound (IMC) layers. However, it can also result in Bi-embrittlement at the Bi-rich PCB side, which can lead to failure during thermal cycling. Hence, considering this Bi-concentration gradient is crucial while modeling the thermomechanical performance of BGAs with hybrid SAC-LTS interconnects.In this study, finite element models of hybrid solder interconnects, formed at 190°C peak reflow temperature with SAC305 spheres and Sn-Bi based LTS paste, were analyzed. Quarter-symmetry models of a CABGA192 package with various Bi-concentration gradients resulting from three different paste-to-ball volume ratios (0.25, 0.5, and 0.8) were developed. Anand constants for solder materials (SAC+x%Bi) were estimated using our previously characterized Anand constants for SAC+Bi alloys, and from literature data. The models were subjected to thermal cycling (0-100°C) boundary conditions according to IPC-9701B. The maximum average nonlinear plastic work accumulation was used to identify the critical solder joint, and the failure region within the critical joint. Then, the Syed model was implemented to approximate thermal fatigue life (TFL), and the values of TFL were used to compare the thermomechanical performance of hybrid joints formed with different paste-to-ball volume ratios.Our analyses have illustrated the effect of paste-to-ball volume ratio on the thermomechanical performance of hybrid SAC-LTS interconnects. These findings suggest that optimizing the SMT process by selecting an optimal paste-to-ball volume ratio can lead to an optimum distribution of Bi across the joint, thereby improving thermal fatigue life (TFL).

articleTitle: IR and Optical Imaging Technique for Stability Analysis of Thermal Interface Materials Under Accelerated Power Cycling
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Understanding the reliability of thermal interface materials (TIMs) in die-level packages is critical for maximizing the performance and lifetime of electronic assemblies. However, testing TIMs with genuine parts can be very slow and expensive, and simulations cannot accurately predict material reliability. There must be ways to quickly and cost-effectively test TIMs for comparisons and allow down selection for genuine part testing. This report covers a TIM testing technique that evaluates TIMs' reliability in days, instead of months, on cost-effective equipment. The test technique also allows for in situ monitoring of TIMs with thermal and optical imaging, giving insight into a TIM's behavior and failure mechanisms.This test technique used a thermal test vehicle (TTV) representative of a package with a central processing unit (CPU) and an integrated heat spreader (IHS). TIM was placed on the CPU die, and a KBr window was placed on top of the TIM (in place of the IHS). The window allowed for simultaneous TIM thermal and optical imaging, while previous techniques used IR or optical imaging independently. The CPU was power cycled to cause temperatures to oscillate between 30 and 100°C. The temperate cycling caused warpage of the CPU and drove mechanical strains in TIMs. A cycle took 3 minutes, allowing for the accumulation of many cycles quickly but still having real-world strains, strain rates, and temperatures applied to TIMs. This coupled thermal and mechanical cycling offered more realistic TIM stressing in accelerated conditions than similar techniques, delivering practical results for how TIMs react in real-world applications.This work was done as proof of concept for the technique design and worked with three repressive types of TIMs: TIMs intended for between a heat spreader and heat sink (TIM 2s), grease TIMs intended between a die and heat spreader (TIM 1s), and phase change materials (PCM) TIM 1s. Results showed the system could drive damage in TIMs in a few days, allowing for quick comparisons and down selection. IR imaging could detect the initiation and growth of phenomena resulting in TIM failures, such as voiding, cracking, and delamination. Correlations between the growth of defects and local die temperatures were determined, highlighting the technique's applicability to relate defects to lower TIM thermal performance.

articleTitle: An Advanced 48U Single Phase Immersion Cooling System Design for Commercial Data Center Deployments
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Liquid Cooling technology for sustainable data center deployments is mainly driven by increasingly higher Thermal Design Power (TDP) microprocessors, sustainability regulation and enforcement, and higher computing power demand at the edge, especially in the harsh edge environments. Recent industry research and engineering success show that power usage effectiveness (PUE) of less than 1.1 can be achieved with immersion cooling solutions. In today’s commercial immersion cooling data center landscape, single-phase solutions have maintained their pioneering status through sustainable coolants that can be commercially deployed in environments that preceded two-phase solutions. This paper introduces an advanced 48U single-phase immersion cooling solution with 1.03 pPUE (partial PUE) that achieved target for commercial deployment in data center. The three major ingredients of this solution are detailed: filling block modules to improve cooling design efficiency, flow field uniformity subsystem for cooling capacity, and heat sink optimal design for cooling performance. Key learnings from this solution engineering practices are also summarized as reference for a sustainable data center with single-phase immersion cooling design.

articleTitle: Experimental Analysis of Heat Transfer and Pressure Drop in Aluminum Metal Foams Immersed in Dielectric Synthetic Fluid
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Metal foams possessing high porosity are extensively employed in diverse applications due to their interconnected hollow structures that enable fluid flow and enhance flow mixing capacity. The unique features of metal foam, such as its high surface-to-volume ratio and stochastic orientation, contribute to an enhancement in its thermal performance. The current study utilized high-porosity metal foam heat sinks as an alternative to conventional heat sinks. The aim of this investigation is to experimentally evaluate the performance of an aluminum foam heat sink when immersed in a single-phase synthetic dielectric fluid. This research investigates the effects of variations in geometrical parameters, specifically pores per inch (PPI), as well as operational parameters on fluid flow, pressure drop, and heat transfer within metal foams. The study employs metal foam that features cores measuring 0.0127m in height, relative densities ranging from 10.7 to 12.3 percent, and PPI of 5, 10, 20, and 40. The metal foams were exposed to varying flow rates of 0.2 LPM, 0.5 LPM, and 0.8 LPM, as well as heat fluxes of 60 kW/m<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> and 80 kW/m<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>, and inlet temperatures of 20°C, 30°C, and 40°C. The experimental results are presented in relation to pressure drop, thermal resistance, overall surface area efficiency, and coefficients of local and overall heat transfer. The metal foam with a pore density of 10 PPI demonstrated the most optimal heat transfer performance, exhibiting the highest values for both local and overall heat transfer coefficient, and the lowest thermal resistance across all conditions. The surface area efficiency demonstrated the maximum and minimum values for the foam with 5 and 40 PPI, respectively. Furthermore, it can be observed that the pressure drop across a 40 PPI foam is 1.5 to 1.8 times higher compared to that of a 5 PPI foam for both the heat fluxes and all fluid inlet temperatures.

articleTitle: Study of High-G Level Shock Damage-Accrual in Doped/Undoped SAC Solders during Prolonged Sustained Operation at 100°C
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
