abstract: Electronic components may experience increased strain rate, high-g loads, and wide temperature extremes in the automotive and aerospace applications during transport, storage, and normal operation. Electronics may be routinely subjected to temperatures between -65°C and 200°C for sustained durations at high strain rates, ranging from 1 to 100 per second. A number of doped SnAgCu alloys have emerged to mitigate the damaging effects of sustained high-temperature operation on the properties. The efficacy of doping in mitigating the detrimental effects of high strain rate operation at high strain rates is not understood. In this study, tensile specimens are prepared from various doped SAC solders and tested at working temperatures ranging from -65°C to 200°C at strain rates of up to 75 per second for up to 1 year of isothermal aging at a storage temperature of 100°C. Mechanical properties like UTS and E, at high strain rate testing are reported and compared for the undoped and doped solders containing different Bismuth content. Mechanical properties of doped solders are found to be higher than that of undoped solders. Also, after high temperature storage for prolonged durations, solders containing higher Bismuth content performed better than the undoped solder SAC305. The experimental results and data were fitted to the Anand viscoplasticity model. Anand constants are extracted for various aging durations and employed for studying the solder joint’s visco-plastic behavior in the FE analysis of Drop/Shock events. For the assembly of CABGA208 packages with PCB, FE analysis for drop/shock events at 1500g has also been carried out for various conditions, according to JEDEC standard JESD22-B111A (2016).

articleTitle: Modeling of Backside Power Delivery and Thermal Management in Semiconductor Die Packages
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Modern semiconductor packaging faces the dual challenges of efficiently delivering power to numerous transistors and managing heat to prevent hotspots and potential component failure. Backside power delivery (BSPD) distinguishes itself from conventional power delivery methods by delivering power from the backside of the silicon die, using unused space for thicker power lines and thereby reducing resistance loss. Embedded microfluidic cooling strategies have investigated microchannels in the back side of silicon dies to direct coolant over hotspots, effectively dissipating heat for chip temperature management. We propose a synergistic integration of microfluidic channels with power delivery on the backside of semiconductor dies that can potentially offer optimized space utilization to allow balanced power and thermal performance. However, this requires modeling tools that can accurately capture coupled electrical and thermal responses in 3D while resolving the small feature sizes relative to the overall die size that can lead to computational complexity. To address this challenge, we develop a model that employs a homogenization method that allows for sub-grid resolution of microscale features, as well as the transformation of the fully 3D problem into an equivalent set of connected 2D subproblem. This work demonstrates application of this method to numerically study a silicon die with both a backside power delivery network (BSPDN) and manifold liquid cooling microchannels. 3D transport is represented by considering the energy and mass exchange between multiple 2D layers. The homogenized representation treats the domain as a porous composite material with metallic power lines navigating between the flow channels. Homogenized conservation thermofluidic conservation equations for the porous medium that consider electrical Joule heating are used to construct the numerical model. Representative steady-state cases are studied where the silicon die generates uniform heating with local hotspots. Through these case studies, we reveal the potential application advantages of integrating 3D manifold microchannels for cooling in a BSPDN for high-power operations.

articleTitle: Forced air cooling thermal design with embedded heat pipes in a heatsink for GaN-based High Power RF Amplifier Applications
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: This paper introduces an approach to efficiently manage thermal dissipation in gallium nitride (GaN) on silicon carbide (SiC) high electron mobility transistors (HEMTs). While GaN transistors possess a high temperature tolerance, it remains crucial to efficiently transfer the heat generated within the transistor-package to the external environment. In this article, a conceptual design for a heat sink is suggested with the aim of lowering the temperature of a GaN transistor module. ANSYS-Icepak software is used to conduct steady-state thermal simulations for forced air convection with different air flow rates, both with and without heat pipes embedded in a heat sink. The comparative simulation results for a 20 mm x 10 mm active area indicate a 31.5% temperature reduction from 100.2 °C to 68.6 °C in the transistor package with proposed embedded heat pipes. In addition to the temperature reduction, heat sinks with embedded heat pipes allow for a smaller form-factor heat sinks effectively dissipating the higher heat flux density from microelectronic packaging devices. The simulation findings also indicate that a heat sink of comparable size but without embedded heat pipes is not a viable option for effectively dissipating the 170.2W of power from the active packaging region of the GaN transistor.

articleTitle: Enhancing Minichannel Flow Boiling with Femtosecond Laser Surface Processed Stainless Steel Surfaces in Water
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: In this work, results of a single-channel flow boiling system using functionalized 304 stainless steel surfaces with DI water as the working fluid are presented. The surface is modified using femtosecond laser surface processing (FLSP), which creates self-organized, micro- and nanoscale surface features that introduce additional nucleation sites and augment the surface area available for two-phase heat transfer. A polished and an FLSP surface were tested up to critical heat flux (CHF) using two different mass fluxes, and their heat transfer performance are compared. The FLSP surface yielded substantial enhancement in both the heat transfer coefficients (HTC) and the CHF compared to the polished baseline. Up to a 139.3% and a 164.0% increase in HTC was observed for mass fluxes of 230 kg/m<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>s and 463 kg/m<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>s respectively. Additionally, the FLSP surface increased the CHF by 22.1% and 11.6% respectively for mass fluxes of 230 kg/m<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>s and 463 kg/m<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>s. This work demonstrates the potential of FLSP functionalized stainless steel surfaces as a viable method for achieving substantial two-phase heat transfer enhancement.

articleTitle: Process Performance Interaction of In-Mold Electronics for Signal-Processing Applications
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: The use of in-mold electronics architectures opens new possibilities in the integration of wire harnesses and human-machine interfaces into body wall plastic for the automotive platform in conjunction with additive fabrication. Process-property interactions of additively fabricated functional circuits have not been sufficiently understood in the presence of thermoforming to make informed choices of process parameters based on known design and material parameters. This study examines the process-performance interactions of thermoformable substrates. Previous research endeavors have primarily concentrated on the advancement process development of stretchable conductive inks that are well-suited for thermoforming applications. In this paper, a test vehicle with stretchable conductive ink is used on the nScrypt platform, and the samples are cured using a conventional thermal oven. Thermoforming has been pursued at various temperatures and times. The electrical properties of conductive traces have been compared before and after thermoforming. The interaction of processes and performance on two substrates materials including polycarbonate and high-impact polystyrene has been compared. The thermoforming process has been validated by printing a functional circuit (integrator) whose data is compared to simulated data using LTspice.

articleTitle: Surace-Enhanced Two-Phase Cold Plate Designs for High Power Dissipation in Data Centers
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Multi-chip modules (MCMs) have become a popular architecture adopted in datacenters to collocate computation, memory, and communications. Their high-power density brings considerable challenges to the use of conventional air-cooling. Higher facility temperatures are preferred because they enable heat capture and reuse as well as simpler heat rejection architectures with low water usage such as dry cooling. This push for higher coolant temperature, alongside the elevated power density, has placed an even more stringent requirement on minimizing the chip junction-to-coolant thermal resistance. Here, we developed a high-performance, energy-efficient, and scalable thermal management approach based on two-phase cooling using R1233zd(E) refrigerant. The approach utilizes custom copper and aluminum microchannel evaporators capable of dissipating heat loads up to 1 kW over a 76 mm × 76 mm MCM-relevant footprint. The custom high-aspect-ratio (~10) microchannel (300~550 µm) evaporators are designed and fabricated using either electrical discharge machining or skiving. Experiments showed that a skived copper cold plate with 550 μm channel width, 375 μm fin width, and 5.25 mm fin height can reach a junction-to-coolant thermal resistance < 0.0083 K/W at a 1 kW heat load. We employ surface structuring to enhance the refrigerant flow boiling performance. Etched aluminum is used due to its promotion of nucleation and rewetting arising from its roughness and wickability. Etching was carried out on an EDM aluminum fin plate with 300 μm channel width, 250 μm fin width, and 2.3 mm fin height. We observed a 1.7× higher refrigerant flow boiling heat transfer coefficient improvement after surface structuring, achieving a thermal resistance of 0.0085 K/W at 1,1 kW heat load. Our work demonstrates that two-phase cooling, favored by low-profile MCMs, can enhance the power density at the server level.

articleTitle: Predicting cell-to-cell thermal runaway propagation in modular battery energy storage systems
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Battery energy storage systems (BESS) are playing a critical role in transportation electrification and the energy transition at large, powering electric vehicles (EVs) and enabling electrical grids to integrate a reliable supply of renewable energy. However, lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) used in BESS still pose an inherent risk for thermal runaway (TR) cell events and subsequent cell-to-cell fire propagation. Recent battery fire accidents worldwide call for the development of safer BESS, which requires a better understanding of TR trigger and propagation mechanisms. This work investigates temporal and spatial TR propagation behavior across multiple large-format pouch cells, leveraging a computational transient heat transfer model as well as single-cell and cell-to-cell TR experiments. This work predicts the TR propagation speed in a battery module with a large series of lithium-nickel-manganese-cobalt oxide (NMC) pouch cells, based on a case study representative of a commercially available modular BESS used in battery-assisted EV fast charging and stand-alone grid storage applications. Finally, the effect of the cell TR trigger temperature is investigated. Overall, this study furthers the system-level understating of TR dynamics, helping BESS developers implement safer BESS designs and pursue certifications that impart confidence that their designs adhere to industry standards.

articleTitle: Thermal Interface Material Analyzer Test Method Development for Gap Fillers: Simultaneous Thermal and Mechanical Stress Cycling
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Thermal management is essential for the performance of electronics in transportation, telecommunication and aerospace systems. Thermal interface materials provide the main pathway for heat dissipation between sources and sinks in advanced electronics and can be selected from a wide variety of material formats that are best suited for a given application. Traditionally, thermal interface materials have been subjected to reliability testing under static conditions to evaluate how extreme conditions impact the materials’ physical behavior and characteristics. However, there is an increasing need to analyze materials under dynamic conditions to better evaluate the performance of a material. Herein, we focus on using a set of non-curable and curable gap fillers to understand how dynamic testing using combined thermal and mechanic stress impacts the physical properties and characteristics of a material. A thermal interface material analyzer was used to subject non-curable and curable gap fillers to combined thermal and mechanical stress. A series of test methods using the thermal interface material analyzer was developed to fundamentally understand how varied temperatures and bond line thicknesses coupled with mechanical strain impacts the performance of the gap filler. A set of non-curable gap fillers were examined with two sets of gaps, large (<2000 µm) and thin (<1000 µm) bond line thickness for ten cycles. The non-curable gap fillers were subjected to temperatures ranging from 23 to 70 degree Celsius while under varying strains of 0 to 25% from the nominal bond line of <2000 µm or <1000 µm gaps. Additionally, a series of test methods were developed to analyze a curable gap filler to understand the physical constraints while under compression and tension at elevated temperatures. Several strain rates were used to understand limitations surrounding the viscoelastic behavior. In return, the analyses give rise to test methods that can be used to assess the failure modes of gap fillers and help improve future generations of gap fillers.

articleTitle: Additively Manufactured Cold Plate with Internal Phase Separator for Hybrid Two-Phase Cooling
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: In the present work, a hybrid two-phase cooling system (HTPCS) was developed that integrated the benefits of both capillary-driven evaporation from wick structures and pumped two-phase cooling. The cold plate included eight heaters that were distributed equally on both sides of the cold plate. The evaporators were wick structures, and an individual heater was assigned to each evaporator wick. The main significances of the present study are (i) preventing the flooded evaporator wicks inside the cold plate by a phase separator inside the cold plate, and (ii) fabricating the entire cold plate through one single additive manufacturing (AM) process. The cold plate was made of an aluminum alloy (AlSi10Mg) through direct metal laser sintering (DMLS) process. The cold plate was tested by utilizing the refrigerant R245fa as the working fluid, and the results were compared to those of a cold plate without evaporator wicks. The capillary-driven cold plate equipped with a phase separator operated from 456 to 468 W/cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">I. 2</sup>, achieved a remarkably uniform thermal resistance as low as 0.15 to 0.20 K-cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>/W, while operating within a low pumping power below 0.3 W. In comparison, the plain cold plate (i.e., without evaporator wicks) operated up to 150 W/cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> with a broad range of measured thermal resistances, spanning from 0.18 to 0.32 K-cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>/W. In addition to a remarkable improvement in the thermal performance of the cold plate achieved by avoiding flooded evaporators, fabricating the entire cold plate through one single AM process significantly reduces the complexity and cost associated with manufacturing current versions of cold plates used in HTPCSs. This streamlined manufacturing approach facilitates the commercialization of the proposed HTPCS as a promising technology for the thermal management of high-heat-density electronics.

articleTitle: Experimental and Numerical Study of Ultra-Thin Heat Pipes for thin and light segment laptops
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: The mobile electronic devices come in different form factor like tablets, convertibles, clamshells, dual display devices, etc. Based on current electronic miniaturization trends, there’s an increased demand for these form factors to be thin and light. To reduce system thickness without compromising on performance, there’s a thermal requirement to enhance heat-spreading solutions, especially for non-active systems or systems without a fan-cooled solution. Most heat spreaders used for these types of form factors are bare copper sheets. To increase the system performance, alternative thermal solutions whose conductivity outperforms the bare copper are required. Heat pipes can be considered a great fit since their thermal conductivity is hundreds of times higher than bare copper spreaders. In this paper, the detailed characterization of 0.6mm heat pipe has been done by experimentally measuring the thermal parameters like steady state Q-max, junction to heat pipe resistance, transient Q-max, thermal spreading resistance and spreading coefficient, etc. This paper will provide guidelines to help system thermal designers to decide on the ultra-thin heat pipe transient performance capabilities along with steady-state performance. A detailed experimental fixture has been designed to provide the required loading to the heat pipe at the heat source area. An extensive statistical study has been performed to showcase the part-to-part variation in the thermal parameters of ultra-thin heat pipe which will be helpful to predict the heat pipe performance for mass production. The heat pipe experimental thermal resistance (R) has been correlated to a computational model using computational fluid dynamics (CFD), specifically the Flotherm solver. Results shows that the 150 mm long, Dia 6 flattened to 0.6mm ultrathin heat pipe can carry a maximum heat of 6.5W in a steady state and can withstand 12W of transient power for 5sec.

articleTitle: Effects of Combined Isothermal Aging and Mechanical Cycling Exposures on the Mechanical Behavior of Lead-Free Solder Alloys
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Solder joints in electronic packaging can fail due to repeated changes in temperature and mechanical loading. For example, electronic components in a car engine compartment or a power plant turbine may experience cyclic loading from vibration, while also undergoing thermal cycling due to frequent power switching. The solder materials used to attach these components are subjected to cyclic stresses and strains caused by the mismatches of the coefficients of thermal expansion (CTE) of the materials in the assembly. Recent studies by the authors have examined the mechanical property degradation and microstructure evolution in lead-free solder alloys subjected to isothermal aging. In separate investigations, we have examined damage accumulation and mechanical property degradation in lead-free solders due to isothermal mechanical cycling. However, there is no prior research on the combined effects of high-temperature isothermal aging and mechanical cycling on the mechanical properties and microstructural evolution of lead-free solder alloys.In our current work, we are evaluating the changes in mechanical properties and microstructure that occur to solders subjected to the combined effects of both mechanical cycling induced damage and isothermal aging. In this paper, various sequential applications of mechanical cycling and isothermal aging have been considered. Cylindrical uniaxial samples of SAC305 lead-free solder alloy were prepared by solidification in glass tubes under a controlled reflow profile. The samples were then preconditioned by subjecting them to sequential application of isothermal mechanical cycling and isothermal aging. Both orders of application of cycling and aging were considered. In particular, the first set of samples were aged first, and then the aged samples were subjected to mechanical cycling. The second set of samples was subjected to the two exposures in the reverse order, with the samples first mechanical cycled at constant temperature, and then subjected to isothermal aging. The isothermal aging conditions included exposure to T = 125 °C for 20 days, while the mechanical cycling was performed at room temperature and a total strain range of ε = ±0.006 for various durations (e.g. 0, 50, 100, 200, and 300 cycles).After preconditioning by sequential application of mechanical cycling and aging, the mechanical behaviors of the specimens were evaluated using nanoindentation testing. In particular, the effects of the various types of preconditioning on the mechanical properties (elastic modulus, yield stress, Hardness) and creep behavior were characterized, and compared to the results for pristine specimens. The results were found to be extremely sensitive to the order of application of cycling and aging exposures. Finally, Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) was used to visualize the microstructures of the preconditioned specimens, and the observed microstructures were correlated to the mechanical behavior measurements.

articleTitle: Enhancement of Direct Liquid Jet Impingement Cooling through Laser-Fabricated Micro Pin-Fins on the Chip-Backside
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: With the ever-increasing use of computing power–for example for AI or in self-driving cars – the need for effective, efficient cooling of the used electronics components is also greater than ever. Both liquid-cooled heat sinks using structures to increase effective heat transfer and liquid jet impingement applied directly to the chip-backside have been shown to be promising approaches to highly efficient cooling. Avoiding the thermal bottleneck of thermal interface materials (TIMs) of structured heat sinks and improving the efficiency of direct liquid jet impingement further, this work experimentally demonstrates the effect of creating pin-fins directly on the chip-backside where coolant is applied. Using laser-ablation, pin fins of 50x50 µm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> and 100x100 µm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> footprint were fabricated on thermal test chips and tested for coolant (DI water) flow rate of up to 2.34 L/cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>min with inlet nozzle diameters of 340 µm and 580 µm. With this, an enhancement of the effective heat transfer coefficient of up to 44% at junction level and a maximum heat transfer of 9.09 W/cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>K, also at junction level were experimentally observed. Extrapolated to an equivalent flat chip-backside as coolant-chip interface, this would amount to a maximum convective heat transfer coefficient of 18.2 W/cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> or a 81% improvement over the heat transfer coefficient on the flat surface.

articleTitle: Design and Characterization of a Thermal Test Vehicle with Embedded Phase Change Material
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Phase change materials (PCMs) are a promising passive thermal management solution for electronics. However, their integration outside of the microelectronics package introduces additional thermal resistance between the PCM and the heat source, and makes them an non-viable solution for mobile devices due to spatial constraints. In this study, we integrate PCMs within the silicon chip in close proximity to the heat source. We fabricate thermal test vehicles (TTVs) with realistic mobile chip form factors to experimentally assess the performance of a silicon device incorporated with metallic PCM (specifically, a eutectic Bi/In/Sn alloy). The embedded PCM TTV demonstrates a noteworthy 2.3× extension in ‘on’ operational time during temperature cycling compared to an all-silicon benchmark TTV. Furthermore, it achieves a 10% reduction in the overall maximum temperature rise and a significant 47% decrease in temperature fluctuations during duty cycling. Degradation in the thermal performance of an embedded PCM TTV is observed due to increases in the PCM melt/freeze temperature. This phenomena occurs as result of incomplete phase transitions during the ‘on’ or ‘off’ portions of the duty cycle. However, temperature cycling for 5000 cycles confirms the stability of the embedded PCM for an extended operational period provided that complete melting/freezing occurs during each cycle. The substantial decrease in temperature fluctuations is crucial for enhancing device thermal stability, emphasizing the potential of embedded PCMs in ensuring reliable performance over extended operational periods.

articleTitle: An Evaluation of Microtube Array Density for Liquid Delivery in Pump-Assisted Capillary Loop Coolers
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Transportation electrification is accelerating the development of high-power-density electric drivetrain components. Such compact packages lead to a significant increase in the heat flux for power semiconductor devices and associated increases in thermal management costs. In this research, a flat plate pump-assisted capillary loop cooler (PACL) is investigated for power electronics device cooling applications. A porous wick at the heat source passively draws in liquid through a microtube array from a pumped parallel bypass flow through the compensation chamber. At high heat flux, the liquid evaporates at the wick surface, and vapor exits through the space between the microtube arrays. Coolers with two micro-tube array densities were fabricated, and their performance was experimentally measured using a flow loop. Cooler performance was found to be limited due to vapor flow resistance before reaching the wick’s capillary limit within experimental conditions. Nonetheless, a maximum heat flux of 650 W/cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> was achieved using water as a coolant with a 2 kPa pressure drop at a flow rate of 322 ml/min.

articleTitle: Unveiling the Dual Limits of Critical Heat Flux and Implications for Immersion Cooling
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Rising electronics power density has led to the adoption of immersion cooling as a thermal management strategy for next generation chips. However, immersion cooling is plagued by the critical heat flux (CHF) limit, which dictates the maximum heat transfer from a surface. Following its discovery in 1934 by Nukiyama, two explanations, namely the hydrodynamic instability theory introduced by Kutateladze in 1948 and established by Zuber in 1959, and the evaporation momentum theory conceptualized by Steinchen and Sefiane in 1996 and formalized by Kandlikar in 2001, have hitherto predicted a similar CHF limit (~ 100 W/cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> for water on a copper surface) despite hinging on contrasting physical phenomena. Here, we show through rigorous experimental and analytical investigation of boiling using liquids with diverse thermophysical properties and planar heater surfaces representing 44 unique experimental conditions, that the critical heat flux limit due to evaporation momentum (CHF<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">EM</inf>) is approximately four times higher than the hydrodynamic instability limit (CHF<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">HI</inf>) predicted by Zuber. Remarkably, this elevated CHF<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">EM</inf> becomes manifest only when the hydrodynamics of liquid and vapor flow above the heater surface are fully stabilized. Our experiments demonstrate the existence of these two asymptotic limits governed by hydrodynamic and surface limitations, respectively, depending on hydrodynamic flow conditions above the heater surface such that the ratio CHF/CHF<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">EM</inf> ranges from 0.2 to 1 across all examined fluids. Evaporation momentum theory encompasses the force balance on a bubble, which is evidenced in our experiments showing the presence of nucleating bubbles even as the surface heat flux approaches CHF. Further, a theoretical model is developed to predict CHF based on the single bubble assumption, and closely matches experimental data. Unlike previous assumptions, we find that the effect of gravity is negligible. This work could provide guidelines for development of surface topologies suitable for immersion cooling.

articleTitle: Pseudo-boiling of CO2 inside a parallel-flow microchannel and an array of micro jets impingement device
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: A parallel-flow microchannel and an array of micro-jets impingement device with carbon dioxide (CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>) were heated variably and pressurized above the critical point (31.05 °C, 7.39 MPa), in order to characterize the heat transfer process during pseudo-boiling. Inner surface temperatures were measured with resistance temperature detectors (RTDs) embedded inside the surface. Heat transfer coefficients were calculated both during the pseudo-boiling condition and before and after pseudo-boiling. A pseudo-boiling mass quality, x<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">pb</inf>, is proposed that provides an account, pertinent to the heat transfer coefficient, of the transition across the region affected by the Widom line, assuming values between 0 and 1, corresponding to the borders of the pseudo-boiling regions. The development of x<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">pb</inf> required quantifying the specific enthalpy change through the pseudocritical region, systematically obtained using a pertinent equation of state. A dimensionless pseudo-boiling heat transfer coefficient enhancement coefficient, E=h<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">pb</inf>/h<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">l</inf>, was then proposed and examined as a function of the mass quality. (h<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">pb</inf> is the heat transfer coefficient in the pseudo boiling region and h<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">l</inf> is the heat transfer coefficient of the single-phase liquid-like region.) The usefulness of the pseudocritical mass quality to reveal the effect of the transition across the Widom line was then demonstrated based on experimental results obtained with CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>. The results were then compared for parallel-flow microchannel and micro-jets impingement device, and discussed accordingly.The experiments were conducted at a range of heat fluxes from 35-60 W/cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> with a mass flux from 3200-5500 kg/m<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>.sec. The parallel-flow microchannel had a rectangular heater with a dimension of 5.84 mm×0.89 mm. The micro-jets impingement device had a serpentine-shaped heater with a total surface area of 4.88×10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-6</sup> m<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>. For these configurations of parallel-flow microchannel and micro-jets impingement devices, the experiments were conducted for reduced pressure, P<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">R</inf>, from 1.04 to 1.2. The heat transfer enhancement coefficient, E, was found to reach a maximum value of ~1.5 in the case of parallel-flow microchannel at 7.9 MPa and a mass quality of x<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">pb</inf>=0.938, attributed to the interplay between the more heated fluid adjacent to the heat transfer surface and the pre-transition bulk fluid. For the micro-jets impingement device, the effect of x<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">pb</inf> was somewhat less pronounced. The heat transfer coefficient enhancement was found to be fairly stable, hovering between 0.8 and 1.3, with mass quality, x<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">pb</inf>, which can be attributed to the effect of the interplay between the jets, the fountain effect, and somewhat uniform temperature all across the heater.

articleTitle: A Research on High Speed Signal Integrity Design Optimal for Immersion Cooled Server
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: With the rapid growth of new applications powered by artificial intelligence (AI), especially recent Artificial Intelligence Generated Content (AIGC) where large models used with massive data analyzed and processed through high thermal design power (TDP) GPUs and CPUs, the conventional air cooling solutions are trending to hit the bottleneck. Recent research and engineering pilot cases in ecosystem have proved the feasibility of immersion cooling technology implementation in data center, but IT equipment design, especially the server to achieve high design quality for the commercial deployment in immersion cooling environment, deserves a thorough research across ingredients of the whole system with solid engineering results. Signal integrity (SI) is one of critical ingredients for a high-quality server design optimal for the immersion cooling environment where the electrical characteristics of high-speed signals are subject to the variations of impedance, insertion loss and so on, which may eventually result in a failed eye diagram and signal attenuation out of spec. The thorough SI research introduced in this paper includes the deviation of coolant select, signal integrity contrast test of air-cooled and immersion-cooled environments, simulation accuracy calibrated with engineering validation results, etc. Key takeaways are concluded from this research that the high-speed signals including PCIe 5.0 and DDR5 signals routed through stripline way in the print circuit board (PCB) in the immersion cooled environment is almost identical to air cooled counterpart, while the signals routed through microstrip way are with big differences mainly due to dialectic constants of coolant vs. air. The impedance of microstrip signals in immersion cooling environment is 4 to 8 Ω lower than air cooled environment. The insertion loss of microstrip signals is basically 0.03 to 0.44 dB per inch at 16 GHz lower than air cooled environment at the same frequency. Higher frequency, bigger delta insertion loss. Following the research results of above, we’ve built an immersion cooling reference solution optimal for high-speed signal integrity design, that’s contributed to a successful commercial immersion cooled server deployment. The results of electric validation (EV) tests have further proved solution accuracy with less than 10% variation signal margin within spec requirements, compared to its air-cooled counterpart.

articleTitle: Experimental and Numerical study of thin Vapor chambers for dual heat sources in gaming notebooks
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: The semiconductor industry has rapidly grown in the past two decades and laptop-based form factors are on the steep rise. With the increase in system-level challenges like minimization of system thickness, decreased PCB (Printed Circuit Boards) real estate, more space for high-speed antenna, etc., the space available to manage heat is becoming a major challenge. To overcome these challenges, the requirement for more efficient and enhanced cooling technology is increased. One of the most demanded form factors is thin and light gaming systems, where the power consumption of the CPU (Central Processing Unit) is higher than typical laptops to provide high performance. For a top-notch gaming experience in terms of system form factor, speed, performance, and graphics, gaming systems need to be thinner and require higher power consumption in CPU and GPU (Graphics Processing Unit). The thermal solution for gaming devices should be capable of performing efficiently with dual heat sources. For such applications, typically thicker heat pipes of thickness 2 mm with complex routing covering CPU and GPU have been used. The thickness of the thermal solution is one of the major parameters that decide the system base thickness. To enable thin and light gaming devices there is a requirement for a thermal solution that is thinner (less than 2 mm) and provide better spreading than typically used heat pipes. Vapor chambers are efficient thermal solutions as its steady state and transient performance has been proven efficient in past research in low thickness profiles. In this paper, we are addressing the challenge of dual heat source cooling by characterizing 1.5mm thick Vapor chamber for steady state scenarios. A complete Vapor chamber loading fixture and power sequencing tool have been developed for the characterization activity. The thermal parameters studied in this paper are selected based on the real notebook constraints. A detailed experimental study has been performed to measure the critical thermal parameters like - maximum heat-carrying capability in steady state (Q-max), inplane spreading resistance, junction to spreader resistance, and. A correlated CFD (Computational Fluid Dynamics) model of a Vapor chamber using Flotherm ® is also being discussed and validated with test results. Results show that gaming systems that require more than 80W of dual source power can be efficiently cooled by a Vapor chamber of thickness 1.5mm.

articleTitle: 3D modeling and mitigation strategies in the thermal runaway of single-cell and modular Lithium-ion batteries architectures
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: As the adaptation of Lithium (Li) ion batteries (LIBs) in energy storage systems is becoming more prevalent by the day, the issue of safe and environmentally responsible design, installation, and operation of these batteries is posing a rapidly growing challenge. It is imperative to develop realistic multi-physics and multi-scale models that are not just useful for analyzing the thermal runaway (TR) events at the single-cell level but also modular LIB designs. This needs to be accompanied by the development of easier-to-follow empirical rules and straightforward analytical models as our knowledge of TR events grows over time. The unpredictable nature of TR events and the grave fire and explosion dangers that are particularly associated with violent TR events at the modular level require employing large-scale real-time evaluation of these events as well. Although more innovative battery health indicators are being developed and employed, it is still very challenging to arrest catastrophic TR events in time. The paper herein reports some recent development in advanced modeling and experimental approaches holistically. The challenges and possibilities of different active and passive thermal management strategies are also critically elaborated for LIB modular designs.

articleTitle: Repairability of Additively Printed Circuits Using Sustainable Aqueous-Based Silver Nanoparticle Ink on Polyimide Substrates
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: The electronics industry is focusing on sustainable processes with a reduced carbon footprint. The emergence of water-based low-impact waste inks for additive circuits poses an opportunity for the reduction or elimination of high-impact waste streams. This transition has led to the creation of antennas for mass-produced consumer electronics and the development of sensor components for the Internet of Things (IoT). Aerosol jet printing has been demonstrated for fabricating 3D structures on a micron scale, and its versatility has spurred extensive research. This paper focuses on the study of the performance and process-property interactions of novel water-based materials in realized circuits, a domain that remains unexplored. The focus is on understanding the repairability of these circuits, which is crucial for envisioning their long-term applicability and sustainability. A progressive approach involving computer-aided design, additive printing of various layers of metallization and electrically conductive adhesive, performance testing using frequency response, and repair of attached components was undertaken. The study has been able to identify key parameters and techniques that can optimize the attachment process, ensuring the durability and reliability of the realized circuits. The findings of this work would enable further advancements in the field, fostering the development of eco-friendly electronic solutions with a minimized environmental footprint. This study underscores the viability of water-based inks in flexible hybrid electronics and elucidates pathways to enhance their repairability, marking a significant milestone toward a green and sustainable electronics industry.

Author Keywords: electrically conductive adhesive SMD attachment process

articleTitle: Acoustics Analysis of Air and Hybrid Cooled Data Center
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Due to advancements in technology nodes, the processor power and heat density is ramping up exponentially to meet users' and computational demands. Air cooling has been a traditional approach for thermal management for systems in the data center where conditioned air is provided from data center mechanical systems to the cold aisles. Server fans are used to facilitate the airflow through IT system heatsinks to remove heat from microprocessors. As a result of increased microprocessor energy consumption and the end of Moore's Law, the thermal margin is shrinking to maintain the required junction temperature limits. Data center operators are compelled to use lower inlet temperatures and higher flow rates to meet the thermal requirements and increase the capacity of heat exchangers. Increased flow rates have introduced additional fans, increasing noise levels of operating data centers. Primarily data center noise sources are the servers' fans, network equipment, heat exchangers (CRAC, CRAH, Rear-door HX, In-row cooler, Sidecar HX, rack mount HX, etc.), and tiles. Due to increased noise levels, data center operators must be aware of and follow OSHA guidelines for hearing protection.This paper estimates the acoustics from server fans and heat exchangers by analytical method, simulation with ray tracing method, and validation to quantify the effect of noise in a standard data center environment with an HPC POD consisting of multiple servers, racks, and aisle containment. Generated noise is mapped with servers as noise sources and the background noises with experimental measurements. Server-level noise calculations are performed analytically, numerically, and validated experimentally prior to the case studies in the data center. The noise level is expressed in terms of the Sound Power Level (SWL) and Sound Pressure Level (SPL) for the source and measurements. The case studies in the data center are experimentally validated for pure air-cooled and hybrid (air and liquid) cooled environments separately when Liquid -to-Air (L2A) heat exchangers are placed and operated inside the data center. The baseline case is considered for the 100% air-cooled environment. Results are presented for varying the airflow requirement per server for the cooling demand of air-cooled vs. liquid-cooled components when there is a cooling transition from 100% air to partial air-liquid hybrid cooling. The outcomes of this paper will be highly beneficial in finding the limits for the operation of servers and heat exchangers (in terms of temperature, flow rate, and humidity) and establishing safety guidelines for noise reduction in air and hybrid-cooled data center environments.

articleTitle: Effect of Micro-channel Cross-section and Coolant Pressure on Two-Phase Cooling
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Pumping a dielectric coolant cooling through micron-scale cavities is a promising technology for high-power three-dimensional (3D) integrated packages. But its development is limited due to lack of high fidelity computationally efficient thermal models that are required for assessing the performance for different cooling designs and under varied operating conditions. In this work, a high fidelity Eulerian multiphase model, previously developed and validated by the author, was applied to study the effects of micro-channel cross-section and coolant pressure on two-phase cooling. Results indicated that compared to uniform cross-section microchannels, expanding channels help reduce the pressure gradient along the microchannel and thereby, reduce the saturation and heated surface temperature variability along the channel. Moreover, inlet orifices help with coolant flashing resulting in reduced convective thermal resistance and wall superheat near the channel inlet.

articleTitle: Accelerated Testing of Thermal Grease Degradation: Combined Thermal Gradients and Forced Mechanical Cycling
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: To enable higher computational power and speed with a smaller footprint, an increased number of semiconductor chips are packaged into smaller areas within electronic packages resulting in high heat flux densities. To dissipate heat efficiently and keep the junction level temperatures below a certain threshold required for reliability, thermal interface materials (TIMs) are leveraged at various interfaces within the electronics package. However, most TIMs, in particular thermal greases, degrade with time due to frequent powering on and off of the device and the associated thermal and thermomechanical cycling. Specifically, the material either flows out from the interfacial region (i.e., pump out failure) or the "phases" separate (for example, the high thermal conductivity filler particles separate from the polymer matrix or matrix dries out). Typical power cycling experiments designed to mimic operational conditions require very long experiment times. Inspired by previous accelerated test systems, in this work, we develop an accelerated testing facility with forced mechanical cycling using a high-precision linear stage, in addition to heat flux control, to induce degradation at faster rates. Specifically, we designed and built an experimental setup capable of squeezing thermal greases at a constant rate until a fixed pressure is achieved. This facilitates squeezing the TIM at controlled rates to specified pressures to achieve different bondline thicknesses (BLTs). Then for mechanical cycling, the BLT is perturbed with controlled amplitudes and rates of displacement. Throughout the cycling, controlled temperature gradients are established using a custom-designed heater (that enables simultaneous heating and thermal imaging) and a forced convection heat sink. Here, we evaluate the degradation of a commercially available thermal grease subjected to input heat flux of 6.1 W cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">−2</sup> and average squeezing rate of 60 µm/s. To quantify the evolution of the thermal resistance and local variations in the thermal resistance, steady-state infrared thermal maps are taken at fixed intervals during the mechanical cycling with controlled temperature gradients across the system. The initial experimental results suggest that thermal grease degrades due to void formation within 6 hours when mechanically cycled, whereas a traditional power cycling test takes several days to induce degradation. More research is needed to understand how the mechanisms that lead to failure in accelerated testing are related to degradation observed in application.

articleTitle: Important factors in the design of systems containing a MEMS sensor and ASIC in relation to a variable temperature environment
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: The integrated capacitive analog readout circuit's characteristics are presented in this work through a static analysis for a broad range of operating temperatures. It presents and discusses a comparison of identical test-benches for multiple application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs). Die-package interconnections of the ASIC inputs were removed from a single test setup in order to expand the comparison. As a result, the package and test board have no further effect. The conducted analysis determines how temperature affects observed signal noise levels and the temperature-relation of the ASIC operating consistency. The mentioned topics include the prospective continuation of practical studies on the heat sensitivity of the ASIC functioning and the implications of the analysis offered.This paper presents extension of research on noise presents in analog ASIC devices and its influence on ADC readout digital values corresponding to capacitance of MEMS sensor. The new two additional specimens of ASIC have been tested and results have been compared to previously collected and discussed data.

articleTitle: Touch Temperature Safety Standards and their Impact on Server Design
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: High server heat loads result in excessive exhaust air and surface temperatures for given server airflows. Increasing surface temperatures are restricted by safety standards that govern how hot surfaces can be such that they can be safely handled. Handling of hot surfaces and components must be considered as part of the server design process as parts in the rear of the server, facing into the hot aisle, often need to be serviced during operation. This paper will focus on reviewing trends in server and data center temperature and air flow as well as the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) touch safety standards and requirements. This paper will also discuss a server design that highlights how caloric analyses of air heating through the server can lead to a significant under-prediction of surface temperatures on touch points and surfaces due to non-uniform airflow and heating within the server. This paper also seeks to help educate the community on the importance of touch safety standards and how such standards can significantly impact server design and potentially limit the ability to lower fan speeds to improve energy and air usage in servers and data centers.

articleTitle: Investigation of the Effects of Sustained High-Temperature on the Reliability of Lead-Free Solder Joint Assemblies in Vibration
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Solder joints are one of the critical package elements in electronic assemblies. Electronics in automotive applications may be installed on-engine, on-transmission in the wheel well in front of the firewall. Electronics in automotive applications may be exposed to high temperatures in the vicinity of +150°C in addition to high strain rates from road vibration. Strain rates may range from 1 to 100 per sec. Prior work on vibration reliability in harsh environments has focused on the use of linear elastic models for solder interconnects. Models for the assessment of damage accrual for solder interconnects at high strain rates are scarce. In this paper, specifically, doped solder alloys have been examined in package format by balling packages with SAC-Q solder for the study of vibration reliability models at high operation temperatures. CABGA208 Package-PCB assemblies were prepared with SAC-Q solder in JEDEC JESD22-B111A format. PCB-Package assemblies were tested to failure under vibration loads of 5g and 10g, and at different ambient test temperatures up to 150°C. FE analysis is carried out for harmonic vibration loading on PCB-Package assemblies under different conditions. Energy based life prediction model is established using characteristic lives and accumulated plastic work densities.

articleTitle: Image driven deep learning based compact model to predict critical heat flux in direct immersion cooling via pool boiling
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: This paper introduces a concise model, based on convolutional neural networks (CNNs), to predict the performance of two-phase boiling heat transfer systems by leveraging data acquired through high-speed visualization techniques. The proposed approach utilizes high-speed digital imaging to meticulously capture and analyze bubble behavior on a heating component. Through this, a quantitative relationship is established between physical data and visual patterns, offering detailed insights into dynamic parameters such as bubble growth, departure, coalescence, and the static parameter of bubble diameter. The Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) is trained using visual patterns and physical data obtained from the visualization technique. Two distinct frameworks are employed for training: the first framework (A1) deploys Mask-R-CNN to extract physical data from images and utilizes a machine learning model trained on experimental data for interpolation. The second framework (A2) focuses on characteristic categorization, classifying test images into specific heat flux categories based solely on visual patterns derived from convolution operations. The study aims to quantify the relative weights assigned to the categorization and interpolation algorithms. Furthermore, this research endeavors to tackle a critical challenge encountered by AI models which is quantification of similarity in the training data to ensure optimal prediction accuracy.

articleTitle: Investigation of Flow and Thermal Performance in a Non-uniform Channel Pulsating Heat Pipe Additively Manufactured from High-temperature Resin
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Pulsating heat pipes (PHPs) have garnered significant attention in contemporary two-phase passive heat transfer devices owing to their remarkable attributes in bolstering energy efficiency and thermal management. This study presents an experimental evaluation of the thermal performance of 3D-printed closed-loop PHP with two turns made from Formlab's high-temperature resin using Stereolithography (SLA) technology. Unlike prior non-uniform channel designs, this PHP introduces a distinctive configuration, with heating at the center and cooling at the ends. To achieve the anticipated performance enhancements associated with non-uniform channel PHPs heated at one end and cooled at the other, the PHP incorporates changes in channel width at both the middle and ends of the device. Electric heating of up to 7 W is applied to the PHP's evaporator area, while cooling blocks were employed at both ends in the condenser areas maintaining a constant temperature of 10 °C. Employing acetone as the working fluid because of its low startup power, the study conducts tests in both horizontal and vertical orientations. The vertical orientation considerably outperforms the uncharged baseline by achieving significantly lower thermal resistance for all input powers up to 6.5 W, with startup occurring at around 4 W. This orientation can reduce the thermal resistance to as low as 12.38 K W<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-1</sup> compared to the 20.06 K W<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-1</sup> for the uncharged PHP. The PHP with horizontal orientation fails to start up within this power input range due to the absence of gravitational force. This study indicates that there is still a minimum number of turns required to make PHP operable in all orientations, in addition to the incorporation of non-uniform channel design.

articleTitle: Flow Boiling Heat Transfer Improvement of PF-5060 Using Femtosecond Laser Surface Processed Aluminum
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: This study investigates flow boiling enhancement using functionalized 6061 aluminum surfaces using PF-5060 as a working fluid. Femtosecond laser surface processing (FLSP) is utilized to create self-organized quasi-periodic micro- and nano-scale structures. The FLSP technique uses a single step creating multiscale structures with nanoscale features. These multiscale structures create additional nucleation sites while also increasing the surface area for fluid interaction. One FLSP surface was produced to investigate the effects surface processing has on heat transfer performance. The FLSP surface was tested up to critical heat flux (CHF) with two inlet temperatures and compared to a polished surface baseline to determine heat transfer improvement and flow stability. Results show enhanced performance for FLSP compared to the polished surfaces with a maximum increase in heat transfer coefficient of 270%. The FLSP surface also reduces temperature overshoot by a maximum of 60% when compared to a polished surface. Pressure oscillations were also reduced with the FLSP surface when compared to the polished surface. These results demonstrate how FLSP on an aluminum surface provides a solution for two phase heat transfer enhancement with increased flow stability of dielectric fluids.

articleTitle: Thermal Conductivity and Interface Strength Evolution of TIM-Copper with Temperature and Humidity Conditioning
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: A thermal interface material (TIM) with high bulk thermal conductivity is inserted between the FCBGA package and the heatsink to reduce the thermal resistance of the heat transfer path. Exposure to high humidity, temperature storage, and wide temperature extremes expected in automotive environments may result in interfacial damage, resulting in the initiation of cracks at the TIM-to-Copper interface, increased thermal resistance and thermal runaway of the device. The research objectives include the study of the effect of hygrothermal exposure and thermal cycling on the TIM-Cu interfaces, the effect of environmental exposure on the thermal conductivity of the interface, and the evolution of the fracture toughness of the interface with the time in the use-case scenario. Presently, there is lack of damage models for the prediction of TIM interface survivability and assessment of performance degradation. In this study, the bi-material samples are stored in a Hygrothermal test chamber for moisture absorption at three conditions - 60°C/C/60% RH and 85°C/85% RH. In addition, a separate set of samples has been kept in a thermal cycling chamber with a profile ranging from -40°C to 125°C for 50, 100, 200, 400, and 1000 automotive-grade thermal cycles. Both monotonic and Fatigue testing are conducted on all bi-material samples for the measurement of the mode-1 and mode-2 critical stress intensity factors and Paris’s Power Law Exponent. The thermal conductivity has been measured using a thermal interface tester. Moisture diffusivity, activation energy, and acceleration factors are investigated for hygrothermal exposure.

articleTitle: Hydrothermal characteristics of P2P loop with ribbed spiral channel in evaporator
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Hydrothermal performances of a P2P loop with its evaporator configured by the spiral ribbed channel with internal effusion using water as the working fluid are experimentally studied. Comparative thermal performances between two P2P loops with the spiral and the four-pass serpentine ribbed channels in evaporators are addressed. Between the two P2P loops, the boiling flow structure, phase-change heat transfer rates, and operating pressures with their attendant saturation temperatures in component level; as well as the thermodynamic cycles, overall thermal resistances, and the merit indices in system level are comparatively examined. Relative to the P2P loop with the serpentine ribbed passage in evaporator, Nusselt numbers in evaporator and condenser are elevated, and the coefficients of performance that accounts the combined effect of loop thermal resistance and total pumping power consumption are raised by 0.4-88% to shed light on the improved hydrothermal performances using the spiral ribbed effusion channel in evaporator.

articleTitle: Reliability of FPBGA Assemblies under Martian Cold Thermal Cycles
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: This paper presents new cryogenic thermal cycle test results on fine-pitch ball grid array (FPBGA) technologies for high-reliability applications. Several FPBGAs were assembled onto printed circuit boards for thermal cycle reliability evaluation. The FPGAs include CABGA 208, CTBGA 228, and CVBGA 360, with ball pitches of 0.8mm, 0.5mm, and 0.4mm, respectively. The reliability results are compared for two thermal cycle conditions with the same ΔT, but with either hot- or cold-biased maximum temperatures. In 2022, the effect of burn-in of the same FPBGAs on subsequent assembly reliability was presented. The thermal-cycle condition was hot biased in the range of - 40°C to +105°C with consideration for commercial applications.In the current work, we present similar results for cold-biased thermal shock cycle testing over the reverse temperature range of –105°C to +40°C closely representative of deep space Martian environment. This cycle has the same overall ΔT of 145°C, while switching the high and low temperature limits with respect to earlier testing for commercial use. Three thousand (3,000) cycles were performed on assembled FPBGAs. Reliability results for assembled CABGA 208 and other FPGAs are evaluated and compared under cold- and hot-biased cycling. Results were compared in Weibull plots for those with sufficient failures. In addition, failure analyses were performed by 3D non-destructive X-ray evaluation to determine if cracking condition could be identified for tailoring subsequent destructive analyses by dye-and-pry and optical micro-sectioning. Results with images showing the level of damages after 3000 cycles were also presented.

articleTitle: Thermal Performance Characteristic of Single-phase Immersion Cooling on Servers with Optimized Heatsink Design
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI), high performance computing (HPC), communication technology and cloud service has been requesting high performance of servers powered by CPU and GPU in data centers (DCs). In order to meet the commercial and industrial demand, the thermal design power (TDP) of both CPU and GPU has been rising from generation to generation due to constant increase on the core count, cache size and heat flux density. Intel XEON processor has reached 350W and Nvidia’s H100 GPU even up to 700W on TDP. This exposes huge challenges on system thermal design with traditional air-cooling solution under current boundary condition of heatsink keep out zone (KOZ), air flow and off-the-shelf heatsink technologies. Therefore, liquid cooling has more attention to address the thermal management challenges from increasing TDP of chips and rack power density in DCs. Among these novel liquid cooling solutions, the singlephase immersion cooling(1-PIC) has emerged due to the special advantages over air-cooling solution in terms of enhanced cooling capability, improved components operation reliability and optimal Power usage effectiveness (PUE).Tencent Cloud (Tencent) has huge amount deployment of servers in DCs globally to respond the demand of all walks of life and consumes huge electricity energy each year. In order to reduce carbon footprint and accomplish green and sustainable DC, one 1-PIC solution prototype with fluorochemical fluid is built to investigate the cooling performance and optimization for application in future. This paper presents both computational fluid dynamics (CFD) analysis and experimental investigation to study the thermal performance characteristic of 1-PIC on servers developed by Tencent on Intel Eagle Stream (EGS) platform. Thermal performance is characterized based on system level to represent the real operation scenarios. Meanwhile, this paper also describes the design of prototype tank, rework on servers for immersion, thermal interface material (TIM) selection and impact on thermal cooling performance from different heatsink design, fluid flowrate and fluid inlet temperature. It is demonstrated that 1-PIC solution could deliver better cooling capability and support higher TDP of CPU than traditional aircooling solution, which could be a promising cooling methodology for high-power server’s adoption in DCs.

articleTitle: Experimental Investigation on Single-phase Immersion Cooling Solution for Data Center Application
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: The continuous advancement of data centers (DCs) driven by the rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI), autonomous driving, edge computing and mobile internet search service has led to severe energy consumption concern globally. It impacts not only the design complexity and total cost of ownership (TCO) of DC but the realization of carbon peak and carbon neutrality (dual carbon) goals. In order to improve energy efficiency and meet the requirement for green and sustainable DC, it is critical to reduce total power consumption of DC to reach optimal Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE). Immersion cooling solution has emerged as a potential and prominent candidate to reduce PUE due to its advantages in terms of enhanced cooling capability, high rack power density and energy efficiency by submerging IT equipment into a pool of dielectric liquid.Baidu Inc (Baidu) has investigated experimentally the technical feasibility of single-phase immersion cooling solution for DC’s application and developed the Scorpio 5.0 immersion cooling rack solution (ICRS) to improve energy efficiency and sustainability of DC under collaboration with Intel. This paper demonstrates in detail the Scorpio 5.0 ICRS, specifically the design of tank, power supply unit (PSU), remote management control (RMC) and servers etc. as well as the experimental data on tank’s shock and vibration, thermal cooling performance, material compatibility and improvement on power consumption and CPU operation frequency. DC level analysis in terms of maintenance, PUE and TCO benefit are also addressed in this paper. According to typical DC operation, the Scorpio 5.0 ICRS could achieve PUE below 1.1, improve the TCO by 7% to 17% in five years operation, promote the computing capability of servers by 7.51% on SPECCPU rate and reduce unit servers power consumption by 30+W.The Scorpio 5.0 ICRS has been completely verified for pilot deployment and provides a technical reference for the application of immersion cooling in DC, which together with Intel Xeon processors not only empowers the construction and transformation of green DC but drives the development of a low carbon digital economy.

articleTitle: Fabrication and Thermal Characterization of Copper Nanowires (CuNWs) Thermal Interface Materials Tapes
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: High-performing thermal interface material (TIM) that exhibits both high thermal conductivity and high mechanical compliance is a crucial component in modern electronics. This paper specifically focuses on the fabrication and characterization of Copper Nanowires/Polydimethylsiloxane (CuNWs/PDMS) composites as a promising TIM. The first section of the paper discusses the shortcomings of existing fabrication methods for CuNWs and proposes a novel on-PCTE evaporative coating method. CuNWs and CuNWs/PDMS of 25-50 gm thick with NW diameter 0.1-0.25 gm and density 107-108 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-2</sup> were fabricated at a high yield rate. The second part focuses on the thermal characterization of CuNWs, highlighting the source of uncertainty in traditional measurement methods[6] and introducing an approach using TIM testers coupled with Infrared (IR) thermography. In the final section, the paper emphasizes the significance of minimizing dry contact resistance(~10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-4</sup> m<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>KW<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-1</sup>) in thermal resistance measurements of CuNWs, which have an expected thermal resistance of ~10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-6</sup> m<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>KW<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-1</sup>. The paper explores the application of gallium-based liquid metal (LM) to mitigate this issue. The results show promising advancements in characterizing low-resistance TIM materials and concluded that the CuNWs (or CuNWs/PDMS tape) have thermal resistance at least one order of magnitude smaller than 10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-5</sup> m<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>KW<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-1</sup>. Further investigation into the roughness and material of the LM-wetted surface should be done to improve LM-wetting condition and enhance measurement sensitivity.

articleTitle: System-Level Assessment of Green Refrigerant Replacements for Direct-to-Chip Two-Phase Cooling
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Thermal management in data centers presents significant challenges, particularly with high-power density chips pushing the boundaries of single-phase cooling systems. This has led to exploring two-phase cooling as a more effective thermal solution. With the anticipated phase-out of high Global Warming Potential (GWP) refrigerants such as R134a, the search for sustainable alternatives is paramount. Employing the Engineering Equation Solver (EES) and empirical correlations, this research rigorously assesses the performance of Hydrofluoroolefins (HFOs) R1234yf, R1234ze(E), and R515B compared to R134a in two-phase cooling systems. The study’s framework includes a detailed analysis of a system designed to support a cooling capacity of 180 kW, comprising three racks, each equipped with six Thermal Testing Vehicles (TTVs). Each TTV has four 2.5 kW heaters with a surface area of 2500 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> each, capable of reaching up to 10 kW. The investigation delves into various operational parameters, including saturation temperature, heat flux, and pressure drop to understand their influence on the system’s thermal performance. Furthermore, it highlights the importance of selecting medium-pressure refrigerants that harmoniously balance thermal performance with system compatibility. This approach significantly advances the goal of achieving environmentally sustainable cooling solutions in data centers. The research concluded that the suitability of the compared refrigerants for replacement depends on various factors, including system size and cost, offering a range of options for different data center needs. Hence, various green refrigerant replacements could be utilized in various systems.

articleTitle: Pulsed flash boiling for high heat flux electronics cooling
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: As demand for computing continues its rapid growth, the required digital processing capabilities necessitate more powerful devices and sophisticated thermal management techniques. Conventional electronic cooling technologies such as air and single-phase liquid cooling technologies are often inadequate for emerging applications due to their requirement of heat spreading to maximize the coolant contact area. We report a pressure-driven boiling approach, termed flash cooling, for thermal management of high-heat flux electronics. A significant innovation is that the operating fluid is flashed in pulses, facilitating higher pressure gradients within cycles. A closed-loop system is implemented, and methanol is used as the operating fluid. Experiments are reported with varying heat fluxes, flow rates and pulse cycle time until steady-periodic conditions were achieved. The heat flux varies from 0.2 W/mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> (125 W) to 1 W/mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> (625 W). The evaporator temperature is observed to be below 85 °C for heat fluxes up to 0.6 W/mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>. The key findings suggest that pulse cycle time is the most important control parameter that influences the operative phase-change regime. The maximum oscillations in evaporator temperature and evaporator outlet pressure are observed to be ± 3.5 °C and ± 9 kPa for 1 W/mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> heat flux. A major advantage of the pulsed flash cooling system is that the flow rates can be dynamically and precisely controlled near the heat source by varying the pulse cycle time without requiring system-level modifications, unlike conventional continuous flow single or two-phase cooling. This feature of flash cooling technology enables it to control the operating boiling regime, and as shown in experiments here, to recover from dry-out conditions.

articleTitle: Evaluating the Efficiency of Machine Learning Approaches for Predicting Solder Joint Characteristic Life under Isothermal Aging and Thermal Cycling Test Conditions
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
