abstract: This research studies the potential of Machine Learning (ML) algorithms for predicting the characteristic life (usually denoted in the literature as N<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">63</inf>) of solder joints under thermal cycling, after undergoing isothermal aging. Currently, the reliability of solder joints is estimated through a time-consuming combination of physical testing and empirical modeling. Existing modeling techniques often demand a diverse range of test conditions, making the process cumbersome. The approach proposed herein applies ML models for determining solder joint characteristic life under isothermal aging followed by thermal cycling tests. The data, consisting of 265 experiment test results, was sourced from comprehensive experiments conducted at Auburn University. The components utilized were Ball Grid Arrays with package sizes ranging from 19mm, 0.8mm pitch to 5mm, 0.4mm pitch. Test vehicles were aged for 0 weeks (without aging serving as baseline), 3 weeks, 6 months, 12 months, and 24 months at 25°C, 55°C, 85°C, and 125°C aging temperatures. The accelerated thermal cycling test profile was from -40°C to 125°C. The solder alloys used for the study were 98.5Sn-1.0Ag-0.5Cu (SAC105), 96.5Sn-3.0Ag-0.5Cu (SAC305), and 63Sn-37Pb (SnPb). The components were assembled on five different surface finishes: ENEPIG, ENIG, ImAg, ImSn, and SnPb. Following the tests, Weibull analysis was conducted to determine the characteristic life for each testing condition. Subsequently, ML models were trained and tested utilizing the derived characteristic life data. A comparison reveals that the characteristic life predicted by ML models closely matches that derived from test results via Weibull analysis, highlighting ML’s potential in this area. The findings suggest that ML offers a more efficient, cost-effective, and streamlined alternative for predicting the characteristic life of solder joints, and may have the potential to revolutionize current practices in the field.

articleTitle: Performance Comparison of Sustainable and Non-sustainable Silver Inks through a Printed Differentiator Circuit
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: The prior generation of additive printable inks used volatile organic solvent carriers. Water-based sustainable ink formulations, however, have emerged in response to the global focus on environmental sustainability and the pursuit of a circular economy that offers a variety of benefits to reduce electronics waste. Studies on the performance of sustainable inks in functional circuits are scarce. This paper studies component attachment and performance of functional circuits fabricated on the aerosol jet printer (AJP) platform with water-based silver nanoparticle (sustainable) ink and solvent-based (non-sustainable) ink. Electrical performance of sustainable and non-sustainable inks has been compared in functional circuits. Interconnection is achieved using electrically conductive adhesives (ECA) in both circuits. Electrical performance of the circuit has been characterized through the measurements of frequency response of magnitude and phase. Several test cases have been run for various operating frequencies. The results show the viability of realizing operational circuits using sustainable ink for additive printing of circuits on the aerosol-jet platform.

articleTitle: Heat Transfer Enhancement for Direct-on-Chip Impingement Jet Cooling using Variable Micro Pin Fins and Tapered Impingement Cavity
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Although jet impingement cooling with microscale pin fins array demonstrates excellent heat transfer capabilities, it requires optimization by a trade-off between maximizing heat transfer and minimizing pressure drop. The present study focusses on minimizing pressure drop and improving surface temperature uniformity by considering fins with variable height and tapered impingement cavity over the traditional setup with uniform fins and impingement cavity. Numerical investigations are conducted to highlight the underlying mechanism that reduces the pressure drop for non-uniform fins and tapered cavity. Among the different cases investigated, the non-uniform fins with tapered cavity are able to combine the benefits of both - low pressure drop like in the case of bare flat surface and low thermal resistance like in the case of uniform fins. The best performing case has a decreased pressure drop of nearly 40% and it still manages to achieve a reduction of 45.4% in thermal resistance along with better surface temperature uniformity. The analysis thoroughly compares all configurations to conclude non-uniform fins considerably outperforms in heat transfer and temperature uniformity.

articleTitle: Maximizing Cooling Potential: A Step-by-Step Guide to Commissioning Liquid-Cooled Data Centers
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: The escalating computational demands driven by artificial intelligence, machine learning, and the Internet of Things (IoT) have resulted in a remarkable upsurge in transistor density within high-end CPUs and GPUs. Consequently, this surge has led to higher thermal dissipation power (TDP) and increased heat flux, necessitating the adoption of advanced cooling methods to minimize thermal resistance and enhance cooling efficiency. Among these technologies, cold plate-based liquid cooling directly applied to the chip has emerged as a preferred option for electronic cooling due to its effectiveness and cost-efficiency. A crucial prerequisite before deploying this technology in a data center is to establish a proper commissioning procedure, which encompasses the commissioning of the Coolant Distribution Unit (CDU), row and rack manifolds, and the cooling loops. This procedure ensures that the liquid-cooled data center facility is fully functional and capable of operating as intended. Commissioning involves functional steps such as the inspection of components and the functional capabilities of all the instruments. This study provides comprehensive guidance on the commissioning procedure that needs to be followed during the deployment of a liquid-cooled data center.

articleTitle: Characterizing Critical Interfaces in a Spacebourne Avionics Unit: Comprehensive Thermal Testing and Model Correlation
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: In our previous work, "Bi-modal Thermal Design of a Spacebourne Rotorcraft Avionics Unit", we presented a comprehensive analysis of preliminary thermal assumptions guided by the harsh design constraints imposed by a high-powered avionics unit that eschews conventional spacecraft design techniques. The paper introduced our primary bottleneck at various interfaces, and detailed pressure paper experiments to estimate thermal analysis inputs and provide a comprehensive thermal design. This paper will further investigate those assumptions by presenting a thorough test campaign and model correlation study that characterizes discrete interfaces of interest using a flight-like prototype.

articleTitle: Thermal Behavior and Visualization of Electrochemical Additive Manufactured Copper Lattice Wicks in a Flat Heat Pipe
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: This study investigates the thermal-hydraulic performance of electrochemical additive manufactured (ECAM) copper wicks in the context of a flat heat pipe during operation. Compared to other metal additive technologies (e.g., laser powder bed fusion), the ECAM fabrication technology employed here enables the creation of significantly smaller and more well-defined geometries and features, resulting in wicks that generate higher capillary pressure while simultaneously being more permeable. Three strut-based body-centered cubic (BCC) lattice wicks were fabricated with strut diameters of approximately 139 µm. The porosities of the wicks (43%, 56.5%, and 67.7%) were varied by altering the BCC unit-cell size. Heat was applied at the evaporator end using a flat ceramic heater (1.9 x 1.9 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>). The condenser end was in contact with a 2.5 x 1.9 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> water block for cooling. The wick samples were assembled with an acrylic cover for visualization purposes. The thermal performance of HFE-7100 as the working fluid was investigated. Various fluid loadings were analyzed to obtain the optimum filling ratio that achieved the lowest total thermal resistance. The effect of varying the heat pipe angle (0⁰, 30⁰, 60⁰, and 90⁰) was examined. Comparisons are made to different conventional and unconventional wick types listed in the literature and show that the proposed wick designs and manufacturing techniques can improve the thermal-hydraulic performance of heat pipes.

articleTitle: Revolutionizing Electronic Cooling: Ultra-short-pulsed Laser Processed Surfaces in Wick-Free Vapor Chambers
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: In the ever-evolving landscape of modern high-power electronics, efficient thermal management solutions play a pivotal role in determining device performance and longevity. Vapor chambers have long been heralded as effective tools for managing high heat-flux scenarios. Traditionally, vapor chambers are wick-lined; however, they have some inherent limitations. These chambers rely on wick structures to resupply liquid to the evaporator, where the fluid undergoes vaporization due to the heat generated by the electronic components. While the effectiveness of vapor chambers has been demonstrated, wicklined vapor chambers face challenges, such as the capillary limit, pore blocking, and added weight. To address these limitations, researchers have turned to wick-free vapor chambers (WFVC). These systems eliminate the need for wick structures, relying instead on the surface properties of the evaporator and condenser surfaces to drive liquid flow. The success of wick-free vapor chambers hinges on the skin-deep surface microstructures present on these surfaces and wettability patterning. In this study, we explore wick-free vapor chambers equipped with uniformly superhydrophilic evaporators created through ultra-short pulsed laser surface processing (ULSP), utilizing two different laser processing methods to functionalize the evaporators. Our findings reveal that ULSP surfaces used in wick-free vapor chambers produce VC thermal resistances as low as 0.12 K/W. What sets the present approach apart is the absence of surface wettability patterning, unlike previous wettability-patterned vapor chambers that combined distributed philic and phobic domains to move condensate as needed in the device, in turn improving performance, as quantified by thermal resistance.

articleTitle: Impact of Thermal Cycling on In-Mold Flexible Substrates Fabricated via Direct-Write Printing
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: In-mold electronics (IME) combines printed electronics with film insert molding in order to fabricate plastic-integrated electronic assemblies. This study investigates the effect of thermal cycling on the performance and reliability of in-mold flexible substrates created through direct-write printing techniques. A multifaceted exploration has been undertaken, encompassing the printing of conductive traces on thermoformable substrates using a direct-write platform, the attachment of passive components, including resistors, capacitors, and inductors, onto the printed conductive traces with Electrical Conductive Adhesives (ECA), thermoforming of the samples with the surface-mount components, quantification of the component performance pre and post thermoforming, and an in-depth exploration of the effect of thermal cycling on the thermoformed samples, spanning temperatures from -40°C to 85°C, over the course of 500 cycles. Process-property-performance interactions between these critical phases of manufacture and assembly of in-mold electronics have been examined. The effect of thermal cycling on electrical performance, mechanical resilience, and structural integrity has been quantified.

articleTitle: Thermal and Mechanical Analysis of Embedded Liquid Cooling with Microchannel and Pin-fin Structures
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Embedded liquid cooling is expected to be a prominent thermal solution for high performance device with advanced packaging such as 3D ICs. It offers significantly high heat transfer performance due to its micro-structured cooling path in close proximity to the active device. In the concept of embedded liquid cooling, electrical interconnect between vertically stacked chip is enabled by Through Silicon Vias (TSV) integrated inside of the microchannel/pin-fin. Therefore, such microstructures play important role not only for the enhancement of heat dissipation but also for the reliability of the device. However, mechanical stress durability of delicate micro-structure becomes serious issues during package assembly process with temperature change. It is crucial to evaluate the mechanical characteristics of embedded cooling system while maintaining the high thermal performance. This paper presents the comprehensive study of two types of embedded cooling structures-microchannel and micro pin-fin, in terms of the thermomechanical and the thermo-hydraulic characteristics. Full-scale three-dimensional simulation model is developed for thermomechanical and Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) analysis to investigate the above-mentioned performances. For thermomechanical analysis, stress distribution and the warpage of the chip are evaluated for each cooling structures. Also, maximum stress on interconnection layer between chip-to-chip, as well as chip-to-substrate are investigated. For thermo-hydraulic analysis, characteristics such as thermal resistance, average chip temperature, pressure drop are compared. Based on the simulation results, novel design with hybrid structure of microchannel and pin-fin are proposed to achieve balanced performance for both mechanical and thermal aspects. By integrating the benefits of microchannel and pin-fin structures, it is numerically demonstrated to achieve high heat transfer and moderate pressure drop while maintaining sufficient mechanical reliability simultaneously.

articleTitle: Interpretable Machine Learning Models Can Outperform Statistical Models in Solder Joint Reliability
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Weibull regression and the Cox proportional hazard model (Cox-PHM) are commonly employed for analyzing the solder joint reliability due to their simplicity and meaningful results. Recently, various machine learning (ML) models have been applied and shown similar or better performance than conventional approaches, yet they do not incur widespread adoption in reliability modeling because of their limited transparency and interpretability. In this research, we compare the predictive capabilities of Weibull regression and Cox-PHM with ML techniques (specifically, Random Survival Forests [RSF] and Gradient Boosting [GB]) using experimental data from an accelerated thermal cycling reliability test and calculating the concordance index (c-index) as an evaluation metric to assess the effectiveness of a model in predicting the sequence of failure times in the tests. The findings with our dataset showed that ML-based models have a similar performance with the traditional Weibull regression (c-index = 0.808), and GB can even outperform with a high c-index value of 0.848. The superior performance of ML models can be attributed to their capacity to capture nonlinearities and intricate relationships within the data. Additionally, we utilized feature importance scores to understand which factors/variables significantly influence the model's prediction. Such interpretable ML methods can provide clear insights into how models make predictions, thereby enhancing trust and the adoption of innovative ML techniques in electronics manufacturing.

articleTitle: Thermal Performance, Stability and Material Compatibility of a New Two-Phase Immersion Fluid
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Two-phase immersion cooling (2-PIC) is one of the leading new technologies for thermal management of server systems and electronic components used in data centers. 2-PIC can provide a significant reduction in energy and water consumption while enabling cooling of higher thermal design power (TDP) chips. One obstacle for wider adoption of 2-PIC has been the lack of dielectric fluids that meet all requirements. In this context, a new dielectric fluid, Opteon™ 2P50, has been proposed and demonstrated to have Global Warming Potential (GWP) of only 10, excellent dielectric and heat transfer properties according to recent publications. In this paper, additional aspects of this fluid are investigated. First, results of accelerated thermal stability tests of Opteon™ 2P50 and legacy fluids in the presence of typical contaminants, such as air, moisture, and plasticizers showed that the new fluid does not break down or generate acids even in temperatures nearly 100°C above its normal boiling point. Second, material compatibility evaluations of Opteon™ 2P50 with several common plastics, elastomers and metals showed excellent chemical compatibility. The potential impact of the presence of moisture and plasticizers on the dielectric properties of Opteon™ 2P50 was also explored and the data demonstrated the electrical insulation properties of the new fluid remain robust even when mixed with those contaminants. Furthermore, the authors investigated the thermal performance of several commercially available thermal interface materials (TIMs) in Opteon™ 2P50. The three thermal greases tested showed similar performance and slightly outperformed a 0.25 mm Indium foil.

articleTitle: Effect of Temperature and Humidity Conditioning on EMC-to-Substrate Interfacial Delamination Subjected to Monotonic and Fatigue Loading
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Epoxy molding compounds (EMCs) are used in electronic packaging to protect semiconductor chips and other internal components against mechanical and chemical stress, as well as heat and moisture. However, challenges arise from material mismatch and stress concentrations caused by metal traces, impacting the interface between the Epoxy mold compounds (EMC) and the substrate solder mask, leading to shear stresses. Over the operational life of semiconductor packages, these shear stresses may result in progressive delamination at the interface. Consequently, significant attention has been directed toward studies on adhesion between EMC and different packaging materials. The research objectives of the study include the investigation of the effect of hygrothermal exposure on the EMC- substrate interface, weight gain measurement of bi-material samples after hygrothermal exposure, investigation of the effect of thermal cycling on the EMC-Substrate Interface, and study of the fracture toughness values, the amplitude of the stress intensity factor for both hygrothermal and thermal cycling conditions. The bi-material samples have been fabricated and stored in a Hygrothermal test chamber for moisture absorption at two conditions - 60°C/60% RH and 85°C/85% RH. In addition, a separate batch of samples has been kept in a thermal cycling chamber with a profile ranging from -40°C to 125°C for 50, 100, 200, 400, and 1000 automotive-grade thermal cycles. Both Monotonic and Fatigue testing are conducted on all bi-material samples to measure the mode-1 and mode-2 critical stress intensity factors. Moisture diffusivity, activation energy, and acceleration factors are investigated for hygrothermal exposure.

articleTitle: High power thermal energy storage from ordered-pore additively manufactured phase-transforming nickel-titanium porous cubes
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Thermal buffering via phase change materials (PCMs) has been proposed as a method to reduce peak temperature in high power switching and pulsed power applications. To improve efficacy at peak temperature suppression, researchers have focused on developing high power and high capacity PCM-based thermofluidic component technologies, and in recent years, additive manufacturing has emerged as a promising fabrication technique for PCM-integrated components.To this end, a new thermal buffering component is proposed, based on additively manufactured porous cubes of nickel titanium (PCNT) exhibiting an above-ambient-temperature structural phase transition (Austenite finish temperature of 92 <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">o</sup>C). PCNT thermal buffering components exhibit unique thermal energy storage properties owing to their high latent heat (>150 MJ/m<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>) and high thermal conductivity (>12 Wm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-1</sup>K<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-1</sup>). The proposed thermal buffering architecture leverages the high thermal conductivity of PCNT and its ability to undergo a reversible phase transformation between austenite and martensite phases, which enables efficient energy storage and release under the appropriate working fluid temperatures.The PCNTs were fabricated using a selective laser melting (SLM) technique, which allows for precise control of the porosity and surface area of the material. The PCNTs were printed to have half of the cube volume occupied by solid material while retaining edges that minimize disruption to the fluid flow. Given the decrease in flow resistance (dropping from ~0.1 kPa for parallel plate flow to ~0.02 kPa through PCNTs), building on prior work by the authors, the fluidic test setup was reconfigured to reduce thermal time constant of the heat input to the test section, and to greatly reduce ambient heat losses by improving insulation and moving to a two-reservoir system.The proposed SLM-printed PCNT structures offer a promising solution for high power, high-capacity thermal buffering of high-power systems, with high potential to reduce size, weight, and power draw in fast switching and high power electronics applications.

articleTitle: Automated Gimbaling of Conical Nozzles for Jet Vectoring Impingement Cooling to Mitigate Workload Dependent Hotspots in High Power Density Silicon
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Direct jet impingement on the surface of the bare die silicon delivers lot more ability to remove heat instantly because of the higher heat transfer coefficients that impinging jets can deliver. High power density silicon dissipates higher heat loads especially in non-uniform power distribution on the silicon in different regions within the die. On a non-uniformly powered die, power tends to be distributed and concentrated on certain areas only thereby driving higher junction temperature (T<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">j</inf>) rise resulting in localized hotspots on the die. Differing workloads produce different distinct hotspots in different regions of the silicon. We introduce a novel approach for improving heat dissipation on high-power density silicon dies even with non-uniform power distribution. The proposed technique involves automatic gimballing of conical nozzles to "jet-vector impinge" on hotspots targeting localized areas of the die experiencing higher power dissipation. Controlled by a micro-controller and a closed-loop algorithm using dynamic temperature feedback, this method continuously mitigates hotspots on the silicon, reducing overall junction tempera ture. The gimballing or jet-vectoring is done based on sensor feedback, ensuring multiple nozzles target different hot zones within the die and is done dynamically. For client silicon, a total of 30 distinct CFD RANS simulations of turbulently impinging jets issued from a single circular nozzle and accelerated under an orifice plate comprising sixteen tapered micro-scaled nozzles in confined channels at different nozzle to silicon wall separation (8 ≤ z/d ≤ 24) distances at angles of impingement, ∅, from 30° (oblique) to 90° (orthogonal), are examined using Ansys Icepak. 15 cases of orthogonal impingement and 15 cases of jet vector impingement on hotspots were simulated. For multi-chip modules, a total of nine RANS cases were investigated, three CFD cases before jet vectoring and six cases after jet vectoring were investigated at angles of impingement, ∅, from 55° to 90°. Application of jet vectoring technique demonstrates a notable reduction of junction temperature by 10℃ for a monolith client silicon and 20℃ for multi-chip modules with higher power density, at identical boundary conditions before jet vectoring, presenting promising results for enhanced heat transfer and more uniform temperature gradien ts across the silicon surface. Results from Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) computational fluid dynamics simulations are provided and discussed for both pre and post jet-vectoring impingement scenarios.

articleTitle: Optimization of Dynamic Wetting and Heat Transfer in High-Power Electronics Cooling: Influence of Impact Parameters, Wettability Distribution and Power input
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: In the pursuit of high-power electronics, effective solutions for thermal management play a crucial role in the performance and lifespan of devices. Droplet train cooling (directing a series of droplets sequentially onto a heated surface) is one way to remove the heat from powerful electronic devices. This cooling technique harnesses the principles of phase-change heat transfer, and has the capacity to handle high heat fluxes. Here, we investigate how the effectiveness of droplet train cooling of heated surfaces can be augmented by using wettability-patterned surfaces. The target surface has superhydrophilic (SHPL) islands laid as a regular array in a superhydrophobic background (SHPB). This configuration serves a dual purpose, preventing flooding (a problem associated with drop train impact on superhydrophilic surfaces) while ensuring efficient evaporative cooling. In the present work, we investigate the effect of droplet train parameters, such as the flow rate and Weber number on the cooling efficiency, which naturally increases with rising flow rate of the cooling fluid (water). We also study the effect of wettability on the cooling efficiency by varying the SHPL island diameter and pitch. The cooling efficiency increases with SHPL island diameter due to more solid-liquid contact area and with increasing pitch due to quicker drainage of the pooled water from the surface. Furthermore, we optimize the design of the wettability-patterned surface and achieve a high cooling efficiency. The current work advances our knowledge of liquid impingement cooling for wettability-modified surfaces with the potential to improve the cooling performance of power electronic devices.

articleTitle: Detection of Cooling Operational Statuses in Data Center Energy Management using Clustering Algorithms
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: In our digitalized world, Data Centers (DCs) serve as crucial infrastructure. Within the DC sector, data processing operations, including processes such as process cooling, hold special significance when investigated from an energy efficiency perspective, as they account for a substantial portion of total energy end-use. Therefore, it is important to prioritize data processing operations in energy management. The objective of this research is to explore the application of AI-powered clustering techniques to identify cooling operational statuses. Additionally, this research offers valuable perspectives on using AI for visualizing and identifying cooling patterns that deviate, which can provide valuable insights into DC energy management. The study object consists of a DC room equipped with Liquid Cooling Packages (LCPs). The findings show that the cooling power density on average is 9.1 kW/m<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>. Through analysis of the elbow curve, the optimal number of clusters is identified to be three. One of the identified clusters, i.e., Cluster 3, is characterized by large time periods with no supplied cooling from the LCPs. When comparing Clusters 1 and 2, Cluster 1 has a higher temperature difference between the chilled water supply and return, but a lower LCP return temperature compared to Cluster 2. Moreover, the quantified cooling characteristics contribute to the understanding of the LCPs’ operational statuses and cooling performance, which is useful for implementing targeted improvements, e.g., adjusting PID parameters, in the cooling infrastructure.

articleTitle: Sustainability and Life Cycling Investigation of Buck Charging Circuits Printed using Gravure Offset Printing
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Conductive inks for additive fabrication of flexible circuits typically comprise metal nanoparticles and several solvents for carrier fluid, surfactants, catalysts, and curing agents. Increased emphasis on sustainability has resulted in the emergence of water-based inks to replace volatile organic solvents. Flexible electronics have the potential for closer integration of form and function while lowering product weight and bulk. In this paper, the use of sustainable inks for the fabrication of additive battery charging circuits has been studied. The objective of this paper is to examine the use of water-based inks with surface mount components for an application with sustained current exposure of a battery charging circuit. The Gravure offset printing technique has been used to print switch mode buck battery charging circuits using water-based silver conductible ink. Component attachment for the circuits has been performed using electrically conductive adhesive (ECA) and low-temperature solder (LTS). The charging circuits have been subjected to accelerated life cycling to study the effect of usage on trace resistance evolution. The output charging current of the circuit has been monitored to track its evolution correlated with line resistance. The printed circuits were subjected to a repairability study wherein the attached components were manually removed; the component pads then underwent site redressal using conductible ink and the respective component attachment material (ECA/ LTS), which were dispensed manually. This was followed by the attachment of new components and subsequent curing. The performance of the repaired charging circuits was also tested and compared with that of the pristine circuits. Finally, the switch mode buck charging circuits were also printed using non-sustainable silver ink, i.e., inks not using water as the primary solvent, to compare their pre- and post-repair performance with the circuits printed using sustainable water-based ink. Elemental analysis of printed circuit interconnects has been performed to corroborate the differences in performance seen within sample types.

articleTitle: Atmospheric Water Vapor Condensation on Ultra-short Pulsed Laser Surface-Processed Copper
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Condensation, a ubiquitous phenomenon with applications ranging from power generation to climate control in buildings, features a complex interplay of surface properties, heat transfer and fluid dynamics. In recent years, Ultra-short Pulsed Laser Surface Processing (ULSP) has emerged as a powerful tool to engineer surface structures with unparalleled precision and control over scales of practical relevance. This study explores how ULSP-structured surfaces are poised to alter condensation studies and applications. One of the primary advantages of ULSP-structured surfaces is their ability to tailor surface topography scalably both at the micro and nano scales. These engineered structures serve as nucleation sites for condensation, influencing the mode of condensation. Herein, high-aspect-ratio (tall) microstructures of (100µm) are fabricated via ULSP on copper plates. The Oplates are characterized for their roughness and wettability when they reveal superhydrophilic properties. The resulting substrates are then characterized for condensation, wherein uniform film-wise condensation is observed throughout the experiment duration. Furthermore, the condensation heat transfer coefficient (CHTC) is compared against a mirror-finish Teflon-coated Cu substrate via gravimetric estimations. Interestingly, the ULSP plates are found to have similar condensation performance to mirror-finish hydrophobic samples, or outperform them at almost all experimental scenarios.

articleTitle: Comparison of Cooling Methods for Underground Electric Vehicle Chargers
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: This paper compares the indirect cooling method using a heatpipe and air-cooled circular fins with conventional cooling methods like forced air convection and forced water convection for cooling power electronics placed underground. A two-module dual active bridge power converter with reconfigurable outputs for electric vehicle charging is used for the thermal analysis. The comparison is based on specific constraints imposed by semiconductor switch surface area requirements and the maximum junction temperature limit. A detailed analysis is presented, and performance parameters like convective resistance, pressure drop, and mechanical pumping power of the cooling systems as the function of volume flow of working fluid are obtained. Commercially available cooling components like extruded fin heatsinks, cold plate, and heat exchanger are used for conventional cooling methods analysis. Whereas indirect cooling using heatpipes and air-cooled circular fins is designed by performing individual analysis on a heatpipe sizing, air-cooled circular fin design, and heatpipe integrated base plate. This work also highlights the equivalent thermal resistance model for each cooling system.

articleTitle: Characterization of Enhanced Two-Phase Jet Impingement on Femtosecond Laser Surface Processed (FLSP) Aluminum Surfaces
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Two-phase jet impingement is a thermal management technique that offers high heat transfer coefficients necessary for dissipating the high heat fluxes in electronics cooling applications. The use of dielectric fluids during jet impingement allows direct cooling of electronic devices but limits the boiling performance due to unfavorable thermophysical properties. Surface enhancements are therefore of interest to increase the boiling heat transfer performance and enable the use of two-phase jet impingement in high-heat-flux electronics cooling applications. Boiling heat transfer experiments are performed using a jet impingement test chamber and a supporting two-phase flow loop. A single 3 mm-diameter jet orifice is spaced 7.5 mm from a 25.4 mm-diameter circular aluminum heater surface. Femtosecond laser surface processing (FLSP) is used to modify the surface structure of the aluminum heater, which creates micro- and nano-scale features. The boiling performance of the FLSP-modified surface is compared to that of a polished baseline surface during impingement with a 1 m/s subcooled jet as well as under pool boiling conditions using the dielectric fluid HFE-7100. Each surface was characterized by incrementing the heat input up to the maximum nucleate boiling heat flux before a transition to film boiling occurred. The surface superheat at the maximum heat flux reduced by 55% and 53% for jet impingement and pool boiling, respectively. High-speed imaging of the boiling process suggests that the mechanism by which FLSP functionalization reduces the surface superheat is activation of additional nucleation sites.

articleTitle: Single-Phase and Two-Phase Liquid Immersion Cooling of Data Center Power Supply Units for Heat Capture
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Data center power supply units (PSU) have high power density due to the increasing power demand and their low profiles. Air cooling proves to be increasingly difficult in mitigating the hot spots, and it also consumes extra energy in fluid delivery, air conditioning, and rejection to the ambience. In this work, we redesign and modify the PSU cooling infrastructure and adopt quiescent immersion cooling. This design removes all active air-cooling elements and enables heat capture. The PSU used in the experiments is a 2 kW 80 Plus Platinum commercial unit (Bel PET2000-12-074RA). The cooling performance was characterized by tracking the steady-state case temperatures of the switching semiconductors. Flutec PP1 was used to study the cooling performance variations with respect to PSU load and capture temperature. Conventional fan-cooled PSU with heat sinks served as the benchmark. Experiments show that two-phase immersion cooling grants an overall enhancement of 4.4× over the original air-cooling approach at 40 °C heat capture. The results suggest that heat rejection from the dielectric fluid to the riding heatsink is the main bottleneck, and further reduction of the thermal resistance would allow heat capture at a temperature closer to the liquid boiling point. The PSU thermal management approach studied here can help lower data center power usage effectiveness (PUE) while increasing PSU power delivery density.

articleTitle: Aging Effect on Drop-Shock Reliability of SnAgCu305 Solder Alloy
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: The reliability of solder joints plays a crucial role in various electronic applications, as it directly impacts the overall performance, durability, and safety of electronic devices. With the global transition towards lead-free alloys, understanding the aging effects on the drop-shock reliability of these alloys has become a primary consideration. Solder joints are pivotal components in electronic assemblies, frequently containing intermetallic compound (IMC) particles such as silver-tin (Ag<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>Sn) and copper-tin (Cu<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">6</inf>Sn<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">5</inf>). During the aging process, these particles tend to course, leading to changes in the structural characteristics of solder joints. This study conducted a comprehensive drop-shock reliability test on SnAgCu305 alloy, focusing on three different aging durations: 0, 2, and 10 days, all performed at a homologous aging temperature of 125 ℃. The test involved using a chip array ball grid array (CABGA208) component with specific characteristics, including a 0.8 mm pitch and a 15 mm body, which was carefully assembled to a test vehicle with Immersion Tin surface finish and Immersion Gold surface finish. The tests were performed with a peak acceleration of 1500 G and a pulse width of 0.5 ms. Cross-sectioning and microstructural analysis were carried out to investigate the correlation between the growth of intermetallic compound particles and drop reliability. The study revealed that prolonging the aging time had a direct impact on increasing the size of the IMC particles and the thickness of the IMC layer, resulting in solder joints becoming less reliable. Consequently, there was a significant decrease in the number of cycles required for failure.

articleTitle: Modification of Flow Boiling Regimes and Mechanisms in Near-Critical Flows
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Carbon dioxide near its critical point provides a promising solution for next-generation electronics thermal management. Its low critical temperature (31.1 °C), low global warming potential, and exceptional heat transfer performance present significant potential benefits relative to current methods for high heat flux electronics cooling. Additionally, near the critical point, low liquid-to-vapor property ratios can improve reliability through diminished impact of critical heat flux (CHF) and flow instabilities. However, the limited knowledge of convective heat transfer behavior at reduced pressures near unity currently makes adopting near-critical systems infeasible. The current work aims to broaden the fundamental understanding of near-critical phase change through high-speed (8000 fps) side-view microscopy and simultaneous heat transfer measurements. Subcooled carbon dioxide (∆T<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">sub</inf> = 3 °C) with inlet reduced pressures ranging from 0.85 < P<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">R</inf> < 1.03 was passed through a microchannel (D<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">h</inf> = 500 µm) in a horizontal, single-side heating configuration to study the effect of P<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">R</inf> on heat transfer performance and visualized flow regimes. Heat and mass flux are parametrically varied to investigate pre- and post-CHF performance in the near-critical region. Collected heat transfer data show an initial decrease in heat transfer performance as P<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">R</inf> increases from 0.85 to 0.96 and the enthalpy of vaporization (i<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">fg</inf>) decreases. However, the heat transfer performance stabilizes above (P<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">R</inf> = 0.96), even as i<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">fg</inf> drops dramatically, suggesting an alternate mechanism, distinct from those encountered far from the critical region, that maintains large heat transfer coefficients at these high reduced pressures. Visualized flow patterns reveal that in this region, the flow regimes deviate significantly from those expected in subcooled boiling processes, affecting bubble ebullition and CHF. This new understanding of the transitioning flow regimes at high reduced pressures, along with an analysis of the changes to property variations near the saturation temperature discussed in this study, help elucidate the heat transfer mechanisms and help to develop a fundamental understanding of near-critical phase change.

articleTitle: Analysis of Additively Manufactured Phase Change Heatsinks for Transient Thermal Management
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: The overall performance of sensors and electrical devices onboard hypersonic vehicles, guided weapons, and other small aerial platforms is often limited by the thermal performance of their respective heatsinks. Heat generated by these electronics, which include radio frequency (RF) and infrared (IR) sensors, processor modules, and communication equipment, needs to be absorbed by internal heatsinks. Phase change material (PCM) embedded in additively manufactured (AM) heatsinks can be used to absorb significant amounts of thermal energy, enabling improved performance such as more sensor output power and more onboard computing power for data processing.The traditional cooling paradigm uses sensible temperature rise in solid metal heatsinks or melting paraffin wax PCM in brazed aluminum heatsinks to absorb heat generated by onboard electronics. Paraffin wax has a low thermal conductivity, so metal finstock is typically brazed into the PCM cavity to efficiently spread the heat. Solid metal heatsinks have limited energy absorbing capacity and the brazing process introduces significant constraints on the PCM chamber and finstock geometry.Additive manufacturing enables complex and optimized internal geometries, significantly improving the size, weight, and power density (SWaP) of the heatsink. This study numerically investigates additively manufactured heatsinks with optimized fin geometries for more efficient utilization of internal heatsink volume to increase thermal performance relative to conventional designs. It will be demonstrated that optimized additively manufactured heatsinks made of aluminum or copper and filled with phase change material can improve thermal performance relative to traditional brazed designs by up to 1.8x by mass and up to 3.2x by volume depending on the specific cooling application.

articleTitle: Investigation of Fatigue Performance for Bulk Epoxy Molding Compound (EMC) in Sustained High- Temperature Environment up to 1 Year Aging
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Electronic mold compounds are used to encapsulate and protect the chip in electronic packages against contaminants, corrosion, thermo-mechanical, and dynamic mechanical loads. Electronic packages in the automotive underhood may be subjected to sustained exposure to high temperatures in addition to wide temperature extremes. Fracture of the EMC provides a path for moisture and contaminant ingress into the package, resulting in premature progression toward failure. EMCs are generally composite materials consisting of silica particles in an epoxy matrix in addition to catalysts, surfactants, adhesion promotors, and curing agents. Relatively little is known about the fatigue resistance of the EMCs. Modeling methods are needed to assess damage accrual and the propensity for failure after sustained high-temperature exposure and wide temperature excursions expected in harsh operational environments. In this paper, two EMCs intended for automotive environments are studied under prolonged exposure to 100°C for a duration of up to 360 days. This study outlines a methodology for assessing the impact of fatigue. Facture toughness is computed. The primary focus of this study involves the examination of stress-life relation in its initial state (pristine samples). Additionally, the research delves into the consequences of prolonged exposure to elevated temperatures on various epoxy molding compounds, exploring the aging process. The load drop versus number of cycles is studied. The inelastic work per cycle as the function of aging is explored. S-N curves are reported.

articleTitle: Porous Liquid Metal-Based Phase Change Materials For Sustainable Thermal Buffer
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Gallium (Ga)-based liquid metal (LM), belonging to metallic phase change materials (PCMs), stands out as an appealing candidate for a thermal buffer due to their high thermal conductivity (~40 W/mK in the solid state) and moderate latent heat (~80 J/g). Despite these advantages, LM-based PCMs encounter supercooling, which refers to the phenomenon where a molten material, having been pre-heated, fails to revert to the solid phase even when the temperature drops below the freezing point. If the supercooling is not addressed during the cooling, the thermal regulation performance may be insufficient. This is because only sensible heat is accessible, limiting the ability to effectively dissipate heat during the repetitive cycles. To effectively tackle the supercooling behavior, this study proposes a porous-shaped LM/PDMS composite. The aim is not only to decrease the free energy needed for heterogeneous nucleation between the LM and its substrate but also to establish a propagation path for rapid solidification, leveraging Cu backbone structure. In contrast to droplet-shaped LM/PDMS composites, our strategy has demonstrated a more sustainable thermal buffering effect, manifesting a propagation of crystallization even at near-room temperature. Thanks to both thermal percolation within the interconnected LM and the high wetting characteristics between the LM and the CuGa2 intermetallic layer, the porous-shaped LM/PDMS emerges as a viable candidate for passive thermal management strategies.

articleTitle: Two-Phase Immersion Cooler for Medium-Voltage Silicon Carbide MOSFETs
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Medium-voltage (MV) silicon carbide (SiC) MOSFETs play a pivotal role in various industrial applications, including electrical vehicles, DC fast charging stations, and renewable energy conversion systems, among others. Compared to their silicon counterparts, the MV SiC MOSFETs feature higher efficiency, faster switching speeds, lower heat generation, and higher power density. Despite their advantages, SiC MOSFETs also lead to higher cooling demands. To address this challenge, we have developed a two-phase immersion cooler, in which the base plate is immersed in the liquid pool, and vapor generated from coolant boiling on the base plate is condensed on the top surface of the immersion cooler under external air cooling. To further improve the cooling capacity, the base plates are textured with microchannels. Experimental tests have been performed to characterize the thermal performance of the two-phase immersion cooler with a state-of-the-art 6.5kV SiC device. The immersion cooler with microchannels exhibits decreasing thermal resistance with the power load and is shown to be superior to conventional air-cooled heat sinks when the power loads are beyond 70 W. Leveraging the feature of reduced thermal resistance with the power load, the fan power can be tuned based on the power load to increase the lifetime of the fans.

articleTitle: CFD Surrogates for Data Center Sustainability Using 3D U-Net Convolutional Neural Network
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Data centers often suffer from energy inefficiencies caused by suboptimal heat flow, cooling imbalances, and temperature disparities. Although Thermal Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) can model these challenges, its computational demand often impedes timely, adaptive energy-saving measures. Addressing this, we introduce an efficient machine learning CFD surrogate model, DCCFD, implemented by a 3D Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) trained on the CFD or IOT-generated data. DCCFD has an innovative input channel design that captures the data center’s 3D geometry, power usage, airflow dynamics, and AC unit set points in three dimensions, enabling 3D CNN models like U-Net to accurately predict and generate the heat map. DCCFD is orders of magnitude faster than the CFD model with high accuracy. This enables real-time control for dynamic reallocation of computational load and cooling system adjustments, yielding significant energy savings. Beyond real-time adjustments, our approach facilitates proactive optimization during the DC installation phase, minimizing potential hot spots and maximizing equipment lifespan. So, DCCFD contributes to carbon footprint reduction and sustainability by maximizing cooling efficiency, reducing energy consumption, and increasing performance while extending the life of servers.

articleTitle: Novel Subcooled Boiling Chamber With Submerged Condensation for High Heat Flux Removal for Data Center Application
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Electronic components, especially the CPUs/GPUs used in data centers are concentrated heat-generating sources. Their large Thermal Design Power (TDP), small die area and confined packaging make their thermal management a unique challenge. While conventional single-phase cooling methods fail to dissipate such large amounts of heat efficiently, recently developed two-phase cooling systems also lack the holistic approach of combining efficient boiling and condensation mechanisms. It is hypothesized that subcooled boiling with submerged condensation and reduced saturation pressure will result in high-heat flux dissipation while maintaining low surface temperatures. The novel boiling chamber presented in this work is demonstrated in a compact configuration that fits in a 1U/2U server rack by combining submerged condensation with subcooled pool boiling. The boiling chamber is filled with 13% and 40% fill ratio of water and Novec-7000 and experimentally investigated on a thermal test vehicle. Results show that the boiling chamber dissipates about 400 W of heat with a surface temperature of less than 80 °C using Novec-7000 working fluid. When tested with water, the device dissipated more than 750 W of heat (heat flux ≈ 67 W/cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>) with a surface temperature of less than 90 °C. Though the surface temperature rose to 120°C, further testing shows the device to dissipate more than 1 kW from a 34.5 × 32 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> plain copper chip. High-speed images identify submerged condensation and small diameters of vapor bubbles. Further enhancements can be achieved by implementing enhanced boiling and condensation surfaces. Lastly, a guide to design considerations and future work is provided to unlock the greater performance potential of the novel boiling chamber.

articleTitle: Assessment of Bubble Pump Model for Fluid Directional Motion from Asymmetric Heated Ratchets
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Passive two-phase fluid cooling systems are of interest for cooling electronics in terrestrial and micro gravity environments due to their compactness and elimination of moving parts. In this paper, the use of asymmetry for the bubble ebullition and growth on a heated surface to passively generate lateral motion of fluid within an open-ended channel is discussed. The asymmetry is affected by locating reentrant slot cavities on one face of a mm-scale 30/60-degree ratchet. Two such ratcheted walls with cavities in every third ratchet form the vertical walls of an open-ended channel. The ratcheted walls are heated using a serpentine thick-film metallic heater and the open-ended channel is located within a quiescent pool of a dielectric fluid. Visualization studies show that bubbles and slugs tend to move in a preferential direction within the open channel. This direction corresponds to the 30-degree slope face of the ratchet, in which the reentrant cavity is located. Prior studies have alluded to two potential mechanisms for this preferential lateral motion-(1) bubble pump model developed by Kapsenberg et al. [1], which attributes the lateral motion to the momentum imparted by the growing bubble to the surrounding liquid, and (2) asymmetry in the curvature of the slug that spans several ratchet lengths, resulting in a net surface tension force along the 30-degree slope of the ratchet [2]. In order to assess the importance of the bubble pump model, bubble ebullition and growth from the nucleation sites are captured using high speed videos and are analyzed using custom image processing. The velocity imparted by the growing bubble on the ratchet to the surrounding liquid is calculated using the semi-empirical model of Kapsenberg et al [1]. This predicted velocity is compared against velocities of detached Stokes bubbles in the field of view obtained using bubble tracking velocimetry.

articleTitle: Experimental Study on HFE-7100 Pool Boiling Heat Transfer in Honeycomb Structures Produced by Additive Manufacturing
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Maintaining new electronic devices within the permitted operating temperature ranges requires effective thermal management technologies. For this reason, much research has been conducted on pool boiling cooling systems for electronic chip design, power generation applications, and data center cooling systems. This study aims to increase the critical heat flux (CHF) and heat transfer coefficient (HTC) and eliminate the incipience boiling hysteresis using surface modifications. Honeycomb fin structures with microscale side gaps are manufactured by Selective Laser Melting (SLM). AlSi10Mg powder is used for this study because of its high thermal conductivity and low density. The working fluid is selected as Novec-7100, and pool boiling experiments are conducted in a saturated condition under atmospheric pressure. Surface modifications decrease boiling incipience superheat and eliminate the incipient boiling hysteresis compared to the plain surface. Side square gaps create a new path for vapor-liquid flow, and liquid replenishment becomes easier. However, the HTC of the honeycomb structure without side gaps is higher than that of other structures above 25 W/cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> because mushroom-shaped bubbles cannot encompass the entire honeycomb structure. The surface modifications enhance HTC and delay CHF. The best-performing structure has a maximum HTC of 1.567 W/(cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>K), 2.96 times that of the plane surface at 0.530 W/(cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>K). Also, it has CHF higher than 74.29 W/cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>, which is 3.20 times that of the plane surface at 23.24 W/cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>. The pool boiling enhancement of surface modifications is attributed to the increased surface area, higher active nucleation site density, and capillary-assisted suction. The results offer significant guidance for creating future surface modifications manufactured by additive manufacturing for boiling improvement.

articleTitle: Advancing Sustainability in Printed Electronics: Low-Temperature Interconnects and Water-Based Ink Performance
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Earlier generations of flexible electronic devices were often fabricated using high-temperature processable interconnect materials. These high-temperature processable interconnects provided distinct benefits, such as low resistivity and higher mechanical strength, but also exhibited drawbacks, including higher energy consumption and the need for high-temperature capable substrate materials. In addition, the earlier generation of printed electronics was realized using volatile organic solvent carrier inks. In this paper, processes for the realization of room-temperature processable interconnects along with water-based inks in printed electronics have been examined. This research focuses on the study of electrical performance and reliability within functional electronic circuitry. The performance of low-temperature processable interconnects in conjunction with water-based inks has been compared with high-temperature processable interconnects for both single components and functional circuits. A differentiator circuit has been realized using aerosol jet printing with both high- and low-temperature interconnects for component attachment. The magnitude and phase response of the circuit has been compared with the theoretically expected output. Fabricated circuits have been studied for consistency of performance and reliability under thermal cycling in the range of -40°C to +85°C required of automotive grade3 components.

articleTitle: Experiments and Modeling of Two-phase Cooled IGBT Module for Rail Transit Applications
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Pumped two-phase cooling for enhancing the thermal management of IGBT in rail transportation has been investigated both experimentally and numerically. The experimental study on pumped two-phase cold plate of IGBT designed for HXD1C locomotives in China was conducted at a mass flow rate of 0.14 kg/s and heat loads of 2640 W to 13200 W, with R245fa as the working fluid. Experimental results indicate that the spatial temperature uniformity of the IGBT cold plate remains within 3 ℃. Under the experimental conditions, local heat transfer coefficients and fluid temperatures in single-phase and two-phase flow regimes were derived using Engineering Equation Solver (EES). A three dimensional (3-D) numerical model for predicting temperature maps of the cold plate was established using COMSOL software, with the results from EES software as the convective heat flux boundary. The combination of 3D and 1D simulation tools, namely COMSOL and EES, significantly increased the efficiency of temperature field calculations. Given the heat losses of the IGBT module and the working conditions of two-phase flow, the results could be obtained within 1 minute, presenting a remarkable advantage for thermal monitoring. The simulation results were compared with the experimental data, and the agreement generally falls within an error band of 2 ℃, satisfying engineering requirements.

articleTitle: Performance Assessment of Hybrid Microchannel-Pin Fin Heat Sink for Hotspot Thermal Management Under Flow Boiling Conditions
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Two-phase microchannel heat sinks are widely used for miniature microelectronic cooling due to their significantly high heat transfer coefficients. However, in complex heterogeneous 2.5D and 3D integrated circuit (IC) architectures, conventional plate-fin microchannel heat sinks often fail to provide uniform cooling across the localized high heat-flux hotspots and low heat-flux background zones owing to their limited heat transfer surface area and eventually result in high temperature gradient, high thermal stress, and ultimate failure. To address this challenge, this paper introduces a novel hybrid microchannel-pin fin heat sink layout consisting of parallel plate-fin microchannels over the background zone and clustered pin fins over the hotspot zone. The clustered pin fins locally increase the surface area in the hotspot region, while parallel plate fins over the background zone ensure uniform coolant flow and avoid flow bypassing around the clustered pin fins. Moreover, parallel plate fins upstream of the hotspot effectively suppress flow boiling instability. A coupled three-dimensional (3D) volume-of-fluid (VOF) and phased-change model has been developed to assess the thermal-hydraulic performance of the proposed hybrid microchannel-pin fin heat sink under flow boiling conditions over a wide range of hotspot heat flux using saturated water as coolant. The flow boiling performance of the hybrid microchannel-pin fin heat sink has also been compared with the conventional plate-fin microchannel heat sink. The results obtained from the developed numerical model reveal that the proposed hybrid microchannel-pin fin heat sink layout effectively dissipates both background and hotspot heat fluxes and subsequently, enhances temperature uniformity across the hotspot and background zones with a marginal increment in pressure drop compared to the conventional microchannel heat sink. The numerical model provides deep insights into the bubble dynamics and corresponding transient thermal-hydraulic response, which can be used for the optimization of the hybrid microchannel-pin fin heat sink layout.

articleTitle: Performance Analysis of Screen-Printed Functional Circuits on Biodegradable PET Substrates Using Low-Temperature ECA for SMD Component Attachment
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Non-sustainable substrates, such as PET and PI, are used for the additive fabrication of FHE due to their excellent thermal, dimensional stability, and mechanical strength. However, their environmental impact is high due to minimal degradation even after decades in a landfill. There is a growing global push for sustainable solutions for printed electronics. Recent studies indicate that alternatives like bio-based PET, polylactic acid (PLA), and regenerated cellulose film, all derived from renewable resources, might not only match but, in some instances, surpass the performance of traditional PET. While these materials show promise in certain environments, comprehensive research on their adaptability across various conditions remains inadequate. With the escalating demand for roll-to-roll manufactured electronics in diverse areas, ranging from packaging to healthcare, it becomes crucial to thoroughly evaluate the efficiency, longevity, and versatility of these renewable substrates. This research endeavors to address these concerns, focusing on assessing the performance of bio-based PET substrates in FHE applications.The research objectives include – (a) studying the significance of Flexible Hybrid Electronics in the context of sustainable and environmentally friendly electronics, (b) determining the compatibility and performance of the biodegradable PET substrate during the screen-printing process, especially while printing with water-based inks. (c) to test the performance of printed circuits and calculate the error percentage between the actual and simulated performance.

articleTitle: Performance Stability and Reliability of Gravure Offset Printed Thermoformed IME Circuits Subjected to Sustained High Temperature Storage
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: In-mold electronics (IME) poses an opportunity for the incorporation of electronic circuits into automotive interior structural plastic. Utilizing IMEs has a number of advantages, including minimizing weight and bulk while upholding ergonomic design. There are several substrates that are compatible with the thermoforming process required for the creation of in-mold-electronics such as polyethylene terephthalate glycol (PETG), polycarbonate (PC), high-impact polystyrene (HIPS). Polycarbonate can sustain relatively higher temperatures owing to its higher heat deflection temperature and Vicat softening temperature, making it a good candidate for automotive applications requiring a high operating temperature capability of 125°C. However, ensuring the long-term performance stability and reliability of polycarbonate-based additive in-mold-electronics circuits under the high operating temperature conditions experienced in automotive environments remains a critical challenge, and its investigation is the objective of the current study. In this study, additively printed traces with specifically thermoformable silver conductible ink have been printed using the gravure offset printing technique on a PC substrate and then have been subjected to vacuum thermoforming wherein the substrates are heated above their Vicat softening temperatures and vacuum formed on an aluminum mold. The printed traces have then been subjected to exposure to the higher operating temperature of 85°C for extended time periods of up to 1000 hours. The resistance evolution of the printed traces has been monitored after every 50 hours of high-temperature testing. Furthermore, printed circuits with RLC components attached have also been subjected to the same kind of testing, and the frequency response characterization of the non-resistive components has also been conducted.

articleTitle: Evaluation of Vapor Chambers Incorporating Square-Shaped and Topology Optimized Pedestals
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Air cooling of high power electronic devices is typically limited by heat spreading. Vapor chamber (VC) technology provides an effective means of heat spreading using passive two- phase heat transfer. In this research, the impact of VC base plate geometry is investigated through numerical and experimental studies. Two vapor chambers were fabricated to experimentally assess the impact of a square copper pedestal on thermal resistance and maximum heat flux. The VC without the pedestal had a total thermal resistance of 0.27 K/W for a maximum power of 560 W, and the VC with the pedestal had a total thermal resistance of 0.2 K/W for a maximum power of 695 W within the test conditions. Experimental results were compared with simulation studies to suggest local dryout occurring when a pedestal is not used. A series of parametric and topology optimization studies are then presented to offer alternative structures to improve VC performance. It is shown that a VC incorporating a pedestal lowers the maximum heat flux over a wider area at the evaporator surface, with thicker pedestals performing better, and engaging a greater number of internal compound pillar fluid return pathways, leading to enhanced performance. Optimal sizes and topologies of the pedestal are numerically investigated to clarify trade-offs in performance versus added mass.

articleTitle: Thermal Management of Omnimagnet for Space Debris Mitigation
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Each year, more and more objects are put into Earth orbits. As the Earth orbits become more crowded, the potential for disastrous collisions between orbiting objects increases. The most problematic objects are space debris objects, which often cannot control themselves and can have a natural lifespan of many years. Several methods of actively eliminating space debris have been investigated, but early tests have not yielded promising results. The omnidirectional magnetic field generator, or Omnimagnet, is a novel electromagnetic device that can manipulate space debris without physical contact. Such a technique is safer and more reliable for satellites than alternative methods that require contact. However, the Omnimagnet is expected to be thermally limited because it generates large amounts of Joule heating. Using forced air convection cooling on Earth, the device is prone to rapidly overheating at high electrical loads. The vacuum environment of space creates radically different thermal conditions to those on Earth, and currently, there is no understanding of Omnimagnet thermal performance in space. It is unknown how much current can be supplied to an Omnimagnet in space before overheating occurs. To address this knowledge gap, this study presents a 1D, steady-state thermal resistance model to predict Omnimagnet thermal performance. Contact resistances, conduction resistances, and radiative resistances have been considered. This model is then used to determine the maximum safe driving current, 1.95A, which avoids overheating. Additionally, thermal resistances are compared to determine the limiting heat transfer mechanisms within the device. Radiative resistances dominate the problem, and thus thermal management strategies should focus on improving radiative heat transfer. Two such strategies, increased emissivity and additional radiating area, are investigated using the thermal model. These thermal management strategies increase the maximum safe current by 26% and 107%, respectively. The thermal resistance model demonstrates that Omnimagnets may be valuable tools to reduce the proliferation of space debris orbiting Earth.

articleTitle: Reliability Performance Analysis of Magnetically-Oriented ACA for Flexible and Stretchable Electronics
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Flexible Hybrid Electronics (FHE) employed in automotive applications may face prolonged exposure to high temperatures, impacting product reliability due to wide thermal excursions. Extended operational periods under high ambient temperatures can compromise the mechanical robustness and reliability of both bulk material and interfaces. In this study, a magnetically aligned Anisotropic Conductive Epoxy (ACA) is introduced as the foundation for producing flexible and stretchable electronics through a rapid and reconfigurable surface mount technology (SMT) production technique. While prior studies have explored component interconnection using low-temperature solder, ultra-low-temperature solders, electrically conductive adhesives, and anisotropic conductive adhesives – a comparative performance analysis between magnetic ACA and traditional materials is currently unavailable. Finite element model is constructed based on the printed samples. The size of electronic components, polyimide substrate, silver ink layers, SAC305, and magnetic ACA connection layers are measured using images of an optical microscope. The real dimensions are obtained from the microscope image. The stress-strain relation is obtained by linear elastic and viscoelastic model. Thermal cycling analysis and shear test are modeled. Thermomechanical analysis is conducted. A hysteresis loop for thermal cycling analysis is reported. The inelastic work per cycle of different materials is plotted and discussed. Reliability performance will be discussed based on the results of the FEA model.

articleTitle: Experimental Study of HFE-7000 Flow Boiling Heat Transfer and Pressure Drop in a Mini Channel Heat Sink for High-Power Defense Applications
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Computing technology demands high-performance cooling systems for defense applications due to the high-power consumption. While controlling temperature distribution and flow fluctuations under high heat flux conditions presents a significant challenge, there exist limited experimental analyses addressing the impact of flow boiling heat transfer on temperature distribution and flow patterns within uniformly heated microchannels. The primary objective of this study is to dissipate elevated heat fluxes using two-phase flow boiling of dielectric fluid. The experimental investigation focuses on flow boiling heat transfer performance in a multi-channel Aluminum heat sink with 8 hotspots subjected to uniform heating. The flow boiling of HFE-7000 engineered fluid at the mass flux of 500 kg/m<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>s was investigated in a mini channel with a cross-section of (14 x 3 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>) divided into three regions by two subchannels and machined staggered elliptical pins with 3mm height (No tip clearance) on each hotspot and distribution pins at the channel inlet. The collected data from temperature and pressure sensors and flow rate were used to assess the heat transfer performance during the experiments. Additionally, High-Speed Camera recordings of flow visualization were analyzed to investigate variations in the heat transfer coefficient along the length of the channel. The temperature and flow instabilities were discussed for the input power of 678 W.

articleTitle: Analysis on Long Term Reliability of Single-phase Immersion Solution based on Data Center Deployment
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Data centers (DCs) are mission critical infrastructures composed of thousands of Information Technology Equipment (ITE) including servers, network switches, Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS), cooling system etc. In the past decade, skyrocketing demand from Cloud and artificial intelligence (AI) has led to explosive growth in number of DCs worldwide, which introduces tremendous needs for electricity as well as significant amounts of heat dissipation. Both ITE and cooling systems are huge-power consuming. In order to conserve energy while maintaining electronic devices under reasonable operation temperature, advanced and efficient cooling technology has become crucial and has attracted more attention from DC’s operators in pursue of optimal performance, reliability, sustainability as well as Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE).Among the novel cooling technologies, single-phase immersion cooling (1-PIC) solution has been deeply investigated by Cloud Service Provides (CSPs).
