Some pioneer CSPs have even adopted 1- PIC volume deployment in DC. However, existing research and literatures mostly focused on thermal design optimization. Industry is lack of long-term operation data in terms of thermal performance degradation, periodic analysis on immersion fluid content and impact on electric performance. Most DCs still hesitate to adopt this novel cooling technology for deployment.Volcano Engine, public CSP under ByteDance.COM, has investigated technical feasibility of 1-PIC with fluorochemical fluid for DC’s application for years. Based on the architecture previously published in ITherm 2023, hundreds of servers under immersion environment have been operating as pilot deployment for six months already out of planned twelve-month research. Massive amounts of first-hand operation and reliability data are being collected to support long-term reliability research, including analysis on variation of CPU Digital Temperature Sensor (DTS) temperature, fluid content, material compatibility, impact on Signal Integrity (SI) etc. This paper presents the data collected with analysis from long-term reliability tests covering multiple perspectives. The collected results and analysis should be able to support long-term stability and maturity of 1-PIC solution, which will support the following volume adoption and deployment of this novel technology in DC for achieving better PUE.

articleTitle: Transient Thermal Buffer for Microchannel Flow Boiling Using Gallium Phase Change Material
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Microchannel flow boiling presents an effective thermal management strategy for high heat flux microelectronics due to large surface area to volume ratios, high heat transfer coefficients, high device temperature uniformity, and relatively low flow rates and small fluid inventories compared with liquid cooling. However, devices such as laser diode arrays or power semiconductor devices often operate under highly transient heat loads such as cold startups or pulsed modes and have performance metrics which are sensitive to device temperatures. The low volume of microchannel packages reduces thermal resistance but often at a penalty in thermal capacitance, leading to large temperature fluctuations during transient heating events. Furthermore, flow instabilities present in microchannel flow boiling at steady state may be exacerbated under unsteady heating conditions. Phase change materials (PCMs), such as gallium, which offer high volumetric latent heat and thermal conductivity, may improve the transient thermal response by dampening the heating rate to the fluid when added in parallel to the heat flow path. The current study investigates the transient thermal response of a low thermal resistance silicon microchannel evaporator with 22 µm x 141 µm (hydraulic diameter, D<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">h</inf> = 38 µm) rectangular channels at the onset of boiling in R134a under a range of unsteady heat steps. Large temperature overshoots above the steady state temperature as well as strong vapor backflow into the inlet plenum were observed. The temperature overshoots increased with peak heat flux. Using the open-source finite difference software, ParaPower (DEVCOM Army Research Lab, Adelphi, MD, USA), the performance of gallium and gallium-copper composite PCMs on the device in single-phase operation was simulated using a range of PCM thicknesses and areas. The transient heat rate to the fluid was extracted and then applied to the experimental device for each case. Boiling initiated at lower temperatures with PCMs of higher thermal conductivity or with increased amount of PCM, but the peak temperatures and backflow were not significantly affected by the addition of the simulated PCM.

articleTitle: Server Level Impacts on CPU Cooling Capability in Single-Phase Immersion
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: The continued demand for increased compute performance has been driving components, such as CPUs and GPUs, and servers to higher power and power densities, to the point where air-based cooling technologies are reaching their limits of cooling capability at reasonable operating expenses/costs (OpEx). High performance data center servers are therefore steering towards more cost effective and efficient liquid cooling technologies such as cold plates and immersion. Single-phase immersion provides a low cost, efficient, sustainable, easily adaptable, and holistic cooling technology for the entire server/IT equipment. Immersion can also be neutral to ambient conditions and air contaminants, making it a preferred cooling technology for edge applications.In immersion, the IT equipment can be immersed vertically in a tank filled with a dielectric fluid such as Polyalphaolefin (PAO). As the IT equipment operates, heat generated by the powered components creates a natural convection flow that drives the fluid through the server (i.e. hot liquid rising), thus cooling the components. This cooling may be further enhanced by using optimized immersion heat sinks for high-power components and/or forcing flow through the IT equipment if needed. The heated exiting fluid is then cooled by the facility water via a Coolant Distribution Unit (CDU) and pumped back into the tank and IT equipment. While tanks in the industry today provide a wide range of fluid manifolds and pump capacities, there is very limited understanding of the actual flow rate boundary conditions for a server in a tank. This poses a challenge to design thermal solutions for the high-power components and to estimate the cooling capability for the IT equipment in a tank. Hence, understanding the specific impacts of different IT components, configurations and boundary conditions on the thermal performance is essential to design efficient thermal solutions and to predict system cooling capabilities.In this paper, an Intel spreadcore server (code name: Coyote Pass, M50CYP) is used to investigate the cooling capability of the 2 CPUs in the 1U server. The two CPUs are 3rd Generation Intel® Xeon® Processor Scalable Family (code name: Ice Lake) CPUs and an immersion heat sink optimized for natural convection is installed on each one. The CPU thermal cooling capability is evaluated under various workloads while running Intel Power and Thermal Analysis Tool (PTAT) at maximum Thermal Design Power (TDP) of 205 W.The impact on the CPU cooling capability by powering on other server components is investigated in natural convection. The results show that the CPU thermal resistance values improve when surrounding components (storage drives and memory modules) are powered on.The impact on the CPU cooling capability by forcing a flow rate through the server is also investigated. The flow rate ranging between 0.9 lpm to 10 lpm. The results show that the CPU thermal resistance values deteriorate if the server flow rate is below the flow rate naturally generated by natural convection. The thermal resistance values improve as the flow rate increases, and at a flow rate of 10 lpm through the server a ~30% improvement is determined.

articleTitle: Optimizing the vapor chamber with liquid supply layers for high heat flux applications using an ANN-based multi-objective genetic algorithm
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: We developed ANN-based multi-objective optimization process to predict the performance of the vapor chamber (VC) with liquid supply layer (LSL), designed for high heat flux applications. We used a numerical model to investigate the thermal performance of the VC and its structural components. An artificial neural network (ANN) surrogate model was developed that can predict thermal resistance (R<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">vc</inf>) and critical heat flux (CHF) through given input variables by bypassing the process of comparing capillary pressure (calculated using the Young-Laplace equation) and pressure drop (computed via a numerical analysis model). We were able to obtain optimal design variables that minimize thermal resistance for various CHFs using the ANN-based Multi-Objective Genetic Algorithm (MOGA) method. At a heat flux of 500 W/cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>, the R<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">vc</inf> of the VC with liquid supply layer (VC-LSL) is 1/3 of that of the VC with no liquid supply layer (VC-NL). Additionally, the junction temperature in the VC-LSL is approximately 100 °C lower compared to the VC-NL. Our approach resulted in a VC with significantly reduced thermal resistance and enhanced critical heat flux (CHF), primarily due to a well-delineated role division between the evaporator wick and the LSL. This work shows significant potential for maximizing heat transfer performance by establishing an optimal VC design responsive to a broad range of heat fluxes.

articleTitle: A novel framework to design phase change material composite for cooling of electronic devices
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Phase change materials (PCM) have been extensively used in the transient thermal management of electronic devices. Organic PCMs are commonly used PCMs because of their high latent heat storage (high energy density) and their availability in a wide range of melting temperatures. However, they often suffer from very low intrinsic thermal conductivity (low power density). Here, the energy density and power density are the total energy available and the rate at which this energy is consumed, respectively. The organic PCMs are often used along with high thermal conducting metallic fillers to promote effective thermal conductivity, however, for a fixed total volume of PCM-metal composite, latent energy storage capacity is compromised. On the other hand, there are metallic PCMs that have high intrinsic thermal conductivity and do not necessarily need a metal filler. The time to reach a maximum temperature limit (cut-off temperature) is considered the performance metric to quantify the thermal performance of PCM-based heat sinks. Ideally, a longer time to reach a cutoff temperature is desirable for safe operations. Previously in literature, a cooling capacity figure of merit (FoM) was proposed for a semi-infinite medium of phase change material. However, the FoM is mainly based on the thermal conductivity and latent heat of the material. Though the FoM can provide an estimate on comparison between different materials and composites, the major drawback is that this metric may not be useful when the influence of the design parameters such as thermal boundary conditions (rate of heat supplied), geometry, set point temperature is taken into account to design the PCM composite. In this work, the authors propose a novel framework based on thermal Ragone plot to determine the optimal design of the PCM-based composite for the thermal management of electronics under a given specific combination of the aforementioned design parameters. The authors believe that this is a first-of-a-kind framework in the context of electronics thermal management. Analogous to the electrochemical energy storage, the plot is developed to understand the trade-off between energy density and power density. Maximizing the energy density for any given power density will translate into maximizing the time to reach the cutoff temperature during the real-time operation. To generate a thermal Ragone plot, energy and power density data from a benchmarked numerical model developed to solve the heat conduction and phase change is employed. The proposed framework is driven by the energy and power density data and leads to determining the optimized PCM volume fraction of organic PCMs that maximizes the energy density and therefore, maximizes the time to reach a cutoff temperature for the specified design parameters. The results also demonstrate the comparison of the organic PCMs with metal fillers and high thermal conducting metallic or eutectic alloy-based PCMs in the form of thermal Ragone chart based on volume and mass constraints. The results from this study pave the way for developing design guidelines for future PCM-based composites for the next generation of electronic systems.

articleTitle: Design and Testing of an Efficient and Rapid Electro-Thermal Pulsed Interfacial De-Icing Framework for Electrified Aircraft
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Ice and frost accretion on the wings of aircraft can destabilize the air flowpath and cause a drastic increase in stall speed and reduction of lift, putting pilots and passengers at critical risk. While conventional jet-engine aircraft can redirect bleed air from the compressor stage to the leading edges to prevent ice accretion in-flight, electrified aircraft must rely on other means of ice prevention and removal while flying through critical icing regions. The current work outlines the development of an ultra-efficient electrothermal pulsed interfacial de-icing framework which can utilize existing battery power on electrified aircraft for resistive Joule heating for ice and frost removal and mitigation. By supplying a high power pulse to a thin film heater on the leading edges of the wings, the temperature of the interface between the wing and the accreted ice layer can be raised drastically in a short amount of time. This reduces heat diffusion losses of the generated electro-thermal energy through the ice layer and substrate, concentrating the thermal gradient to the interface and allowing rapid de-icing by free-stream shear forces causing shedding of the ice chip. The current design proposes a thin film (400 nm) Indium Tin Oxide (ITO) heating layer on an electrically insulated anodized aluminum substrate. A material survey and selection process considering the ideal voltage and current requirements based on the chosen electrified aircraft’s battery voltage and current output limitations guided material selection. Wind tunnel tests under low and high speed freestream velocities of 50 km/h and 100 km/h and sample attack angles of 0 and 45 degrees relative to freestream demonstrate de-icing capabilities for 1-second pulses with power densities < 25 W/cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>. Laboratory de-icing tests suggest further reduction in required power densities is likely with the addition of a superhydrophobic layer atop the heating interface. Infrared imaging of patterned heating elements (e.g., parallel bar, serpentine) during pulse testing indicate that localized heating of heater subsections is possible through constricting current pathways in select locations. Increasing local current density may be helpful for introducing localized thermal stresses near the edges of the heater resulting in ice chip cracking and easier removal, as well as potentially reducing power draw requirements from the battery as a result of reduced pulsed surface area at the interface.

articleTitle: CFD Study of Electrochemical Additive Manufacturing Based Cold Plate Designs for Enhanced Electronics Cooling
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: The continuous advancements in electronics computational capabilities have resulted in ever-increasing thermal loads at the component and data center server level. These strides within the field are soon to be compounded by the rise of artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies. Traditionally, high performance electronics components have been able to be cooled by forced-air cooling; however, the computational performance increases have begun pushing the boundaries of air cooling, necessitating the use of alternative, more effective, cooling methods. Of those methods, direct-to-chip liquid cooling using cold plates has proven to be amongst the most effective. This study details a comprehensive computational fluid dynamics (CFD) analysis on cold plates which are producible only by additive manufacturing methods. The resolution and scale of the cold plate designs are made possible by electrochemical additive manufacturing (ECAM). ECAM is an emerging 3D printing technique which, by its nature, enables the fabrication of exceedingly complex geometries with high resolutions on the micro and nano scale. The ability to produce highly complex and customizable geometries unlocks new thermal management advantages when compared to traditional manufacturing processes. The purpose of this study is to provide a comparison of six ECAM cold plate designs against traditional cold plate counterparts which are producible by conventional manufacturing methods, evaluating thermal performance and pressure drop of the fluid flow using CFD analysis. The cold plate designs were assessed under varying parameters including inlet flow rate, porosities of the cold plates, and wall thickness under a constant heat load indicative of a typical data center server CPU. The results from this study indicate that the ECAM cold plates provide notable improvements in thermal performance when compared to their traditional counterparts. This study bolsters ECAM as a technique to produce cold plates which lead to improved thermal management of electronics, further enabling high power computing and data centers to continue their increase in computational performance.

articleTitle: Screen-Printed Thermoformed Circuits Performance and Reliability under Sustained High Temperatures for In-Mold Electronics
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: In-mold electronics holds the promise of lightweighting on the automotive platform for a reduced carbon footprint. The integration of the human-machine interface can be achieved on automotive surfaces with additive print processes. Screen printing holds the promise of being able to print on large surfaces while providing a high process throughput. The research objectives pursued in this paper include the evaluation of the electrical and mechanical performance of additively screen-printed thermoformed circuits when subjected to sustained high temperatures, the characterization of the long-term reliability and stability of circuits under high thermal stress, and the analysis of the failure modes and mechanisms. Circuits have been printed on polycarbonate and polyimide and performance compared with and without thermoforming. Printed line cross-sections have been measured using laser profilometry. The circuit resistivity and shear load to failure have been quantified for various sintering times and temperatures. Circuit assemblies have been fabricated using surface mount assembly of components on the substrate. Once fabricated, the assemblies have been subjected to sustained temperatures of 85°C for various periods to assess the circuit consistency, repeatability, and deviation from the theoretically expected performance.

articleTitle: Physics-Informed Neural Network on Thin Film Evaporation
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Miniaturization, coupled with consistent performance enhancements in transistors, chips, smartphones, automotive electronics, and server farms, has resulted in heightened power density, thereby escalating the demand for advanced cooling methodologies. Diverse techniques, such as microchannels, sprays, and jet impingement, have been investigated to address thermal challenges. Thin film evaporation, which has been recognized for its potential in applications involving high heat flux, is of particular significance. Over the past twenty years, widespread experimental research has been carried out on the evaporation of thin films within hierarchical structures. Nevertheless, the impracticality of exploring the multitude of potential geometrical configurations through empirical methods, given the associated fabrication costs, necessitates alternative approaches.This research introduces a Physics-informed Neural Network (PINN) platform designed to address the challenge of discovering effective hierarchical structures for thermal management in high-performance photonics and electronics. The PINN platform is versatile and applicable universally, trained on a comprehensive experimental dataset that encompasses various hierarchical structures in thin film evaporation. By incorporating five geometrical dimensions and three dimensionless numbers governing heat transfer and fluid dynamics, the PINN model demonstrates an exceptional ability to accurately predict heat flux curves when provided with geometrical dimensions and the working fluid type. The robustness of the predictive PINN platform is validated independently by two distinct studies, establishing its foundational role as a systematic exploration tool for diverse structures in high heat flux applications, such as electronics, hypersonic aviation, and electric vehicles.

articleTitle: Research of Operation Reliability on Cold Plate Liquid Solution based on Data Center Deployment
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: The 4<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">th</sup> industrial revolution has driven the boom of data centers (DCs) around the world. DCs are becoming the fundamental facility of digital economy and playing a significant role in data collection, processing, and storage. With the rapid development of digital technology such as cloud computing, big data and 5G as well as machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) represented by ChatGPT, there is constant demand on the growth of computing power in DCs. However, this industrial trend is also introducing concern of energy consumption and thermal management due to increase of rack power density and thermal design power (TDP) of silicon chips such as CPUs and GPUs. In order to achieve green and sustainable DC, improve energy efficiency and decrease total cost of ownership (TCO), liquid cooling solution has attained a lot of interest and attention by industry for DC’s application. Furthermore, with the startup of 'East to West Computing' project and Power Effectiveness Usage (PUE) requirement raised by government, new DCs under construction or planned in PRC are required to meet demand for increasing computing power as well as power efficiency. Liquid cooling solution has becoming ever essential and the only choice in certain circumstances within DCs.As one of mature liquid cooling techniques in ecosystem, cold plate liquid cooling solution has been investigated and applied for years. Volcano Engine, the public cloud service provider (CSP) under bytedance.com, has researched and developed cold plate solution for DC deployment with architecture shared in ITherm 2023. Since late 2022, servers cooled by cold plate have been under volume deployment in Volcano Engine DC. Meanwhile, healthy status and key data have been closely monitored and collected regularly to study the long-term operation reliability including temperature variation of key components, such as CPU and DIMMs etc., material compatibility and fluid content analysis at primary and secondary side. Analysis on ingredients’ reliability is also investigated including soft tube, cold plate, blockage, leakage on quick disconnector (QD) etc. The real operation data and analysis from DCs presented in this paper could be a good reference model and learning pool for ecosystem regarding cold plate liquid cooing solution implementation in future DCs’ deployment.

articleTitle: Physical Based Model of Air-Cooled Thermosyphon
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: This study developed a numerical model applicable to air-cooled thermosyphon. The thermosyphon consisted of flat tubes with multiport microchannels in a parallel configuration. The flat tubes were embedded in a heated block at the evaporator, and only one side of the heating block was attached to the heat source. The air-cooled condenser was covered with louver fins with airflow passing through. The model incorporated various heat transfer mechanisms, including falling film condensation and evaporation, nucleate boiling, conduction, and thermal spreading. The analysis was conducted with frontal velocity across the condenser ranging from 0.5 m/s to 4 m/s, filling ratios of 20% to 60%, the heating power of 110 W to 330 W, and geometric influences of thermosyphon such as heater and fin. The result reveals that the total thermal resistance decreases with the rise of power and air flow rate, which spans from 0.03 to 0.05 K/W. For further elaboration of the prediction, it is found that the thermal resistance decreases with a decreasing filling ratio. The pressure drop increases with a rising air flow rate ranging from 10 Pa to 120 Pa. Besides, the power variation imposes a negligible effect on the airside pressure drop. Finally, the current model gives uniform underprediction on the experimental data, and an optimal filling ratio is presented. The pressure drop prediction reveals a low prediction error of 7%.

articleTitle: Prediction of the Mechanical Responses of Single Grain Lead-Free Solder Joints Using Machine Learning
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: SAC alloys, popular lead-free solders in microelectronics, primarily are comprised of over 95% β-Sn, which exhibits varying elastic properties depending on crystal direction. Its plastic deformation involves dislocation movement along specific crystallographic planes. β-Sn has a body-centered tetragonal (BCT) structure, with 10 slip families and 32 slip systems. Our current research focuses on modeling the mechanical response of SAC solder joints, consisting of a very few β-Sn grains reinforced with Ag<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>Sn and Cu<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">6</inf>Sn<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">5</inf> intermetallic particles. Anisotropic elasticity theory for BCT crystals is used for elastic deformation, while Crystal Plasticity (CP) theory predicts post-yielding behavior by considering crystallographic deformation mechanisms.This paper presents a data-driven ML model to forecast mesoscale deformation in single crystal SAC samples. Trained on numerous solder stress-strain curves from various crystal orientations simulated using DAMASK, the ML model was calibrated using experimental data to describe SAC305 alloy material deformation from a crystallographic perspective. To handle the infinite potential orientations for uniaxial loading, 10,000 CP simulations were conducted. The ML model, trained on these simulations, accurately predicted stress-strain behavior for 100 additional orientations, eliminating the need for costly CP simulations. This approach simplifies the complex aspects of numerical crystal plasticity modeling.

articleTitle: Investigation of Rib Characteristics in Structured Cooling Channels
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Cooling systems have a significant role in the development of advanced technologies ranging from gas turbines to electronics devices. The demand for larger processing speeds and utilization of miniaturized electronics components has resulted in higher heat dissipation rate and larger local temperature values in these components. As such, effective cooling setups should be employed to keep the temperature of the components below the safe temperature. In this work, thermal performance in rib structured channels, subject to a uniform heat flux, is numerically investigated for two different cooling setups. In the first setup called crossflow cooling, the air-coolant moves through the confined rib-structured channel. In the second setup, air jet impingement is utilized. For both setups, several rib characteristics are studied. The effect of rib shape is discussed by investigating ribs with rectangular, semi-cylindrical and triangular cross-section shapes. In addition, the effects of rib height, rib angle (45°, 60°, 90°), number of ribs, and rib spacing are investigated for the ribs with a rectangular cross section shape. The results indicate the advantage of utilizing ribs for heat transfer augmentation, when the ribs are properly selected. Comparing the rib cross section shapes, the semi-cylinder rib shape, in jet impingement setup, results in relatively lower temperature values. The rectangular cross section shape results in considerably lower temperature values in crossflow cooling setup. In respect to the rib height, an increase in the height may enhance the cooling performance in crossflow cooling setup. The results also show that the larger number of ribs, correlating with less rib spacing, can provide more temperature uniformity and lower temperature values. In crossflow setup, a reduction in rib angle from 90° to 45° reduces the average non-dimensional temperature value in the base centerline by 45.3%. This temperature reduction is 3.9% in jet impingement setup, while the required pumping power is decreased by 44% by reducing the angle in this setup.

articleTitle: Maximizing the Thermal Performance of Microheaters for Non-Volatile Phase Change Photonics: A Comparative Study of Pulse Width Parameter Effects
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Guiding, manipulating, and detecting light is integral to modern photonic systems that can be designed for displays, memory, data transfer, and sensors. The prospect of realizing programmable yet zero-static power photonics has recently gained attention thanks to the rise of optical phase change materials (PCMs). PCMs have a unique set of properties that make them desirable for this task: nonvolatile retention and reversible switching between their amorphous and crystalline states, which, in addition, display distinct optical and electronic properties. Nonvolatile photonic devices have primarily relied on either electrical or optical switching of PCMs. Electrical switching offers effortless CMOS integration; however, it is predominantly limited to binary output. In contrast, optical switching enables accurate multilevel control but is limited in scalability. This paper studies an alternative electro-thermal approach to nonvolatile photonics by controlling the PCM phase via doped silicon microheaters. The results highlight the significance of precise spatial and temporal temperature control to ensure optimal modulation of the PCM. Specifically, this paper investigates the impact of the electric pulse width (0.2 μs to 10 μs) on the maximum temperature for two different microheater designs. High resolution (≈410 nm) transient thermoreflectance imaging (TTI) is used to measure and analyze the surface temperature distribution across each microheater under pulsed biasing. To assess the impact of varying pulse widths, this study systematically examines their effects on maximum temperature, response time, and maximum power. Shorter pulse widths (< 0.6 μs) enable higher currents, yet their impact on thermal response time can be limiting as the steady-state temperature is never reached. In contrast, longer pulse widths (> 1 μs) provide greater thermal stability but exhibit reduced maximum temperatures due to limited current levels. The experimental results demonstrate a nonlinear relationship between the peak temperature and the power supplied at sub-steady state thermalization time scales. For the specific microheater geometry, the optimal pulse width for achieving the highest temperature is found to be ≈ 0.4 μs.

articleTitle: Enhancing Predictive Capabilities of Pulsating Heat Pipes (PHPs) Through Validation with Diverse Configurations
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Pulsating Heat Pipes (PHPs) are passive thermal transport devices characterized by a serpentine microchannel loop that traverses back and forth from its evaporator and condenser zones. Within this microchannel, liquid slugs and thin liquid films trapped between the wall and elongated bubbles undergo evaporation in the heated evaporator, with the resulting volumetric expansion pushing the adjacent liquid to flow and leading to perpetual oscillations within the device.Despite their now growing significance in thermal management applications, existing PHP models have demonstrated limited predictive capabilities. Furthermore, the empirical values assigned to evaporation and condensation heat transfer coefficients often lack a solid physical basis. For accurate and more widespread implementation of PHPs into industrial cooling applications, such an accurate and broadly validated design code is the key.The one-dimensional transient numerical code developed by JJ Cooling Innovation for PHPs has recently seen its thermal model updated and rigorously validated, exhibiting high accuracy across a range of heat loads (up to 250 W). The predictions of the model align with experimental data, achieving an impressive 97% accuracy within a ±30% error margin (typically a good measure in prediction of two-phase heat transfer).The validation process was conducted using a copper tube PHP featuring a 19-turn configuration with an internal diameter of 2.0 mm and a tube pitch of 12 mm. A microchannel water-cooling plate, maintained at an inlet temperature of 20°C, was employed on the condenser side. Tests were carried out in vertical and horizontal orientations, using R1233zd(E) as the working fluid.Building on this successful validation, the scope of our project expands to include flat micro-channel PHPs with various lengths, orientations, filling ratios and two distinct cooling methods—air and water cooling of the condenser zone. This further validates the current numerical model under diverse operating conditions, extending its applicability and enhancing the understanding of PHP behavior.By systematically evaluating PHP performance across a broader spectrum of configurations, this research contributes to advancing the predictive capabilities of PHP models and their potential for efficient thermal management in various applications.

articleTitle: Closed-loop Analysis of Thermal Energy Storage Device Arrangement in a Thermal Management System
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: There is widespread and growing interest in the design, analysis, and control of latent thermal energy storage (TES) devices that can enhance the performance of thermal management systems (TMSs) for high-powered electronics cooling applications. However, in many complex systems, including air vehicles, footprint and volumetric constraints may create limitations on the configuration or arrangement of multiple TES devices integrated within a TMS. This begs the question, "How does the arrangement of multiple TES devices, along with potentially different phase change materials in different devices, affect closed-loop system performance?" This type of analysis is not trivial, in part because it relies on design and synthesis of a reasonable, or better yet, optimal control strategy to govern closed-loop performance. Often, the models and tools used to optimize and analyze the design of TES devices are not compatible with control algorithm design and synthesis, and vice versa. As an important step towards answering the question posed above, the primary contributions of this work are (1) a graph-based hybrid TMS model that can simulate arbitrary specifications of TES device configurations and allows for specification of different PCM properties within individual devices and (2) a quantification of the effects of select TES device arrangements and PCM properties on the closed-loop performance of the TMS. While not exhaustive, this analysis is novel in relating TES device configuration and PCM composition to transient performance evaluation via scalable modeling and control synthesis tools.

articleTitle: The Impact of Liquid Supply Delivery Methods on the Thermal Performance of a Capillary-based Two-phase Micro-cooler for the Power Electronics
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Conventional cooling solutions such as air-cooled pin-fin, liquid-cooled cold-plate, or even single-phase microchannel coolers are reaching their limit to meet both increased heat flux and power densities in power electronics applications. The two-phase conventional microchannel cooling could potentially address these challenges but suffers from large superheat, flow maldistribution and instabilities, and large pressure drop.To overcome these challenges, we have developed a high-performance microcooler that utilizes the potential of two-phase cooling by capillary-driven flow in microchannels with porous wicks to achieve low superheat (4-6 °C) and specific thermal resistance ~0.015 to 0.02 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>-°C /W at two-phase heat flux ~ 300 W/cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> and a low liquid flow rate 1.5 g/min corresponding to vapor quality of x = 1. However, the thermal performance of the capillary-based microcooler is sensitive to the liquid supply flow rate and packaging solution for x < 1.Here, we examine the impacts of liquid feed packaging configurations and flow rates on the two-phase cooling performance. The flooding at the microchannels caused by excess liquid supply leads to increased superheat and thermal resistance that can be partially prevented using porous tissue that serves as a buffer. We concluded that the optimal operation condition for the microchannel cooler is at vapor quality x ~ 1.0. The higher heat fluxes can be achieved by increasing the supply of liquid at the expense of increased thermal resistance. We have demonstrated the potential to improve the operation efficiency of the capillary-based microcooler to support the growing power density of the next-generation power electronics.

articleTitle: Thin Form Factor Tunable Cold Plates and Locking Tensioner Cooling Assemblies for Next Generation Memory Modules
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Designing thermal solutions for memory is becoming challenging than before. DDRs are getting into the multi-gigabit range and is adopting power hungry technologies like equalization and multi-level modulation that produce distinct hotspots because of higher power density. In conventional Dual Inline Memory Module (DIMM) cooling solutions, heat flux generated on the active layers propagates through multiple layers and interfaces before the benefit of forced convection cooling can remove the heat fluxes thereby generating large thermal resistances. Also, the ever-increasing TDP on these DDR5 DIMMs and the tighter 300 mils pitch between DIMMs makes cooling these devices with adequate thermal margin for higher reliability a challenging proposition. In conventional DIMM passive cooling solutions, DIMMs are increasingly challenging to cool with higher power density and the ineffective capacity of passive system air-cooling solutions to cool them adequately demands active cooling solutions for the tight pitch configurations of the DIMMs.An innovative active DIMM cooling solution such as a tunable cold plate for liquid cooling and a springclip locking tensioner for air cooling is proposed. The springclip retention and locking tensioner heat sink holds the DIMMs captive. The springclip is held captive by a locking tensioner heat sink. The locking tensioner heat sink can be slid out and removed. Once the heat sink is cleared free from the springclips, the clips can be used as a lever to pull the DIMMs out of the DIMM socket. The springclip acts as a retention and no separate retention mechanism is needed. Each springclip is compact in nature and promotes serviceability of DIMMs with ease. The springclips can be made from copper or aluminum and are designed such that the lower part of the springclip is a thin cold plate that exchanges heat from the DIMMs since they are in direct contact with the DIMMs. Thus, the springclips also participate in heat transfer and making them metallic will benefit to spread the heat from the bottom DIMMs to the top heatsinks where the springclips act as an intermediary for heat transfer in conjunction to their primary purpose of retention. In the TDP scenario (24W per DIMM), using embedded Peltier devices showed 25% improvement in DRAM junction temperature. And for the future (DDR6) DIMM TDP scenario (40W), embedded Peltier devices shows a remarkable 41% improvement in DRAM junction temperatures. It is further shown that for higher TDP scenarios, direct cooling with cold plate yields higher than desirable temperature on the DRAMs dictating the need for novel thermal solutions such as the innovation proposed here.

articleTitle: Micro-PIV measurements near supercritical CO2 conditions inside the channel
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: An advanced optical technique, micro-particle image velocimetry (μPIV), is applied to measure the velocity flow field of liquid CO2, methanol, and tracer particles through a T-channel. The captured flow field of the CO2 is processed using a two-direction, two-component (2D2C) cross-correlation method for obtaining the velocity vectors. Non-fluorescent silver-coated hollow glass microspheres with a diameter of 5 to 30 microns are used as the tracers and mixed with the CO2 flow. CO2 has a plethora of applications ranging from the micro to the macro scale, and therefore, better knowledge of the fluid flow and heat transfer processes, such as the flow field, is necessary. The critical obstacle until now is finding the appropriate seeding for liquid CO2. The present experimental study addresses this shortcoming by measuring the velocity distribution of liquid CO2 and methanol mixture inside the T-channel at near-critical thermodynamic conditions.

articleTitle: Graphene-Enhanced Metal Condensers in Wick-Free Vapor Chambers for Thermal Management in Electronics
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Wick-free Vapor Chambers (WF-VCs) have garnered significant attention as an efficient and low-maintenance thermal management solution in various high-power electronic applications. Such chambers can still be further optimized to improve their thermal performance. This study explores the enhancement of wick-free vapor chambers by introducing a dual-layer add-on coating comprising of graphene and Teflon on the metal condenser surface. Graphene, a two-dimensional carbon allotrope renowned for its exceptional in-plane thermal conductivity, and Teflon, recognized for its surface-energy reduction properties, combine to improve the cooling efficiency and overall effectiveness of these chambers. The experimental findings reveal that the combined graphene and Teflon-coated condenser significantly enhances the condensation rate, while dramatically reducing in-plane thermal resistance. Consequently, this opens up opportunities for improvements in the overall cooling efficiency, particularly in high-power and high heat-flux applications, where efficient heat dispersion is paramount. In conclusion, the integration of a dual-layer graphene and Teflon coating on the condenser of wick-free vapor chambers introduces an effective approach to thermal management in high-power electronic systems. The harmonious interplay between graphene's exceptional thermal conductivity and Teflon's surface energy properties has the potential to enhance cooling efficiency. This research not only highlights the immense benefits of this combined coating but also paves the way for innovative thermal management solutions across industries where efficient and robust cooling is of the essence.

articleTitle: Ultra Thin Blowers: A study on parameters influencing flow and thermal performance of notebook applications
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Mobile computing has increased significantly in the past two decades and one of the major trends is the thinning of laptops in addition to increasing the performance of chips integrated within it. Thermal management is a critical aspect in laptops without which ultrathin designs will overheat and result in thermal shutdown. The usage of ultrathin centrifugal fan/blowers has been a recent trend in the industry to actively dissipate the heat from the chip to external ambient. From thermodynamic first principles, thermal performance is governed by fan flow rate. The flow rate provided by the fan is turn dictated by the aeroacoustic limit acceptable by notebook user and the flow rate is determined by several fan design parameters. Existing literature in this domain has largely been the study of large and thick industrial blowers in non-electronic applications. In this paper, we study a commercially available notebook blower of size 65x65 mm, with thickness of 4 mm used in an electronic industry laptop. We assess its performance in terms of flow output using an experimental characterization procedure based on known test standards. Following that, we develop a Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) model and validate it with the earlier generated experimental data. Using the validated model, we study some of the variables such as blade thickness, blade count, and blade height on fan flow throughput. Results indicate that the blade height increases performance linearly, whereas blade thickness and blade count provide diminishing returns after a point. Several notebook segments exist in the market with different thermal and flow performance requirement, and it results in huge cycle time to test different blower designs varying several parameters. The discussed experimental and computational methodology in this paper will be useful for thermal designers to numerically calculate required flow performance upfront and optimize the design variables thereby reducing prototype cost and time.

articleTitle: Explicit FE Failure Prediction of Potted Assemblies Under Inclined High G Shock Loads
publicationTitle: 2024 23rd IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm)
abstract: Reliability expectations in mission-critical applications necessitate the understanding of survivability, failure mechanisms, and efficacy of supplemental restraints such as potting materials in mitigating the propensity for failure. Interfacial failure of the potting materials under high g shock loads is a dominant failure mechanism. Interfacial damage thresholds needed for predictive modeling or the effect of sustained high temperatures on the propensity for failure are largely absent in the state of the art. The research objectives of this study include investigating failure modes of potting-printed circuit board interfaces under the high-temperature exposure effect of mode mixity under end-notch and bi-material specimen geometries. The potting/PCB interfaces have been exposed to high temperatures at 100<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">o</sup>C and 150<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">o</sup>C. The fracture toughness parameters have been measured and used to calculate the cohesive zone parameters at the interface. The effect of shock orientation has been examined on the failure propensity under 30-degree and 60-degree shock orientation for pristine and 100°C, 180-days aged assemblies. A predictive model has been developed to assess interface and interconnect failure. The model has been validated with experimental data acquired from high-speed imaging in conjunction with digital image correlation for measurement of out-of-plane deformation and strains.
